with the New Year, never to leave your side until it so pleases God." Then they sat down, and she told him how, three years betore, atter being lett s widow, she deter- mined to find out what had become of the sweet- heart of her younger days. How, by a chapter of happy accidents, she learnt in Kansas City that he was in London, his address and the name he worked under. How, on knowing, this she hurried over land and sea, and just at the birth of the New Year entered his room. She saw the tears fall from his eyes, heard her name mentioned, and his blessing ',o out to her. All doubts were then at an end. A great joy filled her heart, for she knew his ten years of walking alone and in loveless night were ended.

"My children will be here by the n-xt boat, and you must be to them a father. Now F must go, as I'm weary with the excitement of the ly." Carson drove her to her hotel, and to him the New Year bells never seemed to have rung such merry peals. They rang into his life a New Year in every sense. A few days later there was a quiet marriage, and on the following New Year's Eve, as Carson and his wife listened to the hour of mid- night strike, they thought, with hearts full of love and gratitude, of the joyous meeting twelve months beim.
[TUE END.]

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAR NELLIE, Little girls are thinking with keen pleasure just now of their new frocks for coming holiday parties. Choosing them with the aid of mother is a delightful occupation, and the anticipation of the completed glories of the frock are bright enough to carry one through the ordeal with something approaching equanimity. China silk is still the favourite material for very young girls' dresses, and the usual trimming consists of rows of Valen- ciennes and Machlin, about all of which there is nothing absolutely new. But the faint, pale colours, blue,' pink, citron, and a soft pinkish mauve, gave an air of novelty to the dainty frocks, and thereis always a means of differentiation to be found in the sleeves. Those that come to the elbow, ending in a frill of lace, are the favourites, being in imitation of "grown-up "evening frocks. Insertions, too, have very narrow black velvet run through the spaces and this, too, is imitated from the dresses of the elders, always a distinct recom- mendation in Nursaryland. Veiling is in as much fai our as ever.

itiodei suitable for a girl of any age between' eight and fourteen is of white veiling; the skirt has a deep, shaped flounce edged and headed with bands of ecru guipure insertion laid on white satin ribbon. The deep pointed yoke is of guipure over satin, and the sleeves, which are long, are trimmed with bands to match. Ruffles of white chiffon finish the cuffs and neck-band, and the sash of soft white satin ribbon is fastened at the left side of the front with a paste buckle and long ends. This style of frock can be satisfactorily carried out in pale colour with insertions of white lace. Another pretty way of making a smart party dress for a girl between eight and 12 is with an underskirt of white lace, knife-pleated, and an over- skirt of white Japanese silk edged with a ruche of narrow white satin ribbon. A little lace bolero can be worn over the full silk bodice, although boleros are, as a rule, better suited to wearers of maturer age. If a fancy dress is desired what could look nicer than a little one representing Juliet. The skirt might be of Peacock blue with pattern in silver, whilst the head-dress.should be in black. There should be plenty of spangles on +hP !ace or muslin.

Peasant costumes require only woollen and cotten fabrics, with a slight admixture of velvet, and materials suitable for any of these are specially made for stage purposes, and, although effective, are extremely expensive. One of the simplest is the Normandy peasant, with a woollen skirt and velvet bands, velvet bodice, lacing over a muslin chemisette, which shows in fiche folds above, and elbow sleeves also of muslin. Ancither costume might be of the Scotch fishwife variety. The skirt might be of blue over a blue and orange petticoat, whilst the large white bonnet should not be forgotten. The stockings should be of black silk and patent leather boots with plain steel buckles should lac, procured.

Next to tweed, cloth is the fashionable wear, and for weddings velvet gowns are chosen. In one of a soft tone of dove-colour, the skirt has several lines of piping above the band of chinchilla that trims it above and below the shaped, full flounce. The bolero and sleeves are entirely composed of chinchilla, the cuffs, collar and band round the muff being overlaid with gold braid. A little black velvet waistcoat is just visible between the bolero and a tucked white silk vest, the undersleeves are made of white silk to match the vest. The pleated silk muslin tie is bordered with a slender line of black chenille. The belt is made of the same gold-broidered material as that in the cuffs and collar.

• Though silver fox is the fur of the moment, chinchilla is a good deal worn; but sable is seen on every second well-dressed woman. A charming evening dress is made of rose-pink crepe-de-chine in a very soft, yet vivid, shade. The bolero, velvet sleeves, and skirt are trimmed with a design in ruched silk muslin and silver sequins, NI ith true- lovers' knots carried out in deep pink panne. The full vest and long sleeves are made of pink silk muslin, and the folded, shaped waistband is in the deep pink panne. The rich embroidery on the skirt draws dawn the crepe-de-chine in beauti- ful folds.

It seems that this feeling for gold and silver is but, a return to the earliest instincts of dress; the first-known laces were made of gold and silver thread, and, indeed, so expensive did this beeome, and so numerous were the sumptuary laws regu- lating the cost, that the workers were driven to fiax as a substitute, and from that arose thread lace. Equally barbaric in splendour are the beads with which we should now be hung; beads of all sorts and conditions, the quo.inter and more bizarre the better, are strung together to form chains about a yard and a half ia length, a mixture of turquoise blue, amber, carved gold or silver knobs, and scented Indian wood beads, according to the wearer's fancy. Needless to say, care should be taken to avoid a garish lock, and black is the best background for these gaily-coloured bead strings.
Your loving,
JENNIB.

div.head: ( Copyright.)
div.p: ( Copyright.)
A NEW YEAR'S EVE' VISITOR.
BY ALLAN. DENE, author of "The W4side Inn," "Sheila's .1725,• "A Tragic Mistake," &c.

"New Year's Eve, ten years ago !" murmured Walter Carson, as he leant back in the easy-chair, drawn up before his sitting-room fire at his Duke- street chambers in London. , The cloOks had jmit struck ten, and the sonorous boom from Big Ben came floating over the Green Park as a sort of benediction on the rapidly dying year. The roar of the great city without was not lacking in its elenient of melody, and the noise of merry revellers in Piccadilly completed a strange yet fascinating tout ensenthk. Passing down the street came three young men singing that old Southern song, • "I's! gwine back to Dixey:" .The words and the melody startled Carson from the reverie into which he had fallen. Sitting upright in his chair, he said, aloud:

- - " What memories that song recalls! I How my ;loneliness grows upon met What a fool I was eve, to have indulged in the thing called love I But There, I've tasted the poison, and must abide by zne result. What's that result? Pleasing? Why cannot Ibe of the gay throng outside? Here in this mighty crowded city I am as lonely as a man lost in a desert." He rose, and going to the other side of the room opened a cabinet, and took from it a bundle of letters, some dozen. They were faded and 'bore traces of much handling. After reading, he replaced them, 'and, walking to the photograph of a child on the wall, indulged in soliloquy.

"1 know you not, my sweet child, but your mother was always, and always must be everything to me. How hard and /cruel seems the world! Your mother and 1 parted ten long years ago this night, to meet again in two years' time I What happened to prevent us ? I wrote many times, but no reply ever reached me! Three years after we separated, a letter came from her, and in it 1 read: 'Now that I am married, perhaps you will write.' Life seemed a blank, and I came ,to London, a wayfarer, caring not what became of me. I turned to literature, and have been what people call successful. But what. is success without the power to experience that which makes it other than a metallic gratification? Eighteen months went by before I next heard from your mother, and then your photo only reached me, since when all has been silence I Your mother married a good man And I pray for her and for you too, baby, that you may grow up in her footsteps ! " The circumstances under which his letters to the girl went astray were to him mysterious, but, as a matter of fact, easily explained. The girl was the daughter of a country lawyer, and he had made her acquaintance when she was staying in a boarding- house in Bloomsbury, in which he was also a lodger. Her reason for being in town was that she might improve a somewhat neglected education, and she was taking singing lessons at a school of music in the neighbourhood. A prim little figure, dark-eyed, with delicately- moulded features, mid a flush of colour in her cheeks, Nature's own bloom, her qualities of shy- ness to the company in general, and easy confidence towards those she liked had caught his fancy. It was not his intention to court her, but her friendli- ness to him appealed to his strongest instinct— conceit. It was gratifying to fine himself thus favoured, while others around the table were made to feel their distance. His pride bad satisfaction in the occasional appeals for his opinion, and the contentment with which it was received. A few attendances at the theatres with the incidental comradeship of waiting together in queue on the pavement, mid this demurely frank young lady with her silvery voice had made her conquest. All the while, until she went away, he had regarded the proceeding as a were act of yore:l:lee on his part, graciously accepted by an apprt e itt t ive and onspoilt young person. Then an aunt from the States took away this unwanted daughter from among the large family at home, to be a companion across the Atlantic, and, sutpecting her of flightiness, opened her letters in the capacity of guardian. The first of Carson's epistles—he was a cautious man and diti not commit himself to paper until he could not resist doing so—arrived when the aunt believed she was arranging a highly desirable engagement for her niece, and on the principle of doing wrong that good may come, she kept back the notes of this obviously poor suitor. The Transatlantic event prospered, and then one step down leading to another, it. appeared necessary to destroy these com- munications.

Carson often felt desolate, but never so utterly as then, and as he paced the floor the laughter of the happy crowd seemed to mock him. He rang the bell and ordered some tea. The demure little maid looked at him, and, going downstairs, said: • "Poor Mr. Carson, he looks so strange and miserable!"

Returning, she found him sitting in his chair gazing with half-closed eyes into the fire. Placing the tea on a small wicker table by his side, she attracted his attention by the question: "Anything else, sir? " _

_ "No," was the reply ; "but see, this is New Year's Eve. You've beer good servant to me, at least. Buy yourself something," handing her a sovereign. The amount of the gift bereft the girl of the power of speech ; and with a curtsey, eloquent it itself of gratitude, she left. Carson, sipping his tea, again soliloquised. "It'l now within an hour and a quarter of the New Year. What will that year bring into my life? It cannot bring the light of love and companionship. The same round of weeks and months, and so it will be to the end. Ten years ago, in Old Kentucky, we said' Good-bye.' It was a good-bye' for ever.' Apostrophising the absent woman, he continued: "Leila, Leila, to my grave I take with me the love I bear you. Why did we ever love to be parted sc ruthlessly ? What strange fate has so guided out destinies ? "

Carson could not be called a poetic scholar. His acquaintance with the poets was fair; of the modern poets he knew his Longfellow well; he loved that poet and his works. So now, when he was in the very slough of despond, he turned to the story of Evangeline, and read of the sufferings of that heroic character. Tile reading soothed him, and he fell asleep. The clocks were striking the twelfth stroke of midnight when he awoke. He barely opened his eyes then closed them again, and listened to the joyous salutations of people meeting in the streets, He was not selfish, neither was he bad-natured. No man who ever truly loved can be altogether either. As he listened he said:

"I wish for all a bright New Year,-and Leila, my absent Leila, whom I shall never see again, may your life know no sorrow, may yours never be the aching heart, and may you be blessed in your children growing up around you. My Leila—" He did not finish the sentence,but the tears came trickling down his cheeks as he realised his barren life. Then he became conscious that someone had come into the room and been a witness of his weak- ness and his secret—secret because society said. Walter Carson carried his heart on his sleeve and was incapable of deep affection. So sitting up and turning round, he was startled to see seated on a chair a tall lady, clad in deep mourning and veiled so heavily that he was unable to distinguish her face.
"Madam," he inquired, too taken aback even to get up, "1 should like to know why I am thus honoured ? "
"I came in with the New Year. Not an omen oil ill-luck, I hope," replied a musical voice; "bit / first want to know if Walter Carson is not sin assumed name? "

" Why do you ask such a question?" "For the best of good reasons, and as you will not tell me, perhaps you will allow me to say that I think your real name is Herbert Wilton," pro- ceeded the mysterious stranger. Carson was utterly unprepared for this, and surprise was painfully manifest. Appearing not to notice it, the lady went on: "You are unhappy, I know, Mr. Wilton. I shall not call you Mr. Carson. lam certain of it, becanAe I was watching you for ten minutes before you opened your eyes. Can I be of any help to you? " "I. don't understand you, madam," answered kmrson. "I have no trouble, at least none that you could assist me in."

"Has it any connection with an old love affair ? " very slowly asked the veiled visitor. must decline to discuss my private matters with an utter stranger," replied Carson, jumping up. "Am I an utter stranger, Herbert?" responded the stranger, also rising, and as she did so throwing back her veil.
"Leilia 1" gasped Carson, looking incredulously into her face.
"Yes, Leila," was the answer whispered, while hes. iirsas to round Lis neck "come buck to you

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Following the custom at the peonies over schich she one held sway, the es-Empress Euge iie thieles much mere of le jour de l'an than Christmastide. She herself always makes the moat handsome and inteiesting New Year gifts, and never on this occasion fails to receive one from our Queen. A great number of floral offer- ings too reach the ex-Empress,au le jour de l'an. motility from adherents to the Napoleonic dynasty. Like the Christi/she festivities, the celebration of New Year's Day is of Roman origin. The month with which the year epenee was named "January "in honour of Janus, the G.3d who opens and closes the day, and holds in his bands the dread keys that open up anu exclude pros- perity.' The Rev. E J Hardy states in his new bock "Mr. Thomas Atkins "that the Seaforth Highlanders heve way of their own ot welcoming the New Year. At five minutes to midnight, the oldest man in the regiment, arrayed as Father Time, is played out of rho barrack gate t 3 the tune "Auld Lang Syne." After the clock strikes, comes the youngest drummer boy, as the New Year. "Who goes there ? "says the sentry. "The New Year," replies the small boy. "Advance, New Year, all's well," is the sentry's response. Roses at Christmai time are no longer a rarity, and surrounded as we are at the moment, by a wealth of such blooms, we are apt to forget that the Christmas rote proper, is the flower of the black bellebore. It is an old-fashioned plant, but its large thick flowers of exquisite purity, are very beautiful. The flowers are hite, hut the root is black, and hence its name of helleborus niger—the black hellebore. The root was formerly supposed to hava medicinal qualities of high value, especially in the case of mental disease. There are many legends connected with tee Christmas rose. It is said to have frst flowered in the gardens of heaven, where the angels knew it as the "rose of love." When Adam and Eve were driven from Eden, leaving behind them all the blossoms which they bad Loved to tend, out into a waste world, covered with snow, the pitying angels sought and obtained permission to give them one flower—this "rose of love "—as a sign of the Divine love, and thereupon it blossomed amid the snow. The Duchess of Sutherland, shares with her sister the Countess of Warwick, a fondness for the beauties of nature, which leads her to take as much practical interest in her gardens, as Lady Warwick does in agri- culture, and various rural interests. The gardens at rentham are some of the most beautiful in the country, and the Ductless is quite a ceunoitseur in the growing of orchids, lilies, carnations, and rose?. Whether it is 'gardening, or anything else sbe undercakee, the Duchess is thoroughly practical in all her methods. She has done a great deal to benefit various small industries which she has initiated in the Scottish Highlands, and teat is only one of the many good works in which she is interested, for the Duchess of Sutherland is one of the busiest women iu the country. _

Lady Warwick was able to announce the other day, that some generous donor had ceme forward with an offer of £50,000 for the Women's Agricultural Colleee at Reading. Lady Warwick, it will be remembered, recently stated that it was getting beyond her resources and responsibilities, and she appealed for " a saintly millionaire" t 3 generously help in continuing and developing the work. The name of the " saintly millionaire" has not transpired, but Lady Warwick is to be heartily congratulated upon the success which has astended her appeal. There are many worthy institu- Weis which would be only too glad to as easily raise £5OOOO, but which lack the magic influence which the Countess of Warts ick would seem to posses!. Such a magnificent endowment will do wonders in helping for- ward the work at. the Reading Hostol, in fitting wc,noen for a pleesant and healthful occupation. From time to time fforts have been made, but not with any great measure of success, to revive the lace- making industry in some of the rural dirtricts which were once famous for that art. This was the case in Devoterhire, which was the home of the famous HonTton Point d'Augleterre. and in Bedfordshire, Buckingham, and many of the Midland counties, there were many villages inlwhich the lace pillew was a familar object in almost every cottage. But ever since the introuuction of machinery, it has been a languishing industry, and the Education Acs also struck it another deadly blow. To become a skilled lace-maker, it was essential to com- mence at the very earliest age, but this was hardly pos- sible in these days when the children have to go to school. There was much to be said for the old College industries. Unlike those of the factory, they enabled the people to acquire their independence, and alB3 a large measure of oomestic training, but it is to be feared that their day has gong by, though possibly the Midland Lace Association may do something to revive the ancient and (-liquisite art which used to flourish in so many of our country aistriets. The newest dressing gowns are the cosiest and softest of garments, being built for the nalst part of fabrics made especially for the purpose. The favourite colors are pink, duckling yellow, and blce. The mort luxurious specimens are trimmed with broad bands of tucked silk, and lace is utilised by the far Long for these lovely wraps To be quite correct the decoded version should be patronised, but this is really only possible where is fire in one's bedroom is the rule and not the exception. The floral garnitures for the shoulders of evening gowns, are especially lovely, and have flared premie- Kitty among Christmas and New Year's gifts. To the impecunious, they will prove a blessing indeed, for th,l effect they produce on a middle-aged, or elderly frock, is little short of marvellous. On black gowns a trail of white and mauve clematis, with delicate green foliage looks exceptionally well, as also does a garniture of nasturtium!, or wallflowers. The colouring of artificial flowers this year,leaves absolutely nothing to be desired, and ths mixtures of velvet, silk, and chiffon, of which the best are composed, gives such unusual softness and reality o the blootd, that, gazing thereon, Nature hoe- self, might be deceived. What with the dainty, wer-eut mackintosh coat, wateiproof gloves, waterproof boots, and divers rain- proof fabrics, for gowns, it is an e Ley matter to fortify nutselves against even the British climate. And now it is possible to adorn the waterproof hat, with fascinating bows of watts proof ribbm, which will emerge from the most persistent downpour, as though they possessed not an even bowing acquaintance with the smallest of rum- mer ',hew ens. We have no longer the ghost of an excuse for sallying forth dowdy, and unpleasing to lo:k upon, when the elements are unfavourable. It is as possible to look as smart on a wet day, as on a fine one, though the styles be totally dissimilar. The Countess of Fartorough, and the Countess of Powis, arc seeking to revive certain baronies of their fattier, the late Lord Conyers, in their favour. As a rule it is exceedingly difficult to revive titles that have fallen into abeyance, and the case of the late Lord Steurton, who succsestully claimed the Baroni,s of Mowbray and Selgrave,hae been one of the few instances in which such appeals have been allowed by the Cern- mittee of Privileges in the House of Lords during the last sixty years. The present Lord Mowbray and Stour- ton is also claiming the Earldom of Norfolk. It is one of several genealogical disputes which have lately been revived in the peerage, and it is heieg vigorously con- tem,ed by the Duke ot Norfolk. Formerly the Earldom of Norfolk, and the Baronies of Mowbray and Selgrave were all vested in one and the same person, and as the Stourtons have successfully obtained the Baronies,eo the present Lord Mnwbrav hopes to succeed in hie claim to the Earldom of N3rfolk.

div.head: HOW PARIS WOULD FIGHT.
div.p: HOW PARIS WOULD FIGHT.

calual visitor or hurried tourieo to Paris would never eutpect a tithe of the wondrous defensive works widch encircle the Gay City. Yet Paris has fought before, and may have to fight again ; and it is eafe to Bay that her defences have never before been in such a perfect state of organieaticm. Miles of Forts.

The defensive works cansist of seven great forts round the city, eight miles away from its walls, and nineteen smaller forts, four mile.; out, each containing three acres and mounting two 95-ton guns, hurling 100-pound m2linit, -shells.

Twenty-one miles of continuous fortification surround the town—earthwork walls 150 feet thick at the base and fronted ty forty-five feet moats. Three hundred emplscrmmts exist along this giant wall for as many 95 ton cannon, kept free from rust in the Champs de Mars arsenal, and ready to be swung into place at any .time. In addition thitteen barracks,eleven gnat mobil- 'sing depo!s, all rvithia the city. Concealed Preparations.

Sc cleverly are the forts masked by long slopes of green turf, .rid the walls by trees and bushes, that one can pass in and out of Paris a dozen times and see 'scarcelr a trbce of its famous fortifications, The range of the 95-ton guns is over ten miles—some say four- teen.

Beneath their, at present, untenanted beds on the rampart are stone casemates for ammunition, with email transfer waggons. These casemates open upon the iener basc of the wall, and a set of rails, standard gauge, runs from the doorway to the top of the fortifi- cation. You must look for these rails in the grass, the General Staff is so modest.

div.head: If War Came!
div.p: If War Came!

Supp:se war comes and the three hundred guns must he mounted. Well, the staff has thought of that. The rails that lie ready for the ammunition waggons can be linked with the tramway system of Paris. No ordinary tramway wruld bear ninety-five tons, but that also has been thought of. The Paris tramways are laid on solid oak, dinned to iron trestles, bedded in concrete. To work these guns, were every man of the garrisons drafted away, Paris has 50 000 trained artillerymen among her reservists. She could man every gun twice over, garrison all her forts with infantry reservists, and put a dozen cavalry regiments into the field for scouting purposes. Such a performance no other city on earth could rival. The Scheme of Communications.

The Paris railway stations have immenie acreages of platform space, exclusive of arrival and departure plat- forms, which are made long enough to seceive three trains at a Lime. Paris ha. three circular railways—the Inner, the Outer, and the Grand Ceintures—which form a network connecting th. city and its suburbs. At every thousand yards along the inner slope of the fmt,finations is a three-storey guard-house. Some 20,000 troops could thus be sheltered within call of all attackable points. These guard-houses are connected by the broad Boulevard Exterieur, which is, of course, provided with tramways. The Local Reserves.

Every reservist, whether Parisian horn or provincial immigrant, has a book containing his number, parti- culars of his service, and a memorandum of the barrack to which ha must repair upon the calling of the reserves. In case of war, lines carefully maintained would be switched into use, and the tramway system would be in communication with the enormous goods depots of the Paris to mini.

Not rolling sti,ck only, but horseflesh would ba re- quisitioned' Every horse over four years old is regis- tered, togrther with his typo, owner and probable utility. The General Staff could choose from some 120,000 homes. Thpre are in Paris 16,000 ctbg, with three horses to a o.b-48,000 mounts fairly suitable for cavalry. Add 20,000 -.ram and 'bus horses and 50,000 draught horses —the balance may be taken as in private hands.

div.head: Emergency Stores.
div.p: Emergency Stores.

Th- military stores of Paris ar. boundless. In a day 0)p could clothe and aim 450,030 fighting men, with 70,000,000 rounds of melinite eartridzeg. At the army bakeries she revrves large stores of grain.
In case of ciege the General Staff has a censorship of prices ready in the Paris municipality.which at all times fixes the price of bread and would do so of other pro- visisns.

varis has an invisible defence—the submarine boats that patrol the Seine from Aanieesi and Ivry. Presumably a foreign army might get into Paris again, as one did in 1870-71. but the process would be far more difficult. Experience teacivrt.!—" Science Siftings."

div.head: PROJECTED INVASION OF
div.p: THE PROJECTED INVASION OF
ENGLAND.

Artar dinner Napoleon was again questioned on the sutiject of hie projected invasion of England. Sir George Cockburn said that many people in the country were p.rsuaded it was never irtended otherwise than merely air a felet, and to put ua to expensea. His answer was : " Mr. Pitt never though,, so ; I had well weighed the cons quecces. and I calculated that if I did not succeed the demonstration would do me great disservice, as it would make the English a military nation, and at the same time would give the ministers a command of money, since no other measure could authorise them to call for so large a sum as in this care was requisite. I was very well pleased to 8110 the preparations the Enelish made on the coast opposite Boulogne, at which place it never was my intention to have attempted a landing. I kept up this farce by frequent embarka- tions and by the exercise of m 5 flotilla. My real point of attack would have been somewhere between Margate and Deal. I calculate 4 that I co uld have possessed myselt of the lines of Chatham as a point of retreat. I should then have pushed for London, and, had I arrived there. I should have offered very moderate terms of peace, ~!ong care, however, so far to cripple you that you c ela have done no further m'schief nor have dis- turbed my future plans. Whether I should have suc- ceeded or not I can't say, but such were my pr jecte." He then talked of Ireland,where he said he had as many friends amongst the Pretest:ants as amonst the Catholics. —Fran) "M-,re Light on St. Helena," in the "Coruhill Magazine" fur January,

THE HOUSE BY THE RIVER.
BY MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON, Author of "The Secret. of the Pearls," "The House by the Lock," "Queen Sweetheart," "The Barnstormers," "Her Royal Highness," ike.
CII_ArTER XXIX. THE FACE IN THE COFFIN.

Sybil had no reason to associate Carstairs House, which was only a ',sloe to her, with the mysterious place where she had spent. the most terrible hours of her life. She had Purposely been misled on the day of her first memeratile viSit, by being taken in train and omnibus, boat pod carriage, whereas no such' bewildering variety of conveyance was neces- sary. Now she went by the simplest and shortest way. Instead of driving round to the entrance facing the river, as she had before, and afterwards being hurried into the ball without a chance of observing her surroundings, she approached the house leisurely in the cab which had brought her and Miss Monstance from Kingston, passing a porter's lodge, rattling along a freshly gravelled drive, and stopping at last under a handsome old- fashioned portico. Miss Monstance, having paid the driver, rang the door bell, which was opened by a respectable- looking young man, more like a valet than a butler or footman. They were shewn into a pretty, quaintly furnished, little reception room near the door, where Miss Monstance announced that she would seek Mr. Smith, and find out what room they could have with a window suitable for a sly, peep at the beautiful Miss Wade and her mother, Lady Carstairs. "The funeral won't be for a couple of hours yet," said the youre, woman, "but the ladies are coming here first, I know. I suppose they would want to look at their dead cousin before the coffin is shut up, and as you seem anxious for the same thing, I'll see what can be done." Miss •Monstance disappeared, to return again after an interval of fifteen minutes, which dragged tediously for Sybil. Mr. Smith had said he didn't think Lord Carstairs, his host, would have any objection to their seeing the body of Sybil Wade, and would Miss Ward please come at once ? Sybil rose and followed Miss Monstance, who led her down two or three rather complicated passages and corridors. At the end of the last, a door stood open, and the elder girl stepped aside as if intend- ing her companion to enter first. Sybil's heart was beating fast as she crossed the threshold. Heavy curtains were drawn across the windows, darkening the room, and a row of tall lighted candles burnt on either side of an open coffin, which was supported on a black draped bier. A strange little shudder crept through her veins. In that coffin lay the dead girl who was to be buried as Sybil Wade. What face would she see. lying there, white and still ? • Jack Churchill's words, that it all seemed a horrible dream from which he had just awoke, came back to her. This was like a dream—a dream of gazing at her dead self—only she was in the midst of it and had not woke up yet. Slowly, half-fearfully, she moved forward. As she bent over the coffin the candle-light appeared to make a bright dazzling haze . before her eyes, and for an instant her vision was blurred. But the cloud cleared away as suddenly as it had come. Sybil uttered a loud cry, for the face in the coffin was the face of Hester Frayne. Wildly she turned to rush from the room and demand an explanation of the dreadful mystery.,' from someone, she knew not, who. But Miss. Monstance was gone, and the door, which had., stood open, was closed. She ran to it and tried to fling it open. History had repeated itself for her; the door was locked and she was a prisoner, as she• had been in that terrible room in the house by the river. But now there was no Hester to come to, her rescue. Hester was dead.

div.head: CHAPTER XXX.
div.p: CHAPTER XXX.
TILE LAST ORDEAL.

Sybil went back to the coffin and tears fell hot from her eyes on the marble face of the dead.i "llester ! " she sobbed. "It was all in vain after all—everything you did for me. Oh, I would die a hundred times if only I could bring you back to life."

"She died for you, said 'a voice. And starting, the girl turned to see Lord Carstairs standing in the door. He had Unlocked it noiselessly, and now. he closed it once more, quickly turning a key, and snatching it out again to thrust it in his pocket.l "She died for you," he repeated. "I know now, that you were in a house in Craven-street, where I, found her on Sunday afternoon, only a little more. than a week ago. But I did not know then, and rather than give me a chance to learn the truth she came with me. She pretended then that she came; because she had cared for me all along, and was; rejoiced to see me again, and I was fool enough to., believe her—fool enough to believe that when I got her here she'd tell me everything, as she tried to make me think she would. But it was all a rusel, to help you to escape; I understand that now very well. She told me nothing about you. I had to find out everything for myself." "So it was you who plotted against me ; you, from whom 'Hester saved me before! " Sybil exclaimed, looking steadily into his. pale eyes. She had been afraid before, but she was not afraid now. Her scorn of this man was too great to' admit of fear entering in. "Hester did me the honour to be in love with: me, once," said Lord Carstairs, "If she'd kept it up she wouldn't lie where she does." "You killed her !" cried Sybil. "She was a traitor," Carstairs returned, coolly. "She has paid the penalty of treachery, that's all." "Coward—murderer !" the girl uttered, with ,blazing eyes. "You killed my father as well as 'Hester. I'm sure of that, though I cannot guess why. And I'm sure that now you mean to kill me." "You're sure of too many things for a child of your tender years ma cherc cousine," retorted Carstairs. "For that reason I am under the painful necessity of putting you out of my way." "How is it possible that I was ever in your way?" Sybil demanded. "As you aren't likely to tell the story outside, I don't mind enlightening you, if you really care to hear," said Lord Carstairs. "Thanks to that clever young person, Miss Alonstance, I have plenty of time before it is really necessary to act. The information may pain you, hut—" "I wish to hear everything," Sybil broke in, standing by the coffin, her little cold hand on Hester's hand, so much aolder. "Oh, very well, then. "11You and your father were in my way, for a very simple reason. I didn't know it myself until about the time I first met you. One night, I had two men out here to dinner, for a lark. They were my solicitors. We went into the room that used to be my grandfather's study—for he made Carstairs House his home. Anson, the elder of my two guests, was looking at some valuable books on the shelves that ran round the walls. Behind them he discovered a secret panel, accidentally touching a spring, and there was a document. setting forth that my grandfather repented his harshness to Lancelot, your father. With it there was a will, revoking the old one that left his private fortune to my father, and bestowing it on yours instead. You can guess, my dear cousin, in what a position that left me. It was intolerable. If only Drake had discovered the thing, not Anson, I should have been all right, for Drake was my pal, and we had been together in a good many deals. But Anson couldn't be squared, it seemed. I tried all I knew to get round him, but it was no use. And during dinner at Lady Northmuir's, on the night I saw you and my uncle Lancelot, I got a telegram from Anson in reply to a letter I'd sent him, saying he would only consent to keep the second will quiet if I settled privately with your father. I had begged him not to let the affair be made public talk if it could be avoided, but that was all I got ont of him. Before I parted with my uncle Lancelot that night, I had whispered an invitation here, to Carstairs House.' I made him promise to say nothing to anyone, and the bribe was some old family jewels I thought be ought to have, if they could be put into his hands without my mother knowing anything about it and raising a row. Well, he came; and, as you have heard long ago, he—committed suicide. His body was found in the river, and a letter that made everything clear." "You murdered him !" ejaculated Sybil. "And you forged a letter from him to me, which brought me, I believe now, to this very house." "You are quite right," responded Carstairs. "I don't object to your knowing that or anything now, since no miracle can interfere in your favour this time. It rather amuses me ' than otherwise, to enlighten you, since, as I said, we have still plenty of time. I meant, when I told you that you were right, merely so far as the house was concerned.
lioW your tattier filed aoesn't concern you: Tor even now the subject's not a pleasant one to me. But the letter was not forged. Uncle Lancelot was .--well, persua. . .I,lle blood was _ _ _

_ shed during the per sit., . . peocoss. before he con- sented, and a drop or two tell on the letter. But it had to be sent, for I!,er.. was no hope of getting another genuine doctrilelit ; and it rved its pur- pose. The suicide th,t,ry Aim so .;ieverly proved that Anson never stisperiod, only thought poor Lancelot Wade an unineky chap. And now he thinks the daughter equatly unlucky. For Sybil Wade is dead, you know." "You villain ! " Sybil panted. "Made so by circumstances, which otherwise would have reduced me to beggary—and I couldn't endure that. I'd have married you, and so satisfied everyone concerned, without all this wretched work (which I'm too fastidious, naturally, to enjoy) ; but, unfortunately,l have been secretly married for two years to a woman too handsome, too fascinating to get rid of—ar, actress, who does not want the truth known yet awhile, on account of some money she'll get if she remains unmarried till she's twenty-five. "You promised Hester you'd marry her, said _ _
-"Likely that I mean, that, isn't it, the dat.oter of the half-mad old caretaker of Carstairs House

I had to bribe Hester in some way, and that was the only one which served. IT-pluckily she must have come across some letters from my wife to me in a pocket-book which held some other private anci important memoranda as well, a telegram or two from Anson about that beast of a will, so that she knew I. had good reason for not loving my uncle Lancelot and his daughter. Finding out that I couldn't very well keep my promises to her, and had never meant keeping them, seemed to wake up what Hester called her conscience,' which other- wise might have slept quite peacefully to the end of all things. She turned traitor to spite me. pa trusted her, the little minx, to do for love more than her old brute of a mother did for money, and in consequence\ of her treachery I nearly lost you./ With you gone out of my reach my work was al/ undone. But Drake and I both saw that you would be too scared by Hester's hints or revelations to make trouble if you happened to read a paragraph announcing your own death in the paper. Your one thought, after your past experiences, would be to let well enough alone and keep out of my way."

"Hester never betrayed you," said Sybil. "She told me that I had a relentless enemy, but she never spoke his name, though once by mistake she said ' Ralph, ' and quickly checked herself. She had lost her love for you, but she was loyal to the memory of what had been, even through all her noble efforts to save me."

Carstairs gave a quick, furtive glance at the face in the coffin. "That's something to her credit," he admitted, harshly. "But it doesn't remove the fact of her treachery, and for that she had to pay. Not that she cared; Hester was young, but she wasn't much in love with life. I'd been trying to get hold of some girl who was an invalid bound to die shortly, and then I should have worked the same game, as nobody worth thinking of in England knew her by sight, and a doctor would have had no reason to suspect that his patient was not Sybil Wade. But I was unlucky; I couldn't find a safe sort of person. Of course I had to be careful for my own sake and the family's sake." "Your family's sake 1" echoed Sybil, bitterly. "Were Lady Carstairs and your sister Gladys in this plot, too ? " "Only far enough to bear out my word and follow my instructions without asking questions. I made that worth their while. They never knew there was a Hester, and haven't an idea of the stroke of luck that put her in my way again just as I was beginning to get desperate. You seem curious as to how she died. I won't go into details, but I'll tell you this much, the doctor certified death from double pneumonia. Even Beauchamp Drake, who tried to block my game by snapping you as a wife for himself—betraying me and getting your money for himself—can really prove nothing against me. Only you could absolutely ruin me, ii you were to slip away again and repeat these little cousinly confidences of mine. But you won't slit away; and it's been quite a relief to my mind to talk frankly with someone—even you. My mother and Gladys are inclined to believe that you are really dead, and "—with a horrid coolness he tool out his watch, glanced at it and put it back—" they must not be disappointed." "I believe that you must be insane!" cried Sybil, in horror of him. "No man who was not mad could be as wicked as you and feel no remorse for it." "Perhaps I am mad," he returned, with a slight shrug of the shoulders. "Insanity runs in in 3 mother'. frunily, I understand. .At all events, -thefe's "T -s-:1 of nielhod in my madness, which is the only p. of importance to you. Now, I have a proposal to make you, my pretty little cousin, for you really are exceedingly pretty, yot know. Will you give me the pain of—assuring myself that you are for ever beyond troubling me again (I needn't make lily meaning clearer), Ol will you quietly -drink a nice soothing mixture, which will simply put you to sleep without any discomfort or violence for any of us ? " Sybil looked stiaight and unfalteringly into the man's eyes. She well understood the choice he was giving her. If she did not consent to taking poison, thus sparing him the necessity of violence, distasteful to his fastidiousness, she would be killed in some dreadful way which she dared nol let herself picture. His whole scheme was very clear to her now. It had been essential that Sybil Wade should be seen by a doctor, who would certify that she had died a natural death. Probabl3 some subtle poison had been given poor Hester, which, having rendered her speechless, had counter- feited all the symptoms of pneumonia. No sus- picion of foul play would attach to Lord Carstairs. The world would think that he and his people had been very good to the little alien, bringing her tc Carstairs House to die, and letting her dead body be buried among their common ancestors. Now that the victim had been provided, and all the conventionalities of death properly gone through with, no one need ever know about this latest murder. Her body—the body of the real Sybi: Wade—would simply disappear. When she was safely dead she would be buried, perhaps, in some cellar underneath this old house, while Hester would sleep under the stone engraved with the name of Sybil Wade. The girl shuddered as these grim deductions presented themselves to her mind, but it was not with physical dread of what was to come. She had no longer the faintest hope of preserving her life. But she had either passed beyond the region of fear or she had not yet approached it; which was the secret of her calmness she did not know or stop to question. "Well, what have you decided ? " asked Carstairs, with his first sign of impatience. "In an hour from this .my mother and sister will Le here, and the coffin must be closed up before that if Hester Frayne stays in it. If you would like to take her place there you may, that they may shed a tear upon your pretty dead face. But let me remihd you that there's something to be done before that." "Then you must. do it," said Sybil, firmly, though her voice was faint. "I will not kill myself." Carstairs frowned, and his face, which had kept its colour, grew suddenly pale. He was a coward, and though he had determined on Sybil's death, he would gladly have been spared the unpleasantness that his resolve entailed. "Think again," he said, and drew a stiletto from an inner pocket, letting the blade—scarcely thicker than the long pins by which women fasten on their hats—flash significantly in the candle light. "Think again. This may look like a toy, and scarcely a drop of blood flows where it has fallen. But it hurts, and it steals life." "I tell you again that I will not take my own!" cried Sybil. "I will fight for my life while I have the streibgth left." And flying before him to the locked door, she shrieked aloud: "Murder! Murder!" There had been in her heart no hope of a response; but, as he sprang after her, quick and fierce and stealthy as a panther, she heard an answering shout. Was it an illusion that came to soothe the pangs of death? or was it a voice dear, to her beyond all others? Falling on her knees, she sank against the oaken panels of the door. Over her leant Carstairs with the stiletto uplifted; but—he dared not sheathe it in her flesh. In the pale dilated eyes despair and horror glared. It was true, then, she had heard the voice.
If he killed her now he could not escape

detection and justice. The voice came again, mingling with it a shrill, protesting snarl in woman's accents—Mrs. Fray-ne's. Sybil remembered them but too well. A shout of encouragement, and then a great blow on the door, that shattered a panel and brought through it the blade of an axe. Carstairs, who had hung over the girl in hesita- tion, whether to end her life whatever future eonsequences might be, started back. Flinging away the dagger he snatched frQui We coat a gwall

revolver (kept for some unforeseen emergency, perhaps, when the noise of a shot would no longer matter) and fired straight at Sybil's breast. With- out waiting to see if it took effect he pressed the muzzle against 'his own temples and pullea the trigger. Then his body collapsed. He fell forward on his face and lay still. Another blow on the panel—an athlete's blow— which tore a splintered hole in the door and shewed Jack Churchill's face.

"My darling! Are you hurt ? " he stammered. And even in that moment, thrilling at the sound of these first words, Sybil answered: "No. The bullet only grazed my shoulder." Three minutes more, and the broken lock yield- ing, Jack had sprung into the room. The sight of him, the knowledge of love and safety, after cruelty and deadly peril, were like the opening of Paradise to Sybil. Hardly knowing what she did, she held up her arms like a child, and he caught her to his heart. Only then she remembered, and, shrinking from him, faltered the one word—" Gladys!" "There is no Gladys for me any more!" ho answered. "She was false—utterly. She lied to me, saying you were ill—dying, then dead! That she had seen you nearly every day. She was the tool of that man there, who has died by his own hand, to save himself from the hangman. There is no truth in her. She never loved me. I never loved her. The thought of her as my wife was agony. It was you I loved—always, always you— from the first time our eyes met. My sweet! My precious one!"

Only two persons knew the true explanation of Lord Carstairs's death, though five others—hie mother, his sister, the old chretaker at Carstairs House, and Beauchamp Drake, perhaps, also, Miss Monstance, in a less degree—may have guessed. The truth about Sybil was partially made public, of course, for her identity had to be established. But it was supposed to have been a case of mistaken identity—possibly a fraud upon the family—by a young woman who had been glad of support from. them during her last illness. Jack Churchill's wife did._npt need or desire thro fortune which should have conie to Sybil Wade; and, since the murderer of her father and of poor Hester Frayne was dead, the girl—happy and protected now—wished to shew mercy to the miserable mother and sister.

Beauchamp Drake fled from England on the day. of Lord Carstairs's suicide, taking with him into exile some thousands of his senior partner's money, as well as his own. Mrs. Frayne had also found an opportunity to disappear, during the moments when Jack Churchill had no thought to spare for anything save his newly-rescued love. .A.nd justice was satisfied, so Sybil believed, by the vilest criminal's death.

Great gossip followed on the breaking off of the engagement between Gladys Wade and Jack Churchill, almost on the wedding eve; but nobody quite understood what had led to the parting. Ile had never seemed like the same man after his engagement to the famous beauty, his friends said, therefore he never cared for her. She and her mother had made a dead set at him for his money, and no doubt Jack had somehow found her out just in time. Women had never liked her or her mother, and the two left few, if any, regretful friends when they decided to assuage their sorrow for Carstairs' tragic death in a three years' trip round the world.

"They've enough money row, if such women ever have enough," said Lady Northmuir, who, truth to tell, had had time thoroughly to weary of both during their last long visit to her; "and, after all that's happened, I shouldn't be surprised if they never came back to England. They'll probably settle down in India, where Gladys can make plenty of conquests among a set of youngsters, who won't be too particular or ask too many questions." _ _

- Sybil would have put off her marriage if Jack would have listened to her arguments, but he could scarcely bear to let her go out of his sight; and the only way to keep her within it always was to make her immediately his wife. If he had not decided to seek for some solution for the mystery of Sybil's alleged death, by paying a hurried, unex- pected visit to Carstairs House before it should be time for his appointment with Sybil later in the afternoon, he could not have saved her life. And the memory of his interview with Mrs. Frayne, the fear on her sly face, his insistance against her determination that he should not enter the house, the search from room to room, the seizing of an axe in a lumber-room, the finding of the locked door, the shock of Sybil's cry—all these things together gave him a horror of even a few hours parting from the girl he loved so well. What did gossip matter? They knew that they .had. she_wn meiTz to those who had sinned against them; knmg—That always they could afford to let the world talk. The world would be far enough apart for their new happiness. So Sybil's arrangements were overruled, and she and Jack Churchill were married in a quiet little church in South Kensington, with only the dear old friends, to whose house he had taken Sybil, to listen to the words that made them man and wife._

"All the horrible past seems a dream now, as r used to think even when I was living it," said Sybil, leaning over the rail of the great ship that was taking them away that night for a long honey- moon across the water. "Only the marble cross you have had placed over Hester's grave shines out of the blackness, white and pure as that beautiful moon rising out of the dark sea." "And we'll put it all behind us like a dreara that is ended with the dawn—all but the memory of Hester," answered Jack, with his arm round the slim, girlish waist. "For our dawn has come, darling, the dawn of love's day, and love's day, please God, knows no night." So the moon rose out of the sea. And they watched it together, heart to heart, and the dark dreams of the past vanished for ever in the light. / LTnE END. ]

div.p: great and intelligent countries are concerned, muqt be a subjed of wonderment. Up to now, the newspapeis, which are the only mean that the masses of the pecple have to educate themselves, have fed their readers on " patriotic lies.", instead of teaching them the tru h, Toe greatest need of the twentieth century is a press upright and noble, that will see that its duty is to preach concord, and to help, by their careful discretion and consideration, the work of diplomatists whenever any difficulties may arise between two nadons. If, besides, a law is passed tnat will cause newspaper.; to be pre- secuted for libelling foreign nations, as well aq private individuals, the pPaco of the world will be assured. George B. Burg;n. cERARY earrrc OF THE "DAILY EXPRES

The greatest need for the new century is a little more faith, hope, and charity, and a little le-s pessimism. In the words of a celebratea old divine. let us remember that. "We have a title to be provided for, as we uge Gld's creatures. . . . and, thetefore it is a her a folly and infid,lity to be troubled and lull of care." George Manville Fenn. AUTHOR OF A EIUNDRED POPULAR NOVELS

In my opinion the greatest need of the new century' is a thorough cleansing of the national hive by watts of a short Act of Parliament—one which would enable the magistracy to work in co- Iperation with the Army and Navy in making a clean sweep of the ruffiandom existent in our lar,„e towns, which swarm with able- bodied young men and lads of a class who are a curse to themselves and a constant evil to those among whom they dwell. As matters stand, we are constantly read- ing of Hooliganism and its varieties, which now supple- ment the ordjnary 'petty crimes that fill our prisons. These pests of society will not work; they are perfectly useless, and for their benefit as well as our own, I would give the magistracy the power to hand over to the naval and military authorities every able•bodie d man or youth fit to serve who could not prove that he is getting an honest living It would mean the formation of depots of supply for the twe services, in which excellent sailors and soldiers could be manufactured for enforced service, with the sternest repression and punishment where needed for the vilest and most stubborn, and rapid advance by gradation for the more willing, who should have facility for becoming decent soldiers or sailors fit to be drafted into our regiments or ships. We enforce education with the child and boy. Why not continue it with the growing ruffian ? He would be beyond the reach of the cane so delicately used under the school board, but hers in oases of the very worst there is the lash. Retrograde ? Better than the constant imprisonment which seems only to harden, and its application would be the greatest rarity if stern military discipline were the order of the day.

The Rev. H. R. Haweis, M.A, INCUMBENT OF Sr. JAMES', MARYLEBONE. More prophets, fewer parrots ; mote thought, less ,alk ; more fact, less Nner ; more faith, less form. H. W. Massingham. LONDON EDITOR OF TIIE "MANCHESTER GUARDIAN." Toe greatest need of the New Century is, in my opinion, to teach the individual truth, the state justice, and the Church Christisnity. Canon W. Hay Aitken, OF NORWICH CATHEDRAL• I think that we may get at a conclusi ,n as to what is the greatest need of the Twentieth Centu, y by reflecting on what it is that we most deplore in the --ad of the Nineteenth. I believe that most thoughtful observers of the moral features of the period would indicate this by a somewhat clumsy, but all too intelligible word— Indifferentism. It is not 'merely to Christian religion that the masses are indifferent. It seems scarcely pos- sible to awaken any enthusiasm on any subject of either moral, social, or cyan political reform. The one hopi- tul feature of the hour in this.respect, contrasting with this, and indicating the potentiality of better things, has been the recent outburst of patriotic feeling. Now I suppose that the opposite of indifferentism is earnestness. We need earnestness in other things be- sides football, and indeed even in this there seems a tendency to sacrifice the enthusiasm ot tbe smitten- to the commercially apprised skill of the professional. We need (Oh, that we might begin our new century with it!) "another Pentecost." This will produce ear nestness in every department of reform. I always be- lieve that it was the American Revival that killed salvery, and a simi'ar spiritual movement, conpled with the strong teaching that is now, thank God, so common on the subject of Christian morality, will in- augurate a new crusade against those monstrous moral and social evils which will disgrace our modern civiliss- tion.
J. Keir Hardie, M.P , LEADER OF THE INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY Men !
Rev. W. Carlile,

FOUNDER AND CHIEF SECRETARY OF THE CHURCH ARMY. From a Church Army point of view, the crying need of the Church of Christ is, that she should be truly Catholic in her love both for the best, however much she may differ from some, and for the worst, however much tney-maLy have sunken; as well as Apostolic, itriOntb-oba- puts herself to endless risk and trouble to win them. Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., PASTOR OF CHRIST CHURCH, WESTMINSTER. The greatest need for the new century is a revival of the sense of Reverence, by which I mean the habitual acknowledgment on the part of us all of the reality and worth of the unseen and et.rnal. Our modern life seems utterly superficial. Wealth, display, pleasure monopo- lise us. - We burn so much gas, and spend so much time, far into the night, in its glamour, that we seldom Icok up to the stars burning through the ages, in the infinite spaces of the Universe. How differently Drake, Frobisher, Hawkins, Sir Philip Sydney would have written to Queen Elizabeth of their successes by land or sea, to the style that most corres- pondents and leader writers now employ • whilst the references of Hampden, Pym, and Colonel Hutchinson to God. the Bible, and the eternal principles of the Kingdom of God would be deemed so much cant if used by a' statesman to-day. We are losing oui reverence for human rights, for our liberty, for our word, for the family, for God's Day, God's Book, and G( d himself. And when reverence' for things which lie behind the material and outward vanishes, the dry rot has already struck its fangs into the foundations of our national life. I Corrie Grant, M.P., CHIEFORGAN :ISER OF THE PROGRESSIVE FORCES IN LONDON.

Your question is extremely difficult to answer. Everybody will consider the question of what is the greatest need of the century from their own, and there- fore from a different point of view. My little daughter's answer is "More Liberal M.P.'s," while a struggling friend of mine is confident that the true reply is 6 More money." (should say first that I desire our social and moral progress to be as great in the new century as in the old. The greatest need of the new century is there- fore more citizens of character, of determination, single- eyed, unselfish, simple. What is the greatest stumbling block in the way? The steadily growing greed of wealth.

div.head: Max Pemberton.
div.p: Max Pemberton.

AUTHOR OF "THE FOOTSTEPS OF A THRONE," ETC. I think the greatest need of the new century is : For the Nation—Sobriety and a due sense of proportion. For the Politician—New Voices but old Truths. For the Worker—A wider vision looking across the Channel t 3 ask where the worker stands. The final greatness of this Empire depends upon the fidelity to the old traditions of freedcm and peace. Her commercial greatness, indispensable to her stability, is purely a matter of intellect and application. She must work harder and think more. Perhaps her preat.st need is the knowledge that her commercial supremacy is leaving her. From" THE TEMPLE MAGAZINE" for January.

Railway Outrage nearWarrington. A man, named James Williamson Mauler, London and North-Western scale-porter of Cecil-street, Liverpool, was found on Friday evening shockingly injured in a train near Acton Bridge. He was taken to the railway company's hospital at Crewe. He has two very severe gashes in his neck, from which he lost a large quantity of blood. He is also suffering from shock. He has made a statement that he was stabbed and robbed by a tallow- passenger, who entered the compartment when he was alone as the train was moving out at Liverpool. He describes his assailant as apparently a workman. and adds that he must have known he was carrying a large sum of money. Detectives are making most careful inquiries,

THE GREATEST NEED OF THE
CENTURY.
Symposium by Representative Men, including Learned Divines, Popular Authors, Leading Editors, Well-known Humorists, and two

Dr. Farrar, DEAN OF CANTERBURY. The rmanence or our Empire, the stability of our 'Commerce, the welfare of the Nation, depend on our .showing ourselves capable of developing more Crenuous- ness, more self-denial, a deeper conviction of the truth that there is one thing only—Righteousness—which eXalteth a nation ; and that sin is not only the reproach but the ruin of any people. F. C. Burnand. EDITOR OF "PUNCH." Can there be any queAion as to what is the "greatest peed" to the majority of us in the new century ? Has it not been the greatest need for most persons in the past century, or rhther centuries? Money. Have every good quality possible, be the most charitable person in the world, and if you have no money—eui ibono ? It needs no " symposium " of philosophers or 'men dis- tiu.uishea in Art and Letters to tell us that the greatest need for the new century, and for every other century, Past, present and future, is " money." Without money the next need is miracles. Money or miracles. Remember the tribute money found in the mouth of a fish. Tnere's an example: The miracle produced the money,or.rather, the money was produced by miracle. Had money been Present a miracle would not have been needed. The Rev. Silas K Hocking. AurEon OF OUR 'NEW SERIAL" RUBY LOVEDAY." What is needed more than anything else is a genuine 'ethical revival—the creation of a finer moral sense, of a Purer moral atmosphere. I would say nothing, in die- Paragement of creeds or ceremonials, or modes of woi- ship—three thinga are important no doubt, but they aro nor of supreme importance—:ne one essential thing is

'Character. - We have insisted continuously on whit mit-. be called be formal side of religion, sun as a, tendanee at ()z- -ings, and sacraments. We have urged he necessity of faith ad sound doctrine—and no doubt rightly so—but the all-important question of godliness. ot the higher ethical life, of the fine moral sense that. resents, an I shrinks back, from the least approach of sin, has in my judgment received far too little attention. I hesitate to Bay a word that should seem to reflect on existing organisations, and yet most thoughtful men, I think Will Reedit that the moral tone, and the moral standards of the world leave much to be desired. Nor is there any very clear line of distinction between those who Profess religion and those who do not. As a matter of fact.soms of the noblest characters in the world to-day— and by general consent acknewledged as sucn—make no Profession of rtsligion at all. I fear we must hold it a truth that however successful the Church may have been in christianising the world, the world has been far rdore successful in secularising the Church. Toe Merely rich man has far more influence to-day in Church Councils than the merely godly man. Big houses count for more than great souls, and small sins are winked at when c wered by large contributions. If the Kingdom of Heaven is repre- aented by the ecclesiastical organisations that we call the Church, then a golden key will unlock the door, and money will purchase the •highest seats. The Christian Church to-day is suffering from precisely the same evils that affected and paralysed the Jewish Church in the time of Christ. The poili,3 of analogy may be easily traced by anyone who will take the rrouble to do so. Bence the failure of the Church to meet and circumvent the growing evils of the lad • The power of the drink Seller is steadily increasing both ia the Church and in the state. The Stork Exchange gambler is to the front in ecclesiastical enterprises. Toe company-promoter, the money-lender,the jerry-builder, the rack-renter,have honoured places in the synagogue, and the result is that Morally the nation stagnates. Even religiously we make /to real progress. There are fewer young people in our Sunday schools than there were five years ago ; fewer adults, relatively to the size of the population, attending our churches; fewer additions, in propertion to the agencies, to the roll of Church members. Nor is that the worst, from a merely ecclesiastical point Of view. The Church has lost its bold upon the groat Mass of the people; not one in ten of the working men of England attend Church or Chapel. What we term the masses don't believe in the Church, or in the ministry. They don't believe that we are sincere. They don't believe that we believe what we profess to believe, or we should do differently from what we do. It is a humiliating confession to make, but we had better face it. These people have no quarrel with Christianity. They believe in Christ and reverence Him. But they fail to discover in us any real likeness to the Master. Wherein, they ask, is the difference between those who Profess re.igion and the great mass ot respectable pesple who make no profession? Are we more peaceful, more neighbourly, more ready to forgive, more eager to do good, more wining to suffer wrong.? Is our life simpler.. etveel er, more gentle and generous and heroic? Da We Collle out from among the ungodly ? Do we stand apart—a nat;on within a nation—rebuking national wrong, resissing passion and strife, hol,:ing aloft the banner of brotherhood—fighting against lust and greed and drunkenness, or do we fritter away our life in oiling ecclesiastical machinery and let the world wa g as it will? I may be mistaken—l hope I may be, but it seems to me we have lost the vivid sense of wrong that tught to Characterise us. We really don't trouble about suen matters as drunkenness, and gambling, and prosti. tutioa, and war. Our conscience is not sensitive to the finer shades of morality. We allow evil things to be done in the hope that good may come. We place denominational gain before national righteousness, and Nye have lost sight of the race in our passion for a nation. So I come back to ;he point at which I started. It is an ethical revival that we need. No opening of the flood gates of emotion will meet the case. No DOW acceptance of a creed. When the Church herself has been converted to Godliness then shall we make our influence felt upon the nation. We want a nearer vision ofpod—a realisation of His immanence, an awakening to rightenusnese and a sense of our own accountability, and of a judgment to come. Rev. C. H. Grundy, M.A. Rural. DEAN OF GREENWICH. The pressing need of the new century is among the young men ; a sense of duty instead of a love of pleasure. Toe youth of England lack industry and the Power of "sticking to it." Their minds are full of foot- ball records and entertainments. The one idea is to "get away from the offiee " ns soon as possible. Self- improvement is put on one side for smoking concerts and amateur dramatics, and the tendency is to lean on Parents and to get money from them, instead of pushing forward in life by plodding and efficiency. The "early closing" is the idea everywhere. The dogged intention ta make one's way in the world and rise by sheer tiara 'work is dying out. The limp lover of pleasure, to be paid for by other people, is everywhere. The grit and, determination which built up the old businesses of Enk Land is going. and young men are content to be clerks in'" Limited Companies" because they have 'either the self-respect nor the energy to make a career. Clement Shorter, EDITOR OF THE "Senna." Assuming that there are in this country, and in every -country, many thousands of people who,•without any fault of their own. but through temperament and cir- cumstance, are suffering the most painful fruits of Poverty, I take it the greatest need ot the next century I that it should solve this problem of the undeserved Dr. Jessop, RECTOR OF &MINING, NORBOLIK. I believe the greatest need of the twentieth century, 7.s far as the welfare of our own country is concerned, is ,t the financial position of the Church of England L._u'd be very largely strengthened. Max O'Rell.

AUTHOR OF "JOHN BULL AND HIS ISLAND." ETC. The ignorance of nations on the subject of 'what is going on in other nations is .vomething,r appall- -ii, but when we refl,ct thit Fr,nce it only twenty- )no :siijas from Ecgland, th‘tt ignorance, so far as these two

sallies, and it has since been Dome by his sue- f cessors. Louis Napoleon' like Louis Philippe, I died an exile in England. In 1870 France became a Republic once again, ..nd as a Republic she has just been celebrating by an International Exhibition the close of the nineteenth century. During all these successive revolutions, and doubtless to some extent in spite of them, the national prosperity of France has been steadily maintained. There are in the French character elements of steadfastness, prudence, economy, and sobriety which seem to carry the people safely on through • whatever seasons of disturbance, of apparent national convulsion. When France had to make peace with the Germans after the war of 1870 she was compelled to pay a ransom so enormous that nothing like it had been known in modern history, and yet she paid it to the utter- most farthing, never came near to the brink of national bankruptcy, and, indeed, went steadily on with her manufactures, her commerce' and her culture as if nothing partiLular had happened. Nothing could be more futile than any attempt at confident prediction with regard to the future course of a nation's history, especially, perhaps, of a nation like France, with which the glory of military enterprise counts for So much; but it is certain at least that the present French Republic has lasted much longer than any other form of government since the days of the Great Revolution, and that the visitors from foreign • countries who have lately been studying, with most intelligent • observation, the condition a France have borne testimony to the marvellous prosperity which makes itself evident all over the country. THR PROGRESS OF PRUSSIA.
One of the most remarkable phenomena of the

century, especially in its later-half, has been.the political uprising of Prussia and her establishment as the centre of a German Empire. During the former half of the century Prussia may be said to have counted for almost nothing in the political life of Europe. One who lived in those days might well have forgotten that there ever had been such a Sovereign and soldier as Frederick the Great, or such a statesman as Von Stein. Prussia was gene- rally regarded by the outer world as a land of professors and of beer-drinking students, of pedants and dreamers, and of soldiers drilled to the wearing of uni'form. "Germany is Hamlet," said a gifted and popular German poet, made melancholy by the thought that his country could only, dream and allow itself to be pushed aside,while other countries were imperiously asserting their rights to a share in the government of Europe. It is curious to notice how, up to a comparatively recent date, some of the most experienced even among English statesmen and diplomatists set down Prussia as counting for nothing in European affairs. How such an idea came to exist concerning a people more highly educated as a whole than any other in Europe, and almost entirely free from the distraction of conflict- ing nationalities in one State system, it is not necessary for my present task to inquire too curiously. But it is certain that up to the middle of the century the yearning for German unity,which i found so much expression n poems, and treatises, and discourses, throughout German populations, was regarded in Europe generally as the mere dream , of Teutonic students and sentimentalists. The hour and the man came with the rise of Bismarck to the front, and it was soon evident that the two stars of Austria and Prussia could not keep their motion in the one sphere of Germany; and the triumph of Prussia during the Seven Weeks' war settled the controversy. Then the world began to see that France and Prussia were drifting into rivalry. M. Prevost-Paradol, in words that will long be remembered, likened these two States to two express trains started from the extremes of the same line, and therefore doQmed to inevitable collision. The result of the collision was the fall of the Second Empire in France and the elevation of Prussia to the supreme position in German affairs, with a German Emperor to preside over her councils. and an organisation of minor Sovereigns to support him.
