Some of the States which were formerly Spain's vassals are uow self- governing and prosperous kingdoms.

div.head: STORY OF THE CENTURY.
div.p: THE STORY OF THE CENTURY.
BY JUSTIN McCARTHY.

The story of that century which is now drawing to a close will, I venture to think, prove to be one of the most important volumes in the whole history of civilisation. Ido not say that it will be one of the most brilliant, for there may have been centuries which flashed a broader and a brighter light over the world's fields of intellectual and moral dark- ness; centuries of more startling conquest, of more sudden change ; centuries, even, of greater triumphs in literature and in art. But the nineteenth century has been a time of growth and of development, in all the paths of civilisation, such as the world's history has hardly ever seen rivalled, and in the application of science to the every-day needs of humanity has never seen equalled. When the century opened there 'seemed to be a vast im- passable, impenetrable region of darkness, a cloud- covered "No Man's Land," dividing the old civili- sation from the new. Asia and Africa appeared to have nothing to do with modern civilisation except as a subject for the reader of history, or as an exploring ground for the traveller. Egypt was the land whither Europeans with a taste for antiquities went to study the Pyramids and the Sphinx. India was even still looked upon as the country to, which enterprising Englishmen went to make fortunes. China was thought of as a mysterious old-fashioned region,peopled by countless millions of persons who wore pig-tails, and shut off by a great wall from the visits of intrusive foreigners. The real living world was commonly regarded by Europeans as only to be found in Europe itself, for the New World, as it was called, had not yet begun to count for much as an influence of civilisation, and the still newer world of Australasia counted for nothing at all. It would hardly be too much to say that the whole work of modern science which has to do with the practical affairs of every-day life has, so far as it has got,been acccomplished in the nine- teenth century. Of course there were great scientific discoveries made in the definition and the appli- cation of natural laws to human life at various periods, early and late, in the history of the world, which each succeeding generation has only con- firmed and extended. But what I wish to point out is that the practical science of the nineteenth cen- tury has made more change in the ordinary condi- tions of human life than was made by any century, or all the-centuries, which went before it.

div.head: TRIUMPH OF SCIENCE.
div.p: THE TRIUMPH OF SCIENCE.

Men travelled in the days of Swift and Johnson exactly as they had travelled in the days of Julius Cresar, and in the days when Troy was a city, and back to men's first Journeyings anywhere on this globe; that is to say, they travelled as well as horses or camels, as sails or oars, could convey them. With this century have come the carriages and the ships propelled by steam, and more lately by electricity. The work of electricity is, indeed, even yet only in its early stage of 'development. Up to the present century men strove to send instan- taneous news by beacon lights on hilltops, by flag signals, and by semaphore. Now we have the tele- graph wires on the land and beneath the ocean, enabling civilisation to carry on instantaneous interchange of news, and we are already maturing discoveries and processes which are to render the wire of the telegraph a superfluous piece of mechanism. In no department of human life has modern science been more successful and more beneficent than in all that relates to the mitigation of human suffering during surgical treatment. The peculiarity about all these discoveries and appli- cations of modern science is that they belong to the present century, and distinguish it, therefore, in the history of the world from any century which went before. Perhaps, indeed, if we were seeking for some especially apt and characteristic description of the nineteenth century, some description distin- guishing it from all its predecessors, we should describe it as the century of science applied to the practical business of humanity's every-day life.

div.head: OPENING YEARS OF THE CENTURY.
div.p: THE OPENING YEARS OF THE CENTURY.

The century opened for Europe in an interval of war, which was mistaken, at the time, for a return of the reign of peace. The period of storm brought about by the French Revolution, a revolution which was in itself directly influenced and forwarded by the success of the American struggle for indepen- dence, had come to a temporary lull, and many observers in England and in France fondly believed that the international struggle had come to an end. The history of Europe for many years had been, and still for some years was to be, the story of one man's genius, ambition, and energy. It is not necessary in this narrative to consider what might have been the course of events in Europe, what might have been the effect of the French Revolution, if the other Great Powers had been content to leave to France the working out of her own destinies, and had not made it their policy to force on her their ideas as to the manner in which France ought to be governed. The alliance of the other Great Powers

against revolutionary France gave the military genius of Napoleon an opportunity of shewing its power, and enabled Napoleon to become Dictator with the title of Emperor. "The meteor of con- quest," to quote Byron's words, allured the great Emperor too far. Napoleon attempted enterprises beyond even his power to accomplish; he tried to make himself the Dictator of Europe, and he failed. The interval of peace with which the century opened was followed by the fiercest struggles between France and allied Europe, and the Duke of Wellington brought the whole conflict to a close by his victory at Waterloo. Napoleon may be fairly said to have represented the initiative impulse of war, and Wellington the power of resistance. After the fall and the banishment of Napoleon came what I might call the era of congresses, the days when European statesmen seriously believed that it was possible for a number of diplomatists to meet together in a council-room and parcel out Europe into States and sovereignties according to the desires and the convenience of the then ruling potentates. It did not seem to have occurred to most of the statesmen who took part in these arrangements to ask themselves whether the various populations of Europe ought not to have something to say to the settlements which so directly affected their interests and their happiness. The doctrine of nationalities had not yet become a recognised power in. European politics, and the diplomatists there- fore sat down in their council chamber, with the map of Europe spread out before them, and, pencil in hand, they marked out this part of the Continent as the dominion of the restored King of France, that part as the domain of the Emperor of Austria, another region to the Otto- man Turk, and so on. The great English statesman, George Canning, was the first to set up a systematic, and what may be called a scientific, policy of opposition to these chimerical projects for the settlement of human affaiis in the interests of a few reigning families. The foreign policy which Canning created is now the accepted and avowed policy of England and the United States of America, and even on the European Continent is at least professed and proclaimed as a principle of action by all enlightened statesmen. One by one the arrangements made during the era of the congresses have broken up or crumbled away. Italy, which was divided among Austrian Princes and Spanish Bourbon Kings, has ejected her Spanish Bourbons, has been helped in the ejectment of her Austrian Princes, and is now one kingdom under an Italian Sovereign.

• THE CENTURY FOR FRANCE. For France the century has been one of successive revolutions, or at least of successive changes in government and in political organisation. The Bourbon family did not remain long upon the throne to which the allied Powers of Europe had restored them. The Bourbon Legitimist Sovereigns were succeeded by Louis Philippe, who proved himself to have learnt little of the art of governing men, Other from history, or from personal observation. His reign was brought to a sudden close by the revolution of 1848, and he died an exile in Eng- land. France made another attempt at a Republic, but the Republican leaders, many of them gifted, sincere, and patriotic men, were not equal to the task they had undertaken, and there came a revul- sion of feeling which enabled Louis Napoleon, nephew of the great Emperor, to establish himself as Napoleon the Third. Success seemed for some time to be strewn beneath his feet. He allied him- self with England against Russia in the Crimean war, he took the field against Austria in the interests of Italian independence and his favourite doctrine of nationalities. He overthrew Austria in a short campaign, and contributed his share towards the emancipation of Italy. But he too, like his uncle, was allured too far by the meteor of conquest. He endeavoured to found a sort of vassal empire in Mexico and failed in the attempt, and with the hope of recovering his supremacy at home he allowed himself to become entangled in a war with Prussia, which ended in his capture at Sedan, and the occu- pation of Paris by the German conquerors. His policy, in fact, relieved France from an Emperor, and gave an Emperor to the Germans, for the , Hine of Prussia received the Imperial title at Ver-

div.head: AUSTRIA, AND THE NEAR EAST.
div.p: AUSTRIA, AND THE NEAR EAST.

Austria has had to make great sacrifices during the century, but the sacrifices would be cheap if they obtained for what remains of the empire a more thorough union of interests and of sentiment. The Austrian Empire, as we know it in modern times, has been compelled to try to its utmost strain the experiment of holding together a large number of diverse nationalities under one central authority. The Emperors of Austria had Italian, Hungarian, Bohemian, Polish, and German populations under their sovereignty, and, indeed, the whole Austrian system in this century was the direct outcome of the policy which inspired the Congress of Vienna. Such a policy could come to nothing but failure, and Austria, as its most characteristic embodiment, soon found that her peculiar composition proved an irresistible temptation to some of her rivals/on the European Continent. France assailed her through her Italian populations, and Bismarck later on fol- lowed the example. A little earlier in the history of the century Hungary had gone into rebellion, and would, beyond all question, have secured her absolute independence but that Russia intervened and won for Austria the victories which Austria was unable to win for herself. Of late years Hun- gary has obtained something like recognition of her national right to domestic self-government, and there seems no reason why the Austrian Empire as it now stands should not hold safely and har- moniously together. Russia has grown and con- solidated remarkably during the present century. Her influence is now probably greater than it ever was before, although she is no longer regarded with that widespread suspicion and dread which, about the middle of the century:. seemed to set her down as a mere barbaric Power,thirsting for the acquisition of new territory, and utterly unscrupulous as to the means by which it satisfied its desire. Russia has more than once shewn a willingness which must be regarded as genuine, to co-operate with other great States in promoting a policy of humanity and civilisation, and the closing years of the century saw with admiration and sympathy her attempt to bring about an agreement among the great States of the civilised world which might substitute a tribunal of arbitra- tion for the settlement of international disputes for the merely barbarous force of the battlefield. The empire of the Ottoman Turk, on the other hand, has shewn nothing during the century, but signs of increasing stagnation and decay,politically, socially, and morally. Nowhere in any of the regions covered by the Turkish power does there seem any revival of a healthy growth. Every impartial observer must be ready to admit that there are manly and noble qualities in the character of the ordinary Turk, as he may be seen and studied any day in Europe or in Asia Minor, but the system Of rule in Turkey seems utterly incapable of adaptation to the ways of progress and incapable of improving the condition of any nationality or any class which is brought under its fatal influence. Greece, on the contrary, since her emancipation from Turkish rule under the influence, in the first instance, of the wise and beneficent policy initiated by Canning, has been happily developing in every field of growth, and has now a system of national education which would do honour to any European State. We have not to go far back into the reading of modern history to arrive at a time when the very name of a Greek was held to be the symbol of duplicity, ignoble craft, and chicanery, lust as it used to be in the days of Juvenal. The inspiration of genius enabled Byron to understand the country and the people better, and every year that has elapsed since Greece was set free from Ottoman domination has only served more and more to justify the hopes of the brave men who went out from England and most parts of the civilised world to help her in accomplishing her freedom. For some others of the south-eastern populations formerly under the rule of Turkey there is also good hope of growing prosperity and national strength. Russia and Turkey were engaged in more struggles than one since the days of the Crimean war, and European congresses made some mistakes and blunders in their efforts at the reconstruction of Turkey's ill-managed dominions. But the general result of these efforts, including the work of the Treaty of Berlin, .was to establish the complete emancipation of several Christian provinces *rim the rule of the Ottoman. Power, and their elevation to the ranks of independent and self-governing States. These are good omens for the south-east of Europe.

div.head: TEE DECAY OF SPANISH POWER.
div.p: TEE DECAY OF SPANISH POWER.

At the other extreme of the Mediterranean we find Spain still following the downward catfrse which it has apparently been her destiny to pursue ever since her great days, when her possessions exceeded those of any other European State. The story of the century has .been .for Spain .a melancholy story of Af'scent and decay. She has had many changes of rynasty, and has even known popular revolution, lant no revolution has yet come -which seems to have had the power of breathing into her the 'spirit of progress. Her colonial possessions, the last relics of her greatness, have been in recent years a source of much trouble to her. The manner in which she endeavotred to keep down her colonial popula- tions brought her at last into a hopeless struggle against the ;„rreat and -growing power of the United States. There seems something almost whimsical in the fatality which thus elthibiteciSPain as an utterly • unmatched antagonist for the people of that con- tinent whch first knew civilisation through her, when she was at the of her power and her glory. One would think that any. intelligent Spaniard would have seen, long ago, the impossi- bility of maiiithiniry.,r in our days a system of mediaeval tyranny ever a population living on an island which t;i111 le :=ceit from the.shores of Florida, on the great American .Continent. Every rebellion against Spanish rule in Cuba made the territory of the 11)..itecl States its refuge ,ground after defecit, and its field of preivration for- the next struggje. The war between Spain- and the United States was of short duration, and it enoed, as every un- prejudiced _observer must have known it would end, in the defeat and humiliation of Spain. The friends of Snain—and in one sense at least we

div.head: NETHERLANDS AND NOILTUERN LOROPE.
div.p: THE NETHERLANDS AND NOILTUERN LOROPE.

The story of; the century, so far as Holland and Belgium are concerned, is a story of steady progress in education, industry,_ commerce, and political development. The northern States of Europe—Sweden and Norway, and Denmark—are not merely prosperous at homc, but are making for themselves a distinct reputation abroad in literature and in art. That reputation is a part of this century's story. Denmark has given a Princess to the reigning family in England whose happy marriage, noble character, personal charms, and generous devotion to every charitable and deserving movement must form one of the most delightful chapters in the story of the century.

div.head: EGYPT RECLAIMED,
div.p: EGYPT RECLAIMED,

The modern development of Egypt is the work altogether of the Nineteenth Century. Only a com- paratively short while ago—certainly well within the century, when Belzoni was exploring the , temple! and the Tombs of the Kings in the regions of tht Nile—Egypt was but the vassal State of Turkey. Now it is to all intents and purposes a part .of tha British Empire, and a very important part also o the great highway of civilisation. A system of railways will soon connect Alexandria with Cape- town. "The Englishman," said Alexander Kinglake in his "Eiithen," "straining far over to hold his ioved India, will plant a firm foot on the banks of the Nile and sit in the seats of the Faithful." The Frenchman, too, tried to set a firm foot on the banks of the Nile, and other men of Europe may have had a like ambition, but the Englishman alane seems to have succeeded in the effort, and a project against Egypt would now be a' project against the British Empire. lam telling the story of the century, and it is no part of my purpose to append a moral lesson to every section of the narrative, as the old- fashioned translations of lEsop's fables used to append for the instruction of children a didactic moral application to each fable. I shall not, there- fore, enter into any consideration as to the ethical uprightness of the various movements by. which England became the owner of -Egypt, but it is an important point in my story that Egypt has thus become part of the world's open highway, that every State is free to deal with her, and that the spirit of modern civilisation will breathe upon her.

div.head: EMPIRE IN THE EAST.
div.p: THE EMPIRE IN THE EAST.

The Indian Empire, as we now know it, is also one of the creations of the nineteenth century. An entirely new system of government has been able, at last, to fill the native populations with the con- viction that justice will be done to them and their interests properly cared for under the developing and improving Imperial spirit, and has begun, also, to fill large masses of the native populations with 3 desire to be identified with the new work, and to feel proud of India's place in the Empire. No one who has read history needs to be told that the conquest of India was not always effected by means which were likely to win the allegiance of the native princes and peoples. Little more than midway in the century's course the great Indian Mutiny broke out, which threatened, for a while, to interrupt the whole work of British settlement. There can be no doubt that some of the native rulers and populations had grievances to complain of, and that their national traditions and sentiments, as well as their religious feelings, had sometimes been carelessly or wantonly disregarded by the rulers sent out from England. -Moreover, it cannot be doubted that the events of the Crimean war had some share in arousing the temper among native princes and peoples which brought on the Indian Mutiny—the Indian Rebellion as it might mere properly be called. The Crimean war was undertaken by England, France, Turkey and Sardinia in order to prevent the encroachments of Russia in the south-eastern parts of Europe. What the native princes and populations of India saw, as the campaign went on, was that it took the whole united strength of those four Powers to force Russia into terms of submission, and the con- elusion arrived at in the native mind was that as England could not do the work herself, and even with the assistance of France, Turkey, and Sardinia found it a hard piece of work to accomplish, the reason must be that England was falling off in strength, and was no longer to be dreaded as a master, or relied upon as an efficient protector. No chapters in the world's history are full of more thrilling scenes than those which were enacted dur- ing that Indian Rebellion. The generation which was living and reading; newspapers then could not forget the events, terrible in their tragedy, often sublime in their illustrations of human heroism and patience, which were brought day after day to the knowledge of the civilised world. England was never better served by her Generals and her soldiers than during that epoch of severest strain. The brave, wise, and humane policy Of the Viceroy, Lord Canning, son of George Canning, was criticised severely at the time by some censors in India and at home, but it vindicated itself in the end. The rebellion was suppressed at last, and one of the results of the whole crisis was the extinction of the East India Company, and the transfer of India to the sole control of the Sovereign and Parliament of Great Britain and Ireland. Some lessons were taught by the outbreak, and by the sacrifices made for its suppression, which had their effect on the policy subsequently pursued in the goyernment of India. The main object of Indian rule ever since has been to bring the populations of India into a genuine allegiance towards the Imperial system, to make them feel that they were sure of just and equal treatment, and that whatever advantages the Empire opened to the career of any other of its subjects was open also and equally to every native of India. No doubt there have been mistakes and blunders and shortcomings, here and there, in the carrying out of this great work, but It is only common justice to say that the main. object of the work is such as I have described it, and that its beneficent effect is felt, more and more, every day throughout the great Indian peninsula. Educated natives of Indie,have represented English constituents in the House of Commons, the Civil Service and the Bar of England have given a career to men of Indian birth, and it may well be hoped that the Englishman is destined to hold his loved India—again I quote the words of Kinglake—by other and better means than the strength of a con- quering Power. THE UNIFICATION OF THE AMERICAN STATES.

The nineteenth century would be memorable in the history of the world if it had no other title to such memory than the fact that it saw the develop- ment of what used to be called the revolted North American colonies into the great Republic of the United States. The American Republic is now in population commerce, trade, shipping, industrial science, and political influence one of the greatest States in the civilised world. The Republic has not attained this position without serious internal struggle, and even convulsion. The great Civil War between the Northern and Southern States, which broke out forty years ago, was a strife so long and so fierce that it seemed to outer observers at one time to threaten the disruption of the Republic. The Northern States, however, triumphed at last, after a sacrifice of life and wealth not exceeded in its proportions during ,modern history, and a wise and forbearing policy on the part of the conquerhy- States brought enemies back into friendship, aim established not merely the unity, but the union of the Republic. With the close of the war came the end of the distracting slavery question, so far as North America was concerned, and the United States were left free to pursue their career of prosperity and civilisation undisturbed by that one element of dis- union and of danger which had been their most serious trouble since the Declaration of Independ- ence. The United States have, for the greater part of their history, enjoyed a perfect immunity from the risks and troubles of war. /n the early part of the century Great Britain and the United States were drawn into a dispute about England's claim to maintain the right of search, a tradition, in fact, of the old days when the States were still colonies. The dispute led to a war. It may be safely said that the best intellects in political life on both sides of the water were utterly opposed to the idea of making such a dispute a subject for arbitration of battle, but the obstinacy of the Sovereign on this side, and the excitement of certain politicians on the other, prevailed over wiser and calmer counsels, and a war broke out. Peace was soon restored, seeing that neither country had much heart in the war, and a settlement was agreed upon, which may be fairly , described as an understanding that England was 'never again to raise her claim, and that nothing more was to be said upon the subject. Since then the United States have had a little war with Mexico, and that struggle with Spain which ended so quickly .a few years ago. It should be added, as a fact of sonic historical importance, that both the war with Mexico and the war with Spat( were undertaken in opposition to the opinions of many most enlightened Arneric,ans,who maintained, and still maintain, that the policy of the Republic ought to be the policy laid down by George Washington—the principle of absolute non-inter- vention in the affairs of foreign States.

div.head: GREATER BRITAIN'.
div.p: GREATER BRITAIN'.

The century has seen a remarkable and a most auspicious change in the relations of Canada to the British Empire: Down to the opening of Queen Victoria's reign the population& nt.Upper and Lower Canada—in other words, the populations mainly of French or of-English extraction—had been like two hostile encampwnts, while the only sentiment common to both'fts' the sentiment of hostility to the home Government at Westminster. Early in the present reign this latter feeling 'displayed itself in actual rebellion, and one o£ the first duties forced

on the Governmett of the youa Queen was the subjection of the rebellious Canadian provinces. The Government then sent out a man of genius. Lord Durham, entrusted with almost absolute powers for the work of pacification, and Lord Durham devised for Canada a system of legislative self-government which haraleen completed by the formation of what is now tta Dominion of Canada. Absolute content, devoted loyalty to the Crown and the Imperial system, and a steadily increasing pros- perity have been the results of Lord Durham's policy. The Australasian colonies have grown from what was chiefly regarded in England as a conveniently remote settlement for convicts into one of the most prosperous and promising parts of the British Empire. Art Act of Parliament passed in the last year of the century crowned the work by creating the Australian Commonwealth, and thus doing for the Australasian colonies what had already been a one for the provinces of Canada.

div.head: OTHER NATIONS.
div.p: OTHER NATIONS.

The century has done little for China, the oldest of the old, and much for Japan, the newest of the new, in Asiatic civilisation. Nor has it gre': 'ly changed the condition of the South American Sta es, although it may be .safely assumed that these States have a great future before them, if climate, soil, natural resources, and quick-witted populations can be regarded as safe evidences on which to found antici- pations of coming prosperity.

div.head: PROGRESS, OF BRITAIN.
div.p: THE PROGRESS, OF BRITAIN.

I have purposely left the story of the British islands for the -last in my rapid survey of the cen- tury's dealings with most of the countries in the world. No national convulsion, no revolutionary changes, disturbed the progress of these islands dur- ing the period which it is my task to survey. The reign of Queen Victoria occupies nearly three parts of that time, and during all these long years the safety of the Empire at home has never been threatened by any foreign foe. No English states- man during that time has ever had to confront the risks and dangers which must more than once have pressed upon the mind of a Thiers, a Cavour, or a Bismarck. England, as we have seen, has been engaged in foreign wars, and has had to deal with many a crisis in the north-west provinces of Asia, !Ty Hindustan, in Egypt, and in South Africa. 91 home her career has been one of unbroken and fteadily growing prosperity. The century has been Inv her a period of pacific reform and of political Azavancement. It saw the establishment of a f,enuine system of representative government, it saw the birth and the growth of the great philanthropic reforms which protect the labour of the poor and the young from the old-time tyranny of unscrupulous taskmasters, it saw the passing of the Act which put an end to slavery in the colonies, the abolition of flogging in the army and the navy, and the removal of the odious disqualifications and penalties which were once inflicted upon any manner of dissent from the established religion of the State. The century began with the earnest efforts of a few advanced reformers to obtain something like a system of national education for the populations of these Wands. Some thirty years before the century's close these efforts were, at last, crowned with success, and we have now in England a system of popular education such as some other countries in Europe had been enjoying for many long generations. The whole financial system of the country has likewise undergone a complete change. The doctrines of Free-trade which were commonly held to be the notions of mere theorists, so lately even as the days of Adam Smith, were adopted by Sir Robert Peel as the inspiring principle of practical legislation. Let it be added that the cOntury has seen in the present reigning Sovereign the first really constitutional Monarch whom England has ever known.

div.head: CENTURY OF INTELLECTUAL GREATNESS.
div.p: A CENTURY OF INTELLECTUAL GREATNESS.

The • century has undoubtedly been one of "ntelleetual greatness. "Man's unconquerable suind," to adopt the language of Wordsworth, has 2rad its victories and its triumphs in every field. There have been great statesmen who were also great orators, like Canning, and Peel, and Gladstone, like Thiers, and Gambetta, and Castelar. There have been great statesmen who were not orators, like Cavour and Bismarck. In literature England has had two great epochs during the century. First came the time which is repre- sented by Scott, Byron, Wordsworth, Shelley, and Keats, and Lamb and Sydney Smith, and then the later times which we associate with the names of Dickens and Thackeray, pf Tennyson and Browning, of Macaulay and Grote, Thomas Carlyle and John Stuart Mill, of Freeman, Froudef. and Green, of Charlotte Bronte and George Eliot, of Matthew Arnold, Swinburne, Rossetti, Morris, and many others almost equally celebrated. France has had George Sand and Victor Hugo, the elder and the younger Dumas, Balzac, Alfred de Musset, and a whole host of poets, novelists, and writers of history. The Scandinavian populations have developed quite a literature of their own both in romance and in the drama, and while, in the earlier part of the century, no story-teller could have been more universally popular than Hans Christian Andersen, in its latter half no living dramatist was nearly so much admired, so much imitated, so much criticised, so much denounced, and so much the subject of world-wide discussion as Henrik Ibsen. Russia, too, has developed a literature of aer own during the century, and has compelled the .vhole civilised world to give attention to it, to -"cognise and to welcome it. No names are more samous in living literature than those of Tolstoi I,nd Tourguenief, and these two great novelists have already schools of followers and of imitators wherever romance is associated with a purpose and a mission. Germany has not of late years done much in literature to set the world wondering, but we must remember that some of Schiller's and many of Goethe's finest works, and all of Heine's poems belong to the achievements of the Nineteenth Century. The whole story of America's literature may be said to belong to the present century. It tells us of Washington Irving, of Bryant, Emerson, Wendell Holmes, Longfellow, Hawthorne, Edgar Poe, Lowell, Walt Whitman, Bret Harte; but the great creative genius of American literature is yet to come.
'DIE NEWSPAPER.

The cheap and popular newspaper as we know it to-day is entirely the creation of the Nineteenth Century. The daily journal which brings home to every household an account of. yesterday's occur- rences at the other side of the globe, the weekly paper with its profuse illustrations wrought by the hands of genuine artists, the popular magazines with their contributions by literary men and women of established reputation, the independent daily criticism of statesmen and Parliaments, the full reports of representative assemblies and of public meetings—all these are among the latest products of civilisation, and the forethought of them could never have entered into the mind of Samuel John- ...in, of George Washington, or even of Talleyrand.
MUSIC AND THE ARTS.

m the worlds of literature and art we do not look 4hr progressive development. No one expects that growth of human thought and culture can bring out greater sculptors than those who lived and wrought in the age of Pericles, nobler architecture than that of the Parthenon and the Temple of Theseus, or the Gothic cathedrals of Christianised Europe. We do not look for greater poets than Homer and Virgil, Shakspere, Dante, and Goethe. But in painting, sculpture, music, and the dramatic arts, although yot perhaps in architecture, the nineteenth century hks fairly held its own. The world, it may safely be declared, has never seen greater actors than Edmund Kean and Rachel, and, in our own days, Sarah Bernhardt, and in music Germany has created an entirely new school of her own.

div.head: CENTURY OF THOUGHT.
div.p: A CENTURY OF THOUGHT.

There have been great thinkers in the nineteenth century who may well be placed in the highest intellectual rank, Auguste Comte, and Darwin, and Herbert Spencer. The century has had preachers and divines of the highest order, men whose fame belongs not merelly to any one sect or denomination, but is recognised by all the civilised world. The Century has been gloriously endowed with soldiers, and, indeed, heroes in every field of human self- sacrifice, with missionaries and martyrs. It has been the century especially of organised and scientific exploring. The work of philanthropy, too, has been organised until it has become a recognised institution of civilisation. Even the horrors of the batAlefield have been mitigated by the spirit of the 4u.l.ern time, and the noble work of the Geneva tonvention has done something at least to counter- vilance the destructive business of modern military wcAence on the battlefield. I have already called attention, to the fact that an attempt has once again been 'Wide by one of the greatest European Sovereigns for the establishment of a tribunal before which disputing States might submit their con- troversy to peaceful arbitration. Nothing very decisive has yet come of the recent Congress held at ;The Hague for this purpose, but it is something, at least, to know that the ruling powers of the civilised world were willing to entertain the idea, and united in expressing a' hope that it may before long become a practical reality. The common intelligence of the world is undoubtedly tending that way. The closing years of the century saw the settlement, by peaceful arbitration, of a dispute between England and the United States on what is known as the Venezuela question, which might, at an earlier date, have been referred by these two Powers, as a matter of course, to the arbitrament of war. It has been asserted that civilisation has but two paths of progress—first the path of conquest, and then the path of peace. War, so runs the argument, must first hew down the obstacles and clear the way, in order that the-new path may be opened along which peace is to have its march and its mission. Without Lnquiring too closely into the gerwral accuracy of this somewhat metaphorical declaration, it may reasonably be admitted that civilisation has generally begun its way by conquest. Perhaps there is all the better reason to hope that the other part of the

doctrine may a-46 liavd its Watt-ant of ttutn. zr this be so we may, without indulging in any vain dreamings, admit to otr minds the confident hope that the nineteenth century, with its intellect and its culture, its travel and its science, its broaden- ing philanthropy, and its better understanding of economic truths, must have done something to supersede the work of conquest and to oven the way tor the work of reeace.

div.head: SERIOUS PRONOUNCEMENT.
div.p: A SERIOUS PRONOUNCEMENT.

div.head: IMPOSTERS AT THE HOSPITALS
div.p: IMPOSTERS AT THE HOSPITALS

in an article on the "London" Hospital. appearing itt the Christmas number of the "Windsor Magazine," the writer gives- some curious instances of the übiquitous humbug who from time to time manages to gain ad- mission. "The receiving-room doctors have to be on the alert to guard against the hospital imposter, the man or woman who simulates serious illness in order to get the food and shelter and kindness of the sick ward. As may be guessed, it is no easy task to deceive strawd doctors about one's personal condition, but it has been done. There was one man, quite a finished artist in his way, who knew all about obscure nervous diseases. Be had a glass eye, which helped his deception, and he simu- lated every symptom of the complaints he professed to suffer from in a way that took in even great experts. For some time this man lived going from hospital to hospital, and remaining some time in each, but they all found him out at last. Another man, still more Clever was brought in one day apparently suffering from acute, peritonitis. His story waS that be had fallen from & railway signal pole and injured himself. His abdomen was swollen, the thermometer showed his temperature to be dangerously high, and be was apparently in great danger. He was at once taken up to a special ward,hot fomentations were continually applied, and he was given nothing but hourly teaspoonfuls of soda and milk as food. The sister in charge of the ward fancied she recognised the man as one who had been in some time before fcr the same complaint. The old case was hunted up.the man who came in before had the same symptoms, which he said were caused in the same way; and certain signs on his body made it clear that he and the present patient were one. On being told this, the doctors carefully re-examined the man, taking precau- tions to prevent any " faking " of symptoms. The temperature, which a little while before had registered 103deg8., went down to normal, the abdominal swellings ' suddenly abated, ano the pretence was revealed. This man had deceived numbers of hospitals, and doctors are still puzzled to account for the manner in which he was able to so perfectly assume all the symptoms of one of the most dangerous complaints."

IT will be well for the A Seasonable Caution. good - natured at this

season of the year to re- frain from treating people to intoxicating drinks. If service has been rendered let it be paid for in the current coin of the realm, leaving the recipient free to do what he likes with it. Many men pre- fer this form of benevolence, but do not like to claim it, because it has a greedy look. If, how- ever, the persons treating were to reflect a little they would see that if many people followed their example the result must be unfortunate to the recipient, whose sobriety would be imperilled. There is hardly enough of this consideration in the world, and its increase is hindered by current maxims and a desire to avoid being classed with the churlish, who object to all intoxicants. Good wishes and benevolence are quite consistent with discrimination, however, and when we reflect upon the harm done it this season by a too free indulg- ence in intoxicating liquors it is incumbent upon us all to determine that, as far as we are concerned, no want of thought shall add to it. LORD ROBERTS gave an excellent hint to the patriotic about mis- taken kindness to returned soldiers. The idea ought to be written up in letters of gold every. where. Our beneficence ought not to take a form injurious to the welfare of another. What we give should not tend to demoralisation. It should not begin a series of acts likely to incapacitate the recipient. There are better forms of charity or giving. We are not restricted to one form only, and the practice has grown upon us to the present extent because we have followed a bad custom, and feared to start a new method. The interest of dependents and workmen should be regarded by the giver as well as the expression of good-will. The intention is to do something season- able, and drink, alas! is always in season. Many a mau has found. himself overcome at Christmas- time for the first time in his life. We are not now speaking of what happens in a man's home or amongst his friends, but of what happens to per- sons whose duty calls them from house to house. and who are often treated to drink at almost every house they call at. Such men can hardly refuse what is offered, and therefore the wrong is in offering it. There are many ways of getting over the difficulty. A smart house-wife will find out whether there are children to whom an accept- able present cf small Christmas dainties or fruits will be welcome. There is always the money present, if present there must be, and though it may ultimately go in drink, the responsibility must then rest upon the person spending it. More attention ought to be paid to these small points. They are part of the altruism which conduces to a sound civilised state. They are indications of fraternity that lead to improvement in morals. Am Imy brother's keeper? it is asked. The reply is, you need not be your brother's stumbling- block and tempter. The wise householder will dwell upon these little matters, and decide to run the risk of misapprehension at first.. No moral lecturing is needed, only discrimination in how to give and what is given.
Lord HOPETOLIN seems to

A False Step. have made a false step at starting. To have invited a man to form a ministry who has failed to do so is a blunder, however it may be excused. The Colonial Office ought to have known better, if Lord HOPETOUN did not. But it is held that the Colonial Office had reasons of its own for preferring Sir W LYNE to Mr BARTON. The latter was the chief leader and spokesman of Federal interests when the deputation from Australia was in this country negotiating with Mr CHAMBERLAIN respecting the Commonwealth Bill. He had to try conclusions with the Colonial Secretary on several occasions, and he worsted him over Clause 5, upon which so much ingenuity was spent, and so much time wasted. For these reasons, so people say in this country, Mr BARTON was rebuffed. In Australia it must be acknowledged, every thoughtful politician was astonished at the opening move, becauso it looked so excessively personal. We are now informed that New South Wales, as the senior colony, was con- stitutionally entitled to have its Premier selected as Premier of the Federal Ministry. The idea does not greatly impress us. Sir W LYNE has not been always an advocate of Federa- tion, and he has not done half the work for it that Mr BARTON has ,done. To select the wrong man out of deference to some musty constitutional idea was a mistake. Events luxe proved it to be so. Sir W LYNE has been unable to form a Ministry, and Mr BARTON is now engaged in the task, with every prospect of success. We are learning by painful experience that colonial opinion is a real thing, and that it must be consulted. If we want to have a strong and representative Ministry, we must go the right way to work, and Lord HOPE.. TOUN began in the wrong way. Mr BARTON when in ,London was dead against the constitutional lawyer theory of what should be done. His tussles with Mr CHAMBERLAIN were on this very point. Once more the point has occasioned difficulty, and Mr CHAMBERLAIN has been beaten, as he deserved to be. Politicians and Imperialists will have every confidence in Mr BARTON. 110 is a man of broad views, keen common souse,

He is admired and respected ir: Australia, where is high qualties are well-known, and hopes are now brighter that he is undertaking to form the first Federal Govern- ment in Australia, with himself at the head. Any Ministry that was regarded as weak, or a mere makeshift,or suspected of being formed in response to hints from 'Downing-street, would have had a troubled career before it, and would have dashed the bright hopes of the Federalists at starting. This would have been a great calamity. We want everything to work smoothly and happily, and all personal frictim to be avoided. Australia is enter- ing upon a brilliant career as a Commonwealth,and any cloud of suspicion or uncertainty would have darkened its opening days. We believe that cloud has now been dispersed, and we shall feel that Mr. BAuToN is in his right place, and that Australian and Imperial interests will be safe in his hands. Any other feeling would have been most untimely and unfortunate.

One gratifying circumstance about the close of the year 1900 is that it leaves the population of our workhouses, there is good reason to suppose, at the lowest level which has been attained for several years. The details on which accurate figures for the whole of the country could be cal- culated are not at the moment available, but there can be little doubt that the fact is as stated. Even in London, where the number of the indoor poor has shown such an invincible tenhncy to rise, there is a distinct check in the movement, the total now standing something like two hundred below what it did at the beginning. Unfortu- nately, much of this improvement is clearly due to accidental causes. Labour has been in demand throughout the summer, trade has been brisk, and the winter one of unusual mildness. How rash it ‘Avould‘ be to argue a genn ral improvement in pauperism from a decline of a few hundreds in ten of thousands appears on the reflection that a week of keen frost—almost, indeed, a passing snowstorm—would, in most cases, have sufficed to fill up the ranks of workhouse inmates. It must be confessed that, for all the improved humanity in workhouse treatment. the increased interest in the condition of the poor, and other signs not without encouragement, the close of the year 1900 and of the century leaves the great pro- blem yet unsolved. And there can be little doubt that before many years a solution will be keenly looked for. If workhouse inmates continue to increase slightly in numbers, the expense of the administration of the Poor Law increases enor- mously,and will soon impose on the ratepayer that burden which, as human nature is constituted, 'proves after all the strongest incentive to reform.

Within the next few weeks the Income-tax papers will tell in secret what no tradesman has cared to acknowledge openly—the shrink- age of business through the war. The great shipping agents and those ammunition factories which still remain in the hands of private companies have done very well—" it is an ill wind that blows no one any good " ; but, for tile most part, the tale has been all the other way. The fiction that the war helps the news- papers has been exploded, the fact being that except in . rare instances, the expense of a special war service is greater than the increase in the profits. The milliners, especially those in London who rely for their dividends on the • caprices of luxury, have suffered considerably.; but firms which have a general trade do not appear to have felt the shortening of money. . Neither has it touched the hotels to the extent that might have been expected, the explanation being that people have been reluctant to, drop their hospitality while it could have a cheering effect. The theatres, for the same reason, • have kept up their records ; and the seaside resorts of .our coasts have done even better than usual, because it was unpleasant in all the circumstances, to go on the Continent for a holiday. But the jewellers and the dealers in heavy, costly furni— ture, and many other things not necessary to life or recreation, will have to report a decline in their trade; while individually, among the direct sufferers from the war, there will be many instances of a sad falling away of means of support. It is to hoped that before the year is out the reproach of a C.I.V. being in want of employment will be effaced. That Ps a scandal which can be easily and promptly remedied.

No large employer can afford to disregard trades unions or ignore the right of the working- men to combine for their own interests, and this fact is emphasised by the report on trades unions issued by the Board of Trade last week During the eight years over which the statistics given oi:tend the membership of British trade unions has increased by 20 per cent—from 1,503,232 in 1892 to I,BOPIB last year. The addi- tional members last year numbered just over 153,000, 0r.9 per cent increase upon the previous year. An, increasing consolidation is also shown, for while the membership kas steadily grown, the , number of unions has decreased from 1,310 to 1,292 during last year owing to the amalgama- tion of a number of smaller organisations into larger and .ctronger societies. Altogether trade unionism is ig.st now in a very flourishing condi- tion and is undoubtedly a force in the land which cannot be dep,,p6ed. Some day such men as Lord Yenrhyn will cwaken to this fact.

Warrington-made electricity is now an accom- plished fact pent to everyone, though the tall .standards which are dotted up and down the tprincipal streets still lack their " 41111 of light." ..Alderman Monkc. was some weeks ago committed to a promise that electric light would be available in the shops for Christmas, and it is to the credit .of himself and the electricity department that the promise has beewfulfilled. All the customers are not yet supplied, but the work of connect- ing them with the mains is rapidly proceeding and there will not be many, we believe, who will lia.ve fair occasion to grumble in the oCourse of a day cr two. The task of coming up to time has been no easy one, for the dynamo plant is still incomplete and likely to be for some weeks,so that street-lighting must not.be expected just yet. The electricity already supplied is highly satisfactory as *.lsaraple,and gives some indication of tile immense improvement which will be effected when the light- ing scheme is complete.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

If, as Thc,dore Hook once observed, there is a something in the closing days of the year that ordinarily predisposes mankind to take a sombre view of matters. and be grave, how much more so is it in the closing days of the century? The very thought seams calculated to produce on the gayest temperament" a lovely dejection of spirits, and a delightful slow fever." To say nothing of the mists and the wind, the sleets and the oid, and those Christmas bills which even to a solvent debtor are admittedly not good for the digestion, the fact of this being not only the end of the year, but the fin de sieele, gives us pause, and is enough to disturb the nerves of anyone of ordinary sv.sceptibility. The end of anything, no matter what, is ypical of mortality, and the bare sound .31 that dreary monosyllable " last" is -„-pr,gnant with dismal forebt.ding. The end kit trie year is but the completion of a solar revolu- tion, but the close of a century bears so special a :resemblance to the ending of life, that there is no resisting the suggestion. At such a juncture of couri,e, our thoughts turn zaturally to those of our countrymen who are still in South Africa fighting our battles, and we cannot but admire their superb courage and endurance, while sincerely regretting the new:lefty for their continued detention at this sea-on on the scene of action. The, present, in short, is a fitting opportunity for the modern Schopen. bailer to air his pessimism,by pointing with cynical i-ntisfaction to the fact that despite our being " cratiam,d with the best doctrines till we quite o'erflow." and of the many sermons we hive heard from the words "Peace on earth, wodwill towards men," we are no nearer the realization of that ideal than we were nineteen

hundred years ago. But this is only apparently true. Our, pessimist is, at the best, but a poor philosopher, and very superficial. The nineteenth has been a glorious century in many of its phmes. In literature the works of Ruskin, of Carlyle, of Tennyson, of Wordsworth, and of Browning, and Dickens and Thackeray and George Eliot, have. added a lustre which time cannot dim. As in litera- ture, so also in religion; the teachings of the clergy and of the ministers of various denominations are characterized by a broad humanitarianism, the key note of which is as the best of the nineteenth cen- tury literature, and roughly expressive of the preachings and teachings of Christ. In the world of politics, also, there may be seen forces in opera- tion which, even amid the clash of arms and the din of battle, bid the people hope and believe that a better time will yet dawn for the whole of man- kind, when war shall be numbered with the gigantic evils of the past, and when "man to man, the wide world o'er, shall brothers be."

Christmas is said on good authority to be the time when the farmer's harvest closes, and it may be easily conceived that there are many items that go to make up the harvest. Cheddar cheese is one which this year proves to be much better than for several seasons past. The make is reported as of good quality, the quantity fair, and prices low. The one feature of harvest the farmer does not appreciate, is that for bacon pigs. When he com- pares the price of these with that of barley meal, he begins to feel that some one else has harvested his profits. It is generally the lordly pheasant that upsets the poultry market, but this year is an exception. The price of poultry has not suffered much, and the question was whether that ot beef would keep up. There is said to have been an absence in some places of really high-class beef for the festive season, the reason being that as soon as a farmer had a good animal on the grass the butcher viral after it. The farmer is not usually stand-offish in such matters, because of the prospect of . dear cake, hence a bargain is soon struck. Altogether, the farmer's prospects, like those of many others, were brighter this season than last, and, there is reason to believe, have been fairly realised.

It is still a stubborn fact that the Prevention of Corruption Bill does not look with a friendly eye upon the time-honoured Christmas-hx. The man or woman who gives a Christmas-box may mean it only as a pretty compliment, fitting to the season, and the recipient may accept it in that spirit, and be altogether uninfluenced by any commercial con- sideration. But, if it be so, say the authors of the Bill, why have any secrecy about it? But that is the point. It would seem that what has first to be decided is the question of motive on the part of a giver, and this may sometimes, but not always, be adjudged by the nature and value of the gift. It is a vexed question, and in some respects and to a certain extent, will ever remain so ; but it will never do to abolish the Christmas-tloz entirely, or to disallow employers occasionally to acknowledge ' the special merits and deserts of their employes by giving a Christmas or other offering,in the spirit of goodwill, for instance, which should ever prevail at Yuletide.

So the " distressful country " is to be saved by its peat and, if so, there are parts of England, as in the Lake District,and about Dartmoor, that may be similarly benefited. It is reported that for the past twelve years Herr Zschorner, of Vienna, has been investigating the properties of peat, with a ' view to making use of it in industrial processes, and the results attained are remarkable, From them, the question would appear to be, not what you can make, but what cannot be made from this , wonderful and plentiful product. For instance, a building is exhibited in which everything, from the carpet on the floor to the curtains at the windows and the paper on the walls, was made from peat. It is alleged that the fibres of the remains of the reeds and grasses of which peat is composed, have, of course, their original physical and chemical characters changed, but that the fibrous structure remains intact, while the fibres are vary durable, elastic, and are non-conductors of heat. Fabrics woven from them have the toughness of linen, with the warmth of wool. There is no textile fabric that cannot be woven from these fibres. Blankets and other coverings used for horses and cattle are found in use to excel in warmth and cleanliness. Paper of several qualities has been made, and the uses to which peat fibre has already been applied indicate possibilities that may render the peat bogs of Ireland a really valuable addition to the resources especially of Ireland. -

There is sympathy just now with railway com- pany shareholders as having been doubly hard hit by the inflated price of coal during the year. The companies being the largest consumers of fuel in the Kingdom, the greatincrease in the cost has told most •heavily on them. The receipts of the four principal railways in England have increased, but the expenditure through the cause mentioned has been so much higher that it is reported there will be a drop of one per cent. in the dividends of the North Eastern, the London and North-Westeru, the Midland, and the Great Western. Thus it is seen that those interested are not only paying more for their individual consumption, but also as share- holders in the railways.

Some of the provincial Boards of Guardians:are not only dissatisfied with the Local Government Board's new dietary order for the workhouses, but persist in making sarcastic allusions to the general Local Government authority and rule. In refer- ence to the order in question there appears to be some room for coniplaint, and if the Boards would confine" their remarks thereto, their criticisms would be the more effective. The changes proposed are clearly designed to effect a saving, but it seems questionable whether this would be secured in some of the workhouses. There are so many curious defects in the order that an effort is being made to persuade the central authority to allow it to become optional. It has been pointed out at Bridgnorth, for instance, that the order permitted the Board to give adults broth and bread and butter, but children could not have bread and butter; they must have broth and bread and cheese. An" optional" order, however, would be of little avail.

CONCERT AT THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOLROOM.

' The above place was fiiled with an appreciative audience on Wednesday evening, when Mr 11 liiliidge presided. The Rev W A Eyre gave an in- teresting address, after which the following pro- gramme was gone through :—Pianoforte solo, Mr Ball;II song' Star of Bethlehem " Mr Shingler ; mandoline solo, Miss Temperley ; song " The angels of old," Miss Clare ; violin solo, Mr J C Stubbs; recitation "Trouble in the Amen corner," Miss Saunders,; song, "Holy City," Miss Lloyd; concertina solo, Mr Clarke; song, Mr Stubbs : pianoforte solo, Mr Beckett, ; song, Miss Lloyd; song, "The young Royalist," Mr Hopwood ; violin solo, Mr J C Stubbs; song, "The New Kingdom," Miss Clare ; recitation, " Aunt Tabitha, ' Miss Saunders; song, Mr Shingler ; reading, Mr Rictlardson ; song, Mr Clare. The able accompanist was Mr LI Ball. FIRE IN PARKER-STREET, RUNCORN.

About 4-15 on Thursday the fire alarm sounded ominously over Runcorn, and filled the people of the district with deep concern. On inquiry, how- ever, it was ascertained that a fire had originated in the house of Mr Walter Mather, Parker-street, Runcorn. It appears that there was a baby in bed, and in attendance upon him was a b3y of ten,f.er years. This little fellow, however, it is supposed indulged in the game of playing with matches with the result that the rug and bed were, set fire to. The alarm spread and before any sarioua injury had been done to the child, it was bravely rescued by some of the neighbours. By about 4.30 the Runcorn Fire Brig- ade and a posse of police under Superintendent Hicks were upon the scene, and the fire checked in a very short time. The damage is not very exten- sive, but the baby has susfained slight burns.

RUNCORN NOT ES [By a Correspondent]. The Runorn Fire Brigade are always with us and it is a good job too. But, whilst-it is a pleasure for Runcorn to pride itself on having one of the oldest and worthiest of superintendents in Mr Robert Wright, surely even that worthy gentleman will agree with me when I say it is rather a deplorable fact that the brigade is not better equipped. It may be argued that it i 3 sufficient for our needs. Yet, have we suffiuient for the needs of the future? And to this question I rather think the negatioa is the reply.

The poor fellow, whose wife was imprisoned for a month, for assaulting him with a cruet--itand,was getting the " omplimants of the season" with a vengeance. One hears enough of missions to the " blacks," but surely the disclosures of an ordinary English Police Court, should h 3 the means of estab- lishing a mission to the blackguard. But whether that comes about or not, there is room for a Prison Gate Mission at Runcorn Toough the Runcorn people are not bad themselves, there is a floating population which I " hae ma do3ts about," and it would he as well to save the native from the foreign infidel.

Christmas, the last of the century, has gone, and but a remembrance of it remains. Some have spent it happily, others have gathered together round the vacant chair.bat all save the roysterer who spent is "lathe jug "—his own pet slang for the prison— have been impressed by the mildness of the season's climatic condition. How is to be accounted for? Is the Gulf stream becoming larger and more effi- cient as an Island warmer? Are the season's chat:lying ? Or has the jingoism of the past twelve months had anything to do with it? These are questions which correspondents are troubling me with. If anyone knows the answers please write, but not all at once please!

THE RUNC.)RN WAR FUND, The fund now totals up to .E 1,704 2s 31. ST MICHAEL'S CHURCH DIVIDING CLUB. The annual report of this club just issued shows that the receipts amounted to £139 15s 81; of which £l2O 3s was paid in subscriptions, and £7 53 61 in levies. The amount paid in sick benefits was £43; management expenses, £3 lie; dividend (97 members at 18s 7d each), £9O 2s 7a; leaving a balance in hand of 2s id. RUNCORN POLICE COURT. At this court on Thursday, the. presiding magis- trates were Messrs J Ockleston and W Handley.— Patrick Bones, of Pool-lane, was fined 8c and bound over for six months in ..g5, for assaulting his wife. —John Hoyle, Ca wdor-street, for being drunk and disorderly in Ashridge-street, was fiaed 14s 61; Samuel Johnson, Speakman-street, for being drunk and disorderly on Christmas morning was fined 103 61 and costs. ST THOMAS' CHARITY, HA.LTON. The annual distribution of St 'Peonies' charity took place at the Girls' School. Halton, on Friday, There were present -.—Messrs C L Evans, Thomas Wright (district councillor), J S Jeacock (overseer) and J Gamon. The amount distributed was lUs each to 49 of the oldest and most deserving persons residing in the parish, whose ages ranged from 60 to 82 years. The volumes were a •,vry good selection. The collec- tors who received prizes are --Bessie Coventry, E Simkin, C Povah,A.da Burrow, L Widders,P Coven- try, Flossie Dodd, L Venables, Annie Gerard, A M Norman, Sydney Leach, Alfred Lea, 11 Unsworth, A E Eden, D Norman, ti Handing, F Halding, G A Wilton.

THE ALLEGED BRUTAL ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Vriday, before Mr W Handley, 11nry Spencer and Fanny Spencer, husband end wife, were brought up on remand caarged with inflicting grievous bodily harm on Samuel Lamb, at Runcorn, on the .27th November.— Superintendent Pearson stated that the prosecutor was still unable to put in an appearance, and he applied for a further remand until Thursday, the 27th inst. The application was granted, and pris- oners were again liberated on bail, themselves in £lO oach, and one surety each in the same amount. A VIRAGO AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn. Police Court on Saturday. before Messrs G L Davies (in the chair) and W Handley Ann Kelly, a well-known character, hailing from Manchester, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street, on Friday night.—P.C. Wilding stated that at 11 p.m. on Friday he was called to a disturbance in Stone-street, and on pro- ceeding there he found the primer drunk, and be- having in a disgusting manner. Re requested her to go away, but she reiused, and addressed the most filthy language to him. He attempted to take her into custody, and she then became very violent. She struck at a Mrs Twigg with the open pocket knife produced, but the latter evaded the blow,and took the knife from her. Witness at length got assistance and brought the prisoner to the police station. Mrs Twig g corrohorated. Prisoner, who is no stranger to the police court, was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour. THE D.tvaaroN OF WIDNES PARISH. We learn that the division of Widnes Parish, in accordance with the scheme agreed upon a short time ago, will take effect early in the new year. The present Vicar Rev C E Stocks, M.A., will, by his own request, be assigned to the charge of the older portion of the parish, to be known as ,the Parish of St Mary's and the Rev R E Corlett, the senior curate, will be appointed to the vicarage of St Paul's. The scheme for the division of the parish which has been found to be very unwieldy and a most difficult one for any single incumbent, was set on foot by the offer of Mr Sutton Timmis to give £5,000 for the endowment of Sc Paul's and the building of a vicarage. The Ecclesiastical Commis- sioners were approached,and ic was found that they were willingto comply with the condition of Mr. Timmis' offer that they should contribute a similar sum to be paid by six yearly instalments over a period of six years until the whole ot the sum had been exhausted. The parishioners, at a meeting held in September, also agreed to raise ~..El,OOO towards the endowment fund in six years. THE ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON THE BRIDGEWATER CA NAL.—CAS IC WIT HDR AWN. Messrs J Ockleston and William Handley, sat at the Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday morning, when Henry and Fanny Spencer, boat people, were again charged with assaulting and inflicting griev- ous bodily harm upon Samuel Lamb, an aged boat- man. The facts of the case, it will be remembered, were that when near the Alma Works, Runcorn,the boats were passing when an altercation took place between the parties, which resulted in the Spencers boarding the defendant's boat and assaulting him so viciously as to cause injuries to his pelvis of a very serious nature. —Defendant now stated that the Spencers had agreed to compensate him sufficiently and to pay all the medical expenses.—The Bench, therefore allowed the ease to be withdrawn. A VIOLENT WOMAN SENT TO PRISON. Rose Ann Scott, wife of Benjamin Scott, marine store dealer, Heath-road, Runcorn, was on Thurs- day brought before Messrs J Ocklegton and W Handley, at the Runcorn Police Court,charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with assaulting her husband, about L3O the same morning.—R vid- {ince was given of the woman's violence whilst in drink. She had thrown a glass and several articles at her husband, and wound up a frolick- 80Me half hour by hitting her beloved just a trifle too affectionately on the head with a cruet. —The husband testified to being in bodily fear of her, and independent evidence of drunkennesss was given.—For being drunk and disorderley a fine of 10a. and Is. costs was imposed, and for the assault two months imprisonment without the option of a fine.—Later the Bench mitigated the imprisonment to one month with hard labour. "MAN AT THE WHEEL" TONTINE SOCIETY. The members of the above society have just held their annual meeting and dividend distribution. After meeting all claims there remained a dividend of 19s each for 55 members. The officers re-elected ware William Moston, president; James Hulse, secretary; Henry Le-Couteur, treesurer, Ira With- ington and John Scott, etewaris ; James Sadler and J Virithington, trustees; Messrs Price, Smith, Pea- cock, Pritchard, Sadler and Banner were elected committee. When the business was cleared the annual repast was provided for the members by the kind generosity of sir and Mrs Boardman, the host and hostess of the "Man at the wheel." It was well served and ample justice was the result. Song stud sentiment were the order of the evening. The singing of the "National Anthem " brought a most convivial evening to a close. CHRISTMAS AT RUNCORN. At the whole of the works in Runcorn operations were stopped at noon on Saturday ;until Thursday, morning, the men thus being given a very sub- stantial holiday. Labour at- the docks al.o ceased at Christmas Day and part of Bank Holiday. Throughout the Christmas holidays the weather was more spring-like than wintry, and the sun shone brightly on both Christmas Day and 'Bank Holiday, though there was some rain at night. On Christmas Day the town presented an even more quiet appearance than on a Sunday and as the rail- way station was closed those people wishing to visit friends at a distance had to walk across the bridge to Widnes. Thera were special services in the morning at several of the churches and chapels. At St, Paul's Wesleyan Chapel the Rev. J. Osborne assisted to conduct the service and an appropriate sermon was preached by the Res. Alfred Wells. Special music was rendered. At the Primitive Methodist Chapel, the Rev Mr. Ayre delivered a sermon to a good congregation. In the evening an entertainment was held. The services at the Parish Church ware also well attended. A carol service in the evening was much enjoyed. The I inmates of Dutton Workhouse had their usual treat. I The rooms had been brightly decorated and the dinner of roast beef and plum pudding &c, gave great pleasure to the inmates. The adults were also supplied with tobacco and the young people with fruit and sweets.

Mr, COPLEY : lam not as random a fool as you are. Proceeiieg, he said it had been thouent by their union that the best course to take was to allow him to reply to a letter Signed by Mr Dale,a Copy of which had appeared in several papers. He (Mr Copley) had been charged with sensing a threatening letter to Messrs Crosfield, He emphatically denied it, and it was the firsr, tone that he had ever been charged with such an an ion. He always tried to write to heads of firms or managers as respectfully as he possibly could, and expected to have that respect shown to him in return. He was very often complimented by employers upon the courteous mintier in which he conducted both his correspondence and interviews with them. He thought that it would be no digrace either to the directors of Mors Crosfield or to Dr Markel to discuss the grievances with him. Coming to Mr Dale's letter, Mr Copley did not deny that tbe men agreed to bring all their grievances directly before the managers or directors by a deputation from the men affected. That action was taken by members of their Union in all their grievances with any employers, and it was only after the en had been refused the concessions asked for that they asked the Union's officials to intervene. That method had been adopted at Messrs Crosfield'a. The men did not agree to never allow, under any circum- stences,their Union's officials to ask for better conditions if their direct application was refused. A large majority of employers that they had to deal with, recognised the Union's officials, and allowed them to approach the firms and discuss in a friendly manner all questions of dispute which affected their members. That was all they asked Messrs Crosfield to do. (Hear. hear.) It seemed to be a geneaal opinion amongst the public that these men received a week's holiday each year without any restrictions. From Mr Dale'. letter he t3ok it that before the men were allowed the holiday they must be satisfied with the conditious which the firm thought fit to impose, but if they were dissatisfied no holidays were allowed. What was the good of a holiday if a man could not afford to enjoy it? Referring to point No lin Mr Dale's letter, which said that the men expressed themselves satisfied with the existing conditions of °lmplement, he (Mr. Copley) asked should these men apply for improved conditions if they were satisfied with the conditions then in existence. In answer to point 2, :he men stetel that they did not ex- press regret at the course taken by the Union. Point 3, he had previously dealt with, but again he repeated that the men did not agree net to allow an official of their Union to plead on their behalf. What were the conditions these men had asked for? They were not exorbitant, and were not the conditions which some of their members were working under. When comparing wages and hours they always took a firm that was en- gaged in the same industry. They were asking that these men should receive the same wages, and work the same number of hours which obtained at Messrs. Lever Bros. That' firm was always willing to receive the Union officials to plead on behalf of their members, and all theynasked for was that the men at Messrs. Crosfield's shoald be granted similar privileges. (Applause.) The CereoleetaN intimated that questions could be asked, but they must be on points meetioned in Mr Copley's address. Mr DALE said he must express his sorrow that he was not allowed to speak because he could have combated the statements which had been made. The public of Warrington was being gulled and misted by the state- ments made by Mr Cepley. Mr Copley stated that one of the men had approached the engineer and be had refused to allow them to see Dr Markel on the eight hours question. lie wild like to know the man's name. Mr COPLEY : Do you think it would be to the advant- age of this man to give his name when we know what the firm has done in the past. You know what they did with the soap-cutters. (Loud applause.) NeMr. NEWALL : I am the engineer at Messrs. Croefield's wo ks. 1 should like to know the man's name because I haven't the slightest recollection of it. (Hear, hear.) Mr. COPLEY said if he had used Mr. Newell's name he . _

had made a mistake; the maa ap,oro.a-c-Red-idr Dale and ask.d for certain conditions. The request was refused point blank ; Mr Date t.lling tho men that so far as they were concerned he knew they would not get what they asked.
A VOICE : Are these boilermln of Messrs. Crosfield and Song better paid than any o:hor bpiler men in War- rington ?

Mr. COPLEY : We don't go outside thP particu'ar in dustry t) qu)to rates of wagw. The rates of we asked for wer9 the same as Messrs Lever Bros. had been payine, since 1892. Mr. DALE : I should like to ask Mr Copley where is the:analogy between Messrs,Leyer's and M ,ssrs Crosfields workmen?

TIV! CHAIRMAN said the angwer had already been given ; the some kind of work was carrie lon at both places. Mr. DALE : Soap making is only ono item of manu- facture at Messrs Crosfield's works. Many of these tolermen, are employed in raising steam only. Mr. COPLEY : The only analogy that exists boiiween the two firms so far as I am aware is that Messrs. L,ver',a may be manufacturing more soap than Messrs. Crosfeld's. Mr. NIGHTINGALE : Dl the men at Messrs. Crosfield's do a similar kind of work to those at Messrs. Lev3r Bros ?

Mr. COPLEY : If there is any difference, the work is liahter at Messrs Lever Bros. than at Messrs Crosfie!ds. The following resolution was then put to the meeting : —That this meeting still endorses the action of the men in refusing to sign the agreement and condemns the action of Messrs. Crosfield's in locking them out. f tic CHAIRMAN said the resolution was carried by 85 votes to 8. A vote of thanks to the Chairman having been passed the meeting termins.t,-.1.
