div.head: SHIP CANAL DANGERS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SHIP CANAL DANGERS AT RUNCORN.
Inquest and Verdict.

On Saturday afternoon Mr. E A White, deputy coroner held an inquest at the Runcorn Police Court, touching the circumstances attending the death of Philip Ferris, 48 years of age, wno was drowned in the Ship Canal, Runcorn, on Friday night. Mr. Charles Dutton was foreman of the jury. Robert Archer, seaman, at present residing in Bruns- wick-street, Runcorn, eave evidence as to assisting to recover the body at 10 30 that (Saturday) morning front the Snip Canal at the Old Quay yard. Thomas Lawrence Grady, 90, Trafford-road, Salford, stated that he was fireman on board the steamboat Fidoe. Deceased was Philip Ferris, also a fireman on the same neat. He told witness he lived at Liver- pool. Witness, the deceased and another man left Mrs. Marsh's public-house shortly before eleven o'clock on Friday evening to go back to their boat at the Old Quay lay-by. They lost their way, and deceased, who was ahead of them, suddenly cried out" Oh, I'm in ! can you save me ?" They could not see him, but they immediately detached a mooring rope from a barge and threw it towards him. The deceased, however, did not appear to grasp it, and they heard no more of nim.—ln reply to the Coroner, the witness said they left the boat about 6.30 to come into Runcorn. They went to Mrs. Marsh's public-house and had some beer. Deceased had four pints of beer, and witness had the same quantity, less one glass. When they left the public-house deceased went into a shop and purchased an evening paper. Wit- ness was perfectly sober, and to the best of his belief Ideceased was also sober.

Captain Heasley, who represented the Bain Canal Company, explained that the proper way to the steam boat would be round by the swing bridge. It was a considerabl, distance round there, and as a matter of kindness and courtesy his (the captain's) boat brought the men across the canal, and put them off at the Old Quay yard to save them going by the bridge. It was a perfectly safe arrangement if it was worked properly. These men had takea the short cut as a matter of convenience.

Inspector Hicks gall the men were in a stranze place, which was not lit up like docks, and they lost their way. The spot whore the fatality occurred was the engine fitters yard, 0!d Quay. James Gaskell, dock gateman, in the employ of the Ship Canal Company, t the Old Quay locks, gave evi- dence as to ferrying some men across the canal from the steamboat Fidoe, about six eclock on Friday night! Captain Heasley here explained that the Fidoe came down the canal and tied up opposite the Old Quay yard. The witness Gaskell brought the men across the canal in a small boat.

The witness, continuing, said if the men had re- turned he should havo ferried them back to the boat. The last witness Grady came and informed him that his mate had fallen into the canal, and witness made a search for him, but failed to recover the body. Snrgeant Gregory deposed to assisting to find the body at the Oil Quay yard. There was a bruise over the left es'e which witness concluded had been caused through deceased falling down the wall. He searched the cloth- ing, and found an evening paper, some twist tobacco, a clay pipe, and a pouch. Thera was no money.—The jury returned a verdict that the man was accidentally drowned.

div.head: WIDNES MAN FOUND DROWNPID ON CHRISTMAS DAY.
div.p: WIDNES MAN FOUND DROWNPID ON CHRISTMAS DAY.

On Wednesday, at the Widnes Accident Hospital, an inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, touch- ing the death of William Cardiff, who was found drowned on th 3 b,ach of the Mersey on the morning of Christmas Day oppsite the West Bank Promenade, Widnes.

Timothy Larkin stated that the deceased was his uncle by marriage. He lived at Appleton Lodge, Apple- ton, and was a chemical labourer. He was about 56 years of age. Toomas Ridley, Royal Britannia Hotel, Terrace-road, state] that the deceased came into the house on Christmas Eve about 6.40. He left about 7.30. Witness had a tontine club and Cardiff Came to draw his dividend. He paid five women before be paid him. He was perfectly sober. Witness gave him £1 and a two- shilling piece. When he paid him, deceased wanted witness to take a shilling out for a drink but he refused. After shaking hands with witness he wished him a " Happy new year." That was the last time he saw him allve.—By the Coroner : It would be easy for deceased to slip in the river accidentally. Ho mug have gone down to the end of the rail for something, and then stumbled. It was a sloping beach, and ran into the water. The tide came right up against it. If the man stumbled he would go right down to the bottom, and then the tide would wash over him. He must have been stugned after falling over, and could not help himself. George Satton deposed to finding the body at eight o'clock on the sea shore of the river Mersey, opposite the West Bank Promenade. He went and told the police. PC. Evans said that, in consequence of information received he went to the river and found the man Cardiff quite dead. In answer to the foreman, witness said there were no marks of violence on the body. The Coroner,in suggesting a verdict ( f found drowned said it appeared to be a straightforward case. The man was evidently sober when it happened. It was a danger- ous place, and people wen; in the habit of going there. The man was shortsighted, and all the circumstances combined took away any suspicion from the ease. The jury concurred and returned a veriict accord- ingly.

div.head: CHRISTMAS arVIARRINGTON
div.p: CHRISTMAS arVIARRINGTON
Celebrations at the Workhouse.

Every effort was mad:' Joy the Guardians and officials of the Warrington Union to enable the inmates of the Workhouse to spend a happy Christmas. For the nonce the inmates were asked to forget their poverty ad to spend Christmas as m-m.rily together as in the more pros- perous days of earlier years. There we re 591 inmates altogether, and without exception they spent an enjoy- able Christmastide. Christmas day commenced with carol singing in the wards by the inmates and at 7.30 breakfast was served. Divine service was conductel at 9.30 a.m. by the Chaplain, the Rev E R Tarbuck. Miss , Ward efficiently presided at the organ and toe singing was considerably improved by the welcome assistance of a few choir boys from Ss Paul's Church. The Roman Catholic inmates went out to mass as usual. At noon the inmates assembled in the dining hall for the custom- ary Christmas dinner of roast beef and plum pudding with beer. The cooking of the viands was in the hands of Mr Powell, and this work had been carried out with skill. The dining hall had been very skilfully decorated with evergreens by the male inmates under the direction of Mr Dobson, the pulpit coming in for special attention at the bands of Mrs Dobson. The dinner was tnaroughly enjoyed,the wants of the inmates being carefully looked atter by Mr and Mrs Ward (master and matron), Miss Ward, Mr Shearer, Mr Fern- side, and others. Amongst the visitors present were the Mayor and Mayoress and Miss Roberts. Mrs Clay, and Messrs A J Jolley (chairman of the Board), Hickman, Thornton, Malkin, Alfred Jolley, and Asticroft (guar- dians), and Alderman Shaw Green, the Rays E R Tar- buck (chaplain) and C a 11 icken, and Mesas J W Hay. ward, Elijah Place George Holford, J Bailey, and Frank Hickman.

tilrace having been sung, the ChriAmas meal was commenced. A number of visitors proceeded to visit the Infirmary where every effort was made, as usual, to minister to the comforts and happiness of the sick. The nurses did all in their power with that purpose in view. The decoration of the Co )3 in each institution abund- antly testified to the festive character of the se.sson. The usual Christmas dinner was provided for the 150 sick patients who were waited upon by the nurses. Fruit, Chris mas cards, tobacco (with toys for the children), were distributed during the day all over the institutions.

At tle conclusion of the dinner in the Dining Hall, the Master remarked that the dinner had consisted of roast beef and plum pudding, with beer, mineral waters, and c3ffeo. A box of oranges and a barrel of apples would be distributed later on in the day with tobacco and snuff. Vie Guardinns had also provided toys for the children, and they were indebted for evergreens to Mrs Broadbent and Messrs J Crosfield, F Monks, T 13 Lyon and Robert Garnett ;while gifts had been received from, Mr and Mrs 0 wensof Latchford;tobacco from Mr Samuel Wakefield, toys from the Mayoress, Christmas cards from Miss Dakin, and Mr Herbert Naylor and Mrs Broad- bent. Half a barrel of stout had been received from Mrs Brundrett (which the Guardians had accepted, and which would probably be consumed on New Year's Day.) El 3 asked the inmates to accord a hearty vote of thanks to the Guardians for their liberality and to the officers for preparing the meal. He could not take much credit to himself, for all the officers had been very busy indeed. (Applause). Threa hearty cheers were then given for the Guardians on the initiative of Mr Ward. The inmates then gave three cheers for the Master and Matron.

Mr A J JOLLEY in acknowledging the compliment on behalf of the Bard, wished the inmates a happy Christ- mas and a happy New Year. He expressed the pl as ure it afforded the Guardians to promote the welfare of all coanected with the house. He hoped the rest of the day would be spent in a happy manner; if it was not it would not be the fault of the Guardians. (Hear, hear). Mr HICKMAN in the course of a speech said he was pleased to see the inmates looking so happy and joyous. The officers had had a hard time in preparing the dinner, and he hoped the inmates would appreciate their services. (Applause). The Guardians desired to do the beat they could for tee inmates, and when he said that he spoke the sentiments of all the members of the Board. He would conclude with an old toast " May the present moment be the worst in our lives." (ipplause). The MAYOR having been called upon to make a few remarks, thanked the inmates for the cordial reception given to himself and his wife. He could not refrain from ' expressing his admiration at the way the room was de- corated last year, and was under the impression that it was the work of the officials But he was wrong,and he had been told it was entirely the work of the inmates own hands. It did them infinite credit, and there must , be some amongst them with natural and artistic talent He was pleased to see it exercised in that agreeable I way. This life was a big battla, from beginning to end, and acme poople fell by the wry. Everyone could not be conqueror in the battle of life. They might say:" It is all very well for people like you, who seem to have done tolerably well,to speak to those who have not done quite so well," but they must believe hiss when he said mat if a man or woman had been tolerably successful In this worl I he or she ought to have a more abun- dant sympathy with chore who had fallen by the way. (Applause.) When he looked around the room and saw some he had known years ago in better circumstances ha could not help feeling a con- siderable amount of regret that they had not been quite so successful as oneself. But, in spite of all these mis- fortunes, they were receiving a considerable amount of cemfort and consideration. They all had the sympathy of the Guardians and officers. He did not think he was exaggerating when he said that the Board of Guardians was never so efficient or determined to do its duty to the ratepayers on the one hand and the unfortunate inmates on the other. (Applause). He hoped they would all live to see the dawn of the new century, and that they would all do the best they could to make those about them as happy as possible. To use the words of an old writer : " May good digestion wait on appetite, and health on both."_ (Applause.)

The Cr:am thanked the Mayor and Mayoress for their presence, and alluding to the supply of beer to the inmates, said it had been seriously debated by the Guardians whether it should be supplied or not this year However, it had been supplied, and he hoped, speaking as an abs luel life teetotaler.that there would be even less cause this year on the part of the Guardians to re- gret having made them the allowance. The Rev C H HOCKEN. in the course of his remarks, commented on his visit to the new infirmary. He was in London not long ago, and had an opportunity of visit- ing seine of the hospitils there, and he could testify that the arrangements here for the poor and th:se in need were better than what he saw ire the great me- tropolis. (Applause.) He hoped they would do what they could to make each other happy, and that God's blessing would continually abide with them. (Applause.) Tea was supp'ied at 5 30 and at seven a concert was given in the Dining Hall by Mr Brobbin and family, who have given their services in this respect for the past eight years. Altogether a most enjoyable Christmas was spent in every part of the house.

div.head: CHRISTMAS SERVICES.
div.p: CHRISTMAS SERVICES.
Wycliffe Sunday School.

A special Christmas service in connection with the above Sunday school was held in the schoolroom on Sunday afternoon. There was a good attendance of scholars. Special Chri6trn3s hymo3 were sung by the scholars. Mr. Gauld delivered a very appropriate Christmas address. A solo was renclered by Mrs. Gleave, as also was a cornet solo by Mr. F. Ford. The Wycliffe Orchestra also assisted in the service.

div.head: Wycliffe Congregational Church.
div.p: Wycliffe Congregational Church.

A large congregation assembled in Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church on Sunday evening on the occasion of the annual Christmas choral service. The devotional part of the service wasconducted by Mr Tnomas Hawthorn. An augumente I choir under the conductorship o! Mr NV H Payton, Nlus Bac contributed items from " Tne Messiah." Mr Frank Hickman presided at the organ, and the instrumental part of 7 the srvice was enriched by the assistance of a small orhestra composed of the following :—First violins,Mr R H Pearson, Mr W Brown second violins, Mr A Knowles, Mr T Wallington, and Miss B BoucLier; 'cello,Mr H Bond;Bass,Mr H Whitfield. The service opened with the heßutiful overture from "The Messiah" and Mr A Griffiths sang the recit and air "Comfort ye" and "Every Valley," in which his pure toned tenor voice was heard to great advantage. Mr W H Wallington very feelingly ren- dered the recits and airs. "Thus saith the Lord," " For behold darkness," and "Why do the Natioas " the latter especially being well sung, Mrs. REi Pearson was in capital voice and contributed three solos in an excellent manner. Her singing of the air "I know that my Redeemer" was eycenotionally fine and was greatly ap- preciated.Misi E Knowles was also very successful in her singing of the recit. " Frl3 shall feed His flock." Mrs A E Longshaw (contralto) sang with taste and skill the recit " Behold a Virgin " and the air " 0 Taoa that tellest." The choir sang a number of choruses with pre- cision and ability, concluding with the" Hallelujah " chorus which was given with great power. A coltection was taken on behalf of the choir funds.

div.head: Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel.
div.p: Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel.

Special Christmas Services were held in the above place of worship on Sunday. There wag a good congre- gation in the morning when the preacher was Mr William Light. The choir creditably rendered the Christmas AntLems "Oh cime all ye faithful" (Arranizel by Novello) and "Christians awake" (Maunder) and several Christmas hymns were heartily sung. The chapel was completely filled in the evening, when selections from Handel's oratorio " The Messiah " were given by an augmented choir. The preacher was the Rev R J Cook, who based an appropriate discourse on Isaiah ix. 6. Tho musical portion of the service was a complete success and reflected infinite credit upon Mr Walter Brougn, who conducted. The choruses" And the Glory of the Lord," "For unto us," "Behold the Lamb of God," " All we like sheep," "Lift up your heads," and "Hallelujah chorus," were admirably rendered and were listeued to with pleasure by the con-

gregation. The tenor solos "Comfort ye," " Every Valley" and "But thou did'st not leave" were ex. pressively mug by Mr. Levi Richardson, and Mrs. H. Cotterell was heard to advantage in " 0 thou that ' tellest " and the plaintive air" He was despised." The duet" He shall feed His flock " received capital treat. ment at the hands Of Mrs. Cotterell and Miss Morrell. Mr. T. Breugh presii4ed at the organ with his usual ability.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON

CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, NEWTON. On Sunday afternoon, a muAcal service, embrac- ing selections from "The Messiah," was given in the above church by the Congregational choir augmented by members of other choirs, to the number of GO. Mr A Knight conducted, and Mr S Tiring officiated at the organ. The following items were given :—Recit "Comfort ye"; Air "Every valley shall be exalted" Mr G Kidd ;chorus " And the Glory"; Air and chorus "0 thou that tellest " Miss Mather and choir; Recit " For behold darkness," Air" The people that walk in darkness," Mr J White; chorus "For unto us," Pastoral symphony, organ; Air "lie was despised'' Miss Mather; chorus " All we like sheep"; Air "But thou clid'et not leave"; Mr J Sepliton ; chorus " Lift up your heads"; solo, "Star of Bethlehem," Miss Nellie Mather; chorus, " Hallelujah " ; air, " I know that my Redeemer livetli," Miss Corlett ; chorus, " Worthy is the Lamb." The service was given in an excellent manner, and the items were marked by capital taste.

div.p: LIBERAL POLITICS IN 1900.
BY AUGUSTINE BIIIDELL, Q.C.

In the teeth of warnings from able editors who know the wants of the newspaper-reading public, I cling, in my anwial review of Liberal politics, to the Statute Book. Ministers come and go, are shifted from one department to another, make a little fame or incur a little infamy for some brief season—it redly matters not; but the Statutes remain, to be interpreted by the judges, and obeyed (when not merely permissive) by the people. Therefore, if you seek to estimate the real force of Liberalism in politics during any given year, the Statute Book should first be examined. I therefore propose before I am done tt, take my readers through 63 and 64 of good Queen Victoria. It is, no doubt, only too true that the great achievement of her Majesty's Ministers during the year is not writ large in any public general statute, though allusions to it, direct or indirect, may be discovered in the Statute Book. For example, the second Act of the last session of the late Parliament is intituled "An Act to provide for raising money for the present war in South Africa " ; whilst the 15th section of the Finance Act reeks of blood- shed--" Income-tax for the year beginning on the 6th of April. 1900, shall be charged at the rate of one shilling."

The war with the two South African Re- publics is the groat political event of the year. Mr. Chamberlain, with a jauntiness some may admire, has referred to this war as a possible feather in his cap—a blood- bedraggled feather; but there it is, and if the Colonial Secretary likes this style of decoration nobody is likely to dispute his right to wear it.
The connection between the war and Liberal politics and the effect of the war upon the Liberal party are subjects ill fitted for a place in a brief summary.

The situation was from the first one of immense difficulty. Would Lord Salisbury, at the instigation of Mr. Chamberlain—and it may be of Sir Alfred Milner—have dared to make war upon the Transvaal Republic on such cases belli as he possessed at the date of Mr. Kruger's ultimatum ? Personally, I am per,uaded he would not. Great timidity reigned in Tory breasts as to the likely popularity of such a war; nor was sympathy with the South African Republic confined to the Liberal party. Sir Alfred Milner himself had no confidence that he had the home Government behind him. The two Presidents, by declaring war and publishing their ultimatum, changed the whole situation. What, then, became the true attitude to be assumed by those—whether Liberals, Tories, or non-partisans—who thought Mr. Chamber- lain's diplomacy had been provocative, and believed that the horrors of war might have been honourably avoided P In times of great agitation, when men's minds move in masses and are swayed by a common 'passion, it behoves those who seek to stem the tide to make it as plain as a pikestaff what they would have their country do. The opponents of the war never made this plain, either in the House of Commons or in the country. They deprecated the war, but they did not oppose it. They could have done so by making and supporting a motion that, on the withdrawal of the enemy's forces from the Queen's territories, the points in dispute, or some of them (naming them), should be re- ferred t arbitration. Neither this nor any- thing like it was done, and, consequently, thri only thing left was to prosecute the war •li the utmost vigour to the bitter end. Thus from the first annexation was ine7itable, unless we were defeated.

My own conviction is that the anti-war feeling in the country was far stronger than it ever had a chance of proving itself to be. On the ether hand, the terrible disasters of the early campaign, the obvious unprepared- ness of the War Office, the apparent 'light- heartedness of Ministers, the hostility of Europe—and in no small measure of the United States of America—made the actual military situation one of a gravity to which we were quite unused; whilst the pluck and good feeling of our common soldiers, and the enthusiasm and assistance of our Colonies, aroused in men's breasts emotions and senti- ments which transcended and overflowed the usual boundaries of party. It was no longer a question of Outlanders and their grievances, but of our existence as a great colonising nation. So, at least, men thought. In the midst of this seething cauldron the Liberal party in the House of Commons, honestly divided in opinion as to whom the war was imputable, was reduced to practical impotency, and cut an almost ridiculous figure. The General Election of 1900, so far from destroying the Liberal party, as Mr. Chamber- lain fondly hoped it would do, has greatly strengthened it, as time will show. In Great Britain there went to the polls two million one hundred and five thousand five hundred and eighteen Liberal voters, as against two million four hundred and twenty-eight thousand four hundred and ninety-two Tories. When Ireland is added the 'Tory majority is reduced •to one hundred and twenty-two thousand nine hundred and seventy-four. The odd man is indeed well represented in the new House of Commons; but he is only the odd man.
And now, having rid my bosom of all this perilous matter, I take up 63 and 64 of the Queen and examine its slender contents in search for Liberal politics. I do not find much.

The first place must be given to the Work- meit's Compensation Act, 1900, which extends the benefits of the Act of 1897 to workmen in agriculture. The hasty adoption by the Government of this private member's measure was intensely comic. The whole House shook with laughter as the bill galloped through. And yet there are those who deny the utility of the franchise. If Hodge had no vote 63 and 64 Victoria, chapter 22,w0u1d never have been. The Tories were quite good-humoured over it. Their conversion, they admitted, was sudden; but it was genuine. The House of Lords recognised the situation—the counties would be jeoptirdised if the bill did not pass; so pass it did. CrtILD LABOUR IN MINES.
This little measure was introduced by Sir Charles Dilke, and met with no opposition. No boy under thirteen can, after the Ist of next July, be employed underground.
RAILWAY ACCIDENTS PREVENTION.

This is an excellent measure, provided always the administration of the law is placed in vigorous hands, for it enables the Board of Trade to make rules as to dangerous railway work; and after allowing a reasonable time and establishing a procedure for making objections to any proposed rules the Act provides that such rules, when made, shall be binding on the railway companies under penalties. THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT, 1900. This timid but, so far as it goes, useful measure seeks to secure for the tenant com- pensation for the improvements specified in

div.head: EXAMINER, FRI!) AN, DECEMBER 28, 1900. THE FRItIE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRI!) AN, DECEMBER 28, 1900. THE FRItIE CHURCHES.

the first schedule. Sixteen in number of these specified improvements cannot be compensated for unless the previous consent of the landlord to their making had been obtained. The Act also contains arbitration clauses. Measures of this kind are merely the seguelea of past controversies. A time will soon come when a step forward will be taken. Our whole Land Law needs radical reform.

THE HOUSING Or THE WORKING CLASSES ACT. This little Act has a tincture of Liberalism about it, since it authorises certain public authorities to acquire lodging houses for the working classes outside their districts, and endeavours to simplify procedure as to the acquisition of land. lam not able to discover any other dis- tinctly Liberal measures in the legislation of 1900, unless the Burial Act is entitled to a humble place. Nothing is more characteristic of an ecclesiastical Establishment than disputes over dead bodies and interment fees. Mr. Carvell Williams and Professor Jobb— Hebraist and Hellenist—met in conclave, and (so it is believed) settled the question. So may it be.
Two important Acts of a non-party character are to be found in 63 and 64 Victoria.
THE COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA ACT.

This interesting measure, though duly recorded in the Statute Book, camo to us "from the long wash of Australasian seas." The House of Commons had nothing to do with it. The fussiness of Mr. Chamberlain nearly wrecked it, awl a. good deal of the language used by the Colonial delegates who had the bill in charge was not suggestive of Willi respect; but wise counsels prevailed, and the Colonies got their bill practically as they drew it. It provides a written Constitu- tion for New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Queensland and Tasmania with power to add to their number. We are not familiar in this country with written Constitutions. Our own grew, and nobody knows at any given moment what its exact height or dimensions across the chest may be. Mr.Wbilter Bagehot's book is the only one much worth reading on the subject, and it is already out of date. A Constitution like ours has at least one great advantage—it saves us from the clumsiness of written language and the muddle-headedness of Parliamentary draftsmen. In the opinion of experts, the Australian Constitution is badly drafted; and it is never easy to alter a written Constitu- tion. The 128th section of the Constitution (which as a whole occupies eighteen closely printed pages) deals with alterations, and if this section is studied the difficulties of the process stand revealed. Everybody wishes well to the new Common- wealth. No nation is saved by its Constitu- tion, but a good Constitution is a great blessing. The Australian Constitution is a Radical one, placing the ultimate power in the hands of the people, who in Australia approach the settlement of political questions free from tin prejudices and prepossessions of the governing classes here at home. The drawing together of the Colonies and the Old Country, if it ever gets beyond the nebulous regions of sympathy and reaches the stage of a political union, will be the ending of that mixture of Landlordism and Church of Englandisra which still gives the flavour to and directs the course of so much of our home politics.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

div.head: CENSUS.
div.p: THE CENSUS.

On Sunday, the 31st of next March, we are to be numbered. The forty odd millions— mostly fools—who will be alive on the date aforesaid will be duly recorded, to the joy of statisticians, by a whole armyof enumerators, under the supervision of the Registrar-General and the Local Government Board. No doubt as the time approaches our ever-active Press will stimulate interest in population questions and increase their own circulations by offering small sums in cash to those of their readers who may guess with the greatest degree of accuracy the figures of Mr. Mantalini's " denmed total." It is too early to begin guessing yet. THE MONEY-LENDERS ACT.

I will conclude my review of the legislation of the year by referring to three more measures. The Money-Lenders Act enables County-court Judges and Judges of the High Court, when satisfied that a money-lender has charged his customer an excessive rate of interest, or piled on other charges to an excessive extent, so as to make the transaction in the opinion of the court harsh and un- conscionable, to set aside the original contract, and to make a fresh one for the parties. Making new contracts instead of the old ones is a task strong judges hate, but it is one in which weak judges take great delight. The Act contains a very admirable clause compelling professional money-lenders to register themselves and disclose their real names. Nobody can complain of being re- quired to carry on his business in his own name. Pious brewers and church-building distillers could not possibly object to seeing their honoured names over the grog-shops in thirsty neighbourhoods which, in real fact, belong to them.
THE COMPANIES ACT.

The Companies Act, 1900, is the last brave attempt of a never-discouraged Legislature to prevant the money of fools from finding its way into the pockets of those who are not fools. It makes company-promoting a some- what perilous pastime. So far good. Whether it will prevent smart fellows in the City, Lord Mayors and Baronets to be, from selling dear to the public what they bought cheap for themselves is doubtful. As a matter of fact, the public is not quite such a fool as some make out. They buy shares in questionable companies not to keep, but to sell again, and to sell very soon; and what chiefly interests them is not the genuineness of the concern, but its chances in the market of getting its shares quoted at a premium.

div.head: MINISTERIAL INCAPACITY.
div.p: MINISTERIAL INCAPACITY.

The only other measure worth a word is a little one-clause Act which he who rims may read. "The Uganda Railway Act, 1896, shall have effect as if £4,930,C00 was substituted for £3,000,000." Only 1:,1,930,000 out! Oh, wise Ministers! Nor is there the least reason to suppose we have the true figures yet. Could Cabinet Ministers be treated as bank directors sometimes are, one or two of them would be found closeted with their solicitors, who would tender them the advice to put their private securities into the names of their friends as quickly as possible. The sheer, downright incapacity of the men who manage the country's business is part of the only un- challengeable verdict of history. And yet we still retain a touching confidence in them, and cried out for a reconstruction of the Cabinet as if Lord Salisbury had at his disposal rows of men of proved intellect, capacity and foresight. His lordship has done his best to disabuse the public mind of so absurd a notion by sending two well-connected clerks to the heads of the two great spending departments of the nation, whilst employing his ablest available man of business in killing pigs. _
THE DIT.E*EIt SESSION

of the new Parliament was not illuminated by any Liberal principles and made no promises as to the future. r.l he Government is distinctly a weaker Government than it was before its reconstruction, and the dissatisfaction with it is widespread in the ranks of its nominal supporters. ___

div.head: WAR AND TAXATION.
div.p: WAR AND TAXATION.

In the meantime the unpcpularity of the war grows daily greater; many—probably a majority—of the officers and men who have come home are centres of disaffection. And, as times are not what they were in the matter of trade, the burdens of impending taxation loom largely in men's imaginations. It cannot be said that politically the century is making a good end. L BIBRELL

div.head: SIMULTANEOUS MISSION.
div.p: THE SIMULTANEOUS MISSION.

With the advent of the New Year the subject that fills the minds of most Free Churchmen is the simultaneous mission. The campaign starts in London on January 26. The Free Churches of the metropolis are divided into fifty-six districts, and fifty-four of these are engaging in the mission. Even the apathetic citizens of London will be stirred out of their lethargy by the campaign. All the arts of advertisement will be used. Notices of the mission will be displayed on all tramcars, omnibuses, and hoardings, as well as outside the Churches; and motor-cars, which are still such novelties that people stare hard at them, will thread the streets of London in all directions and announce to the busy crowds, by means of large placards, that e. r.!mr;t enterprise, in which they should be intimately concerned, is going forward.

div.head: PPESS AND THE MISSION.
div.p: THE PPESS AND THE MISSION.

The London newspapers, morning and evening, have devoted considerable attention to the .coming campaign. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, MA., who has worked indefatigably for the snoress f the enterprise in London, contri- butes n 7, interesting article on the mission to the January Free Churchman. Mr. Meyer reealls that the first suggestion of a simul- taneous mission for the whole country came f-orn the Rev. ThomaS Law, the Secretary of the National Free Church Council. The need for the mission, says Mr. Meyer, is obvious. "There is a conspicuous and growing decrease in average Church attendance. It is said, for instance, that in London the attendance at all the places of worship put together is as low as ton per cent."

div.head: DR. PARKER AT THE GUILDHALL.
div.p: DR. PARKER AT THE GUILDHALL.

Perhaps the most striking item in the London programme will be a sermon by Dr. Parker in the Guildhall to which the Mayors of all the metropolitan boroughs are invited. It is said that over yet has a sermon been preached within these famous walls. The lincrcring echoes of many mayoral banquPts will be startled and put to flight by the trumpet sound of the gospel. The day in which Dr. Pal kf...T warns and exhorts the merchants of the City of London in the Guildhall of the Corporation will justly be regarded as memorable in the history of the ancient City and of the Free Churches. Many of the most dis- tinguished Free Church ministers in the pro- vinces will take command in the London campaign, men like Dr. Fofsyth, Rev. J. H. Jewett, M.A., Gipsy Smith, Rev. John Mc_Neill; and Dr. Barrett.

div.head: MISSION HYMNAL AND TUNE-BOOK.
div.p: THE MISSION HYMNAL AND TUNE-BOOK.

The National Council, in view of the mission, has issued a special mission hymnal at one half- penny. In its preparation some of the most successful missionaries of the day rendered service by selecting hymns and sacred songs. In less than a month orders for more than two hundred and fifty thousand copies of this hymnal have been received, and we understand they are still pouring in in un- diminished volume. This would seem to be a record rate of sale for such a publication. And ten thousand copies of the hymnal and tune- book combined, which is published in either notation and in four editions (Is., is. 6d., es., and 2s. dd.) have also been sold. These facts are an indication of the hold that the project has taken upon the interest of the Churches.

div.head: ALDEnMAN GEORGE WHITE, M.P.
div.p: ALDEnMAN GEORGE WHITE, M.P.

Alderman George White, the new member for North-west Norfolk, is a deacon of St. Mary's Baptist Church, Norwich, and an accession to the ranks of Nonconformist M.P.'s of whom great things are expected. The Free Chvrc:ll Chronicle in a brief sketch of Mr. White says that twenty years ago when Norwich boasted of a local parliament of a thousand members he was the Prime Minister, while Mr. Massingrham, late editor of the Daily Chronicle, was his Chancellor of the Exchequer.
REV. R. J. CAMPBELL, B.A.

We are glad to hear that the popular young Brighton divine is now making good progress towards recovery. He has taken up part of his pulpit work, and is again regularlST contri- buting Christian Endeavour articles to the During his lonL:,, weary deten- tion at Shirley Mr. Campbell received much In dness from Free Churchmen at Southampton. He has expressed a wish that that town shall be the first in which he shall speak when suffi- ciently recovered to undertake outside work.

div.head: UNIQUE VOLUME OF SERMONS.
div.p: A UNIQUE VOLUME OF SERMONS.

Towards the end of January a volume of evangelistic sermons, to which the most eminent evan7eiists and leaders of the Free Churches will contribute, will be published by Rev. Thomas Law, of the Memorial Hall. Dr. Monro Gibson, Rev. F. W. Bourne, Dr. Townsend, the Rev. J. H. Jewett, M.A., the Rev. J. Tolefree Parr, Rev. G. Campbell Morgan, the Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., the Rev. H. Elvet Lewis, Dr Clifford, and others will supply discourses. It is quite safe to say that such a volume will possess a unique distinction. The book will be well printed and handsomely bound. A large sale is anticipated.

div.head: MILLION GUINEAS.
div.p: THE MILLION GUINEAS.

Mr. Price Hughes describes "the wealthier and more privileged members of our Church, as all those who have an income of at least -5:1000a year. One hundred thousand guineas are still nee(le:l to make Mr. Perks's great fund a triemphant success, and Mr Hughes holds that if "the wealthier and more privileged members have any adequate consciousness of what tiny owe to Christ, they will contribute at lea.t, (me-tenth of their income." Free Cluirelnnon, to whatever denomination they belong% earnestly desire the success of this ent,,,pri, and will/e.joice with the Wesleyans NVhell it is carried to victory.

div.head: LATE PRINCIPAL CAVE.
div.p: THE LATE PRINCIPAL CAVE.

The death of Dr. Cave, Principal of Hackney College, r,t the age of fifty-six, is a great loss to the Congregational body. For eighteen years 11,4 presided over his college with dignity and distinction. His rank :As a theological teacher, his gloat organising and business faculty, and his power as a preacher formed a combination of qualities for the position which it will be most difficult to replace. One of his special characteristics was the depth and fervour of his evangelical convictions. Dr Cave leaves a widow and one danahter

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. –
div.p: NORTHERN UNION. -
LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Warrington v. Oldham. Accident to Four Warrington Players.

The popular Oldham team paid a visit to the Wilders- pool enolo6ure on Saturday and succeeded by a narrow margin in gaining the much desired two points in the League Competition. Warrington were unfortun“te with their players from the outset and before the close ot the match no fewer than four players had to leave the field of hostilities owing to ii:jurtes. There was not as large an attecdance as was anticipated. A special train was run from Oldham, but not more than twenty enthusiasts followed their team to Warrington. There would Le about 6,000 spectators when the game com- menced. The following were the teams :

Warrington : Hallam, full buck; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Bockenir three-quarters; Burgess and Duckworth, ; Taylor, Boardman, Mere- weather, Eden, Scholtz.. ift, Andrews, and Fairhurst, forwards.

Oldham : Thomas, full back; Williams, S. Lees, Fletcher and Ike Tse icr. three-quarters; Lawton and A. Les, halt back, : Ferguscn, Mcffatt, Wilkinson, Teller. Wortnald, Eais, Williams and Taylor, Both teams were as selected, with the exception of Huzzey, whose place was taken by Ike Taylor. There was no response to Fergu 011'8 hick, and from the first scrummage Oldham got going., but Williams failed to clear, Fish not only tackling his man hut sending play back zo centre. Airreweather had to leave the field with an injured ankle, and Warrington continued the game with fourteen men. Twice the Oldham backs locked dangerous, but the tackling was accurate, and Warrington in response sent the ball along, Fish forcing Oldham back on their line. Thomas was floored near the posts, and relief came to Oldham when Burgess was penalised. Exchanges were witnessed between Thomas and Hallam, but premature tackling by Eden robbed Warrington of the advantage. A grand run and pass by Williams to Ellis saw Lherwood respond with a neat run, which lauded the locals once more agressive. War- rington missed a fine opening when Taylor made a poor pass to Fish, and profitieg by this let off, Oldham rushed the game to tbe centre. They were quickly repulsed by Hallam, who punted to Thomas, whose exchange CAM. pelled the game to be fought at neutral ground. Williams obliged with a brilliant run, and parted with the hail to Ella. the Warrington goal being suejected to a hot fusilaoe. Hallam defended cleverly, and a tackle of Williams when the Oldham wing man looked dangerous was applaud( d. Fish changed the venue and a lengthy period ot defensive work was indulged in by the Oldham hacks, Fletcher, Williams, Lawton and A Lees obliged with special efforts, but all to no purpose; the Warringtouians, despite their weakened force, com- pelled the gatne to be fought in Oldham quarters. Eden charged a kick by Thomas, but a chance was missed whilst Taylor made a poor pass to Fish when practically the main reposition had been overcome. A moment later the ball was worked over tbe coveted rut, and Thomas kicked dead whilst Fish was in the act of grounding the oval. Following this hard luck came a rapid incursion into the home quarters, and after a round of passing along the threeequarter line, Williams completed a movement by scoring a try which saw Oidham leading at the interval by three points. Warrington went away with great dash after the , interval despite the fact that they were one man short and Fish was checked on the line. The subsequent play saw disasters attend the locals, for in saving a rush at centre field Duckworth was hurt, it being afterwards ascertained that he had sustained a broken collar bone. Immediately after the half back's removal Williams scored another unimproved try, and Warrington suffered another misfortune, by Burgess also get- ting damaged and taking no further part in the match. With their depleted ranks, the Warriegtonians qruggled hard to make the most of a bad jab. The lime side were penalised in such a position that a goal was readily booked. The shot by Lees, however went astray and though Oldham came near scoring again, it was not to be. Boardman, one of the home forwards, retired a few minutes from the call of time. With only eleven men, the Warrington team struggled bard against the heavy odds and they succeeded in keeping their opponents at bay . Time was shortly afterwards called, the cessation of hostilities coming as a relief to spectator and players alike. Score :—Oldham two tries (six points),Warrington nil.

div.head: Runcorn again defeat Warrington.
div.p: Runcorn again defeat Warrington.

Runcorn added another to their long sequence of victories over the Warrington club, on Wednesday at Wilderspool. The home team still suitered from the absence of Burgess and Duckvorth (half backs) and Mereweather and Mcrrison, forwards. Hockenhall was also an absentee, his place being taken by Harris, who had played with the "A." team during the morning Runcorn brought a string team with them though Faulk- ner was missing from half-back. Ttv, weather was very pleasant, and the crowd rolled up in large numbers,fully 6,000 being present when Mr S Williams (Salford) took the following teams in hand. Warrington • Hallam, lull back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickensen and Harris, three-quartets; Scott and R Bate, hall-backs; Taylor, Boardman, -Eden, Scholtze, Swift. Fairhurst, Andrews and Cunningham; for waros. Runcorn : Houghton, full back; Wilkinson, H Jones. Warder and D Jonea, three-quarters; Jolley and Richardson, halves; Farmer, Walker, Lightfoot, Geyter, Tomlinson, Reece. Dixon and Hughes, forwards. Warrington lost ill • lass, Swift starting against the wind. Play seteed in the Fuccorn quarter, Bate and Fish testing Houghton early on. The veteran was safe and cleared with a huge punt. Warrington were soon back again and gct down to the corner where Richard- son relieved from the scrimmage,Hallam failing to bring off a difficult retch. Flarria picked up very martly from the loose and made a fine run only being brought 11 down a yard from the line. Warrington showed promis- ing form at this stage, forwards and backs playing very well together. Runcorn defended stubbornly and a free- I kick eventually enabled them to enter the home bait. ' Jolley secured from the scrimmage and smartly dropped a goal to the joy of the Runcorn section of the crowd. Excellent exchanges between the backs of both teams followed, and play once more settled at centre. Fish took a pass from Bate and beat all opposition until Houghton bowled him in touch. Warrington attacked. Eden grassing Jolley near the line, but the stay here was only brief. Runcorn got down by strong play, Jones in- tercepting Scott's pass and dribbling to the line, where Hallam saved finely. Jollry,Richardson ard Jones passed nicely, the latter being tackled by Fish when near.): over. A hot attack on the home line followedißichardson drop- ping at goal when be might have run in. Jolley made a desperate effort and lost the ball on the line, getting hurt at the same time. Isherwcod brought relief with a short run and punt, but D Jones was quickly back again Fish stay ing his progress at the critical time. Warring- tan rallied again, Isherwood running strongly to centre, where play ; emained until half-time, Runcorn then lead- ing by a goal to nil. Farmer restarted, Bate replying. The visitors got poste ssion and attacked. Warder intercepted and looked a certain scorer when he knocked the ball for- ward near the line. Jolley was hurt twice in a couple of minutes and had to retire for acme time. The hem; eters made great efforts to get on even terms but found an impregnaVe defence opposed to them. There was a lack ot judgment in kicking by the borne team, for Runcorn always;had ample time to reply. Houghton made a couple of mulls near the touch-line, but Warring- ton obtained little advantage: Just aa Jolley returned, [ Fish was laid out and prove of little further use during

div.head: THOMAS FODEN 84 CO, Cumberland Street, MANCHESTER.
div.p: THOMAS FODEN 84 CO, Cumberland Street, MANCHESTER.
the game. Even play followed neither side Eho win g any likelihood of scoring, and the final came with Runcorn winning by one goal (2 points) to nil.

Runcorn beat Wigan. At this match on Saturday there was nothing to com- plain of from a spectator's point of view, an throughout the hostilities were of a vigorous description, and were maintained at a brisk pace. Runcorn were evidently bent upon at once overwhelming their opponents by forward rushes well backed up by the three-quarters, and these tactics were imminently successful, as within the first few minutes Herbert Jonrs received a timely pass, and scampered over the Wiean line close to the posts, Jolley increasing the points by a well-directed goal kick. Then the Wiganers , resorted to similar tactics, their front rank swooping down the field, and the incursion led to Ruecorn being penalized near their "25 " line. The home lot had thus a capital opportunity of gaining something tangible but Nelson's effort was not attended with success. Play fluctuated considerably, but was never uninteresting. Houghton on the one side executing several capital saves when pressed whilst on the other side Nelson as often extricated the Wiganers when their position was menaced. Barr, the ex-Tyldesley three-quarter, who was making his debut with the home contingent, was subsequently conspicu- ous in a lengthy run along touch, and had only to face Houghton when ha parted with the leather, which was sent across the field, where Warder easily cleared. A second penalty kick fell to Wigan, and on this occasion Harris disappointed the crowd, whilst just before the interval the sturdy Prescott undertook to carry out a further penalty against the visitors, to whose gratifica- cation the ball was badly piloted to a position which could scarcely have been improved upon. The second moiety was entered cis at a ding-dong pace, hut the visitors were gradually forced back and cempelli d to act on the defensive. Houghtnn now appeared at his best, for when it seemed as thcugh tho home lot were bound to get through the nimb:e Sam came away smiling and repeatedly landed the leather into the Wigan half when surrounded by the home men. A pack was formed close to the Runcorn line, and it was thought that Eckersley had scraeobled over, but it war 'ruled that he was a few inches short—decidedly hard lines. Keeping up the pressure, the Itunccre 'sacks had all their work cut out, and Harris had another chance of lowering the visitors' goal from a penally, hut all to no purpose and the leather went wide. In their attacks Wigan lost heavily in consequence of want of cohesion among the backs, and several splendid chances of getting on level terms were thrown away by White. Towards the finish Jolley became exceedingly active 1 behind the pack, and scrummaging ensued in dangerous proximity to the Wigan posts, but no further scoring took place, and Runcorn had the satisfaction of notching a couple of lucky points in the table, the score reading : Runcorn, one goal one try Wigan, nothing. It was fortunate for W.gan that they had to resort to several important changes in their team at the last moment, the absence of Owen necessitating the inclusion of Peet as full-back, Ball going to the three-quarter position. These altera- tions, however, would not have earned much weight against Wig chances of success had White acquitted himself in like good style. But, as often as not, White WAS hopelessly at sea, and was practically a hindrance to his colleagues, with the result that during the greater portion of the game Barr was neglected. On repeated occasions the leather should have been transferred to Barr's wing, but the former Tyldesley player seldom got the opportunity of handling the ball. Eckerley,too,was anything but a success behind the "serum," and by this time it will be recognised that the position is not con- genial te him. Nelson was again the pick of the home backs, though what little fell to Barr was done in ex- tremely business-like fashion. Of the Runcorn repre- sentativss Houghton was a host in himself. He was certainly worth any four of the other players lumped together, for beyond the efforts of Jolley at half-back there was little brilliancy in their operations, and there is not" the slightest shadow of a doubt " that Runcorn would have gene under had they not had the assistance of the agile Houghton.
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. CUP.
Warrington Enter the Final,

Warrington and St. Helens met on the Wilderspool enclosure on Monday afternoon in the semi-final of the South-West Lancashire and Border Towns Cup. There was a large attendance. Owing to injuries Burgess and Duckworth were unable to take their places behind the pack,but two capable substitutes were found in Scott and R. B+te. Mereweatherle place in the forward ranks was taken by Cunningham. St. Helens started, the breeze favouring neither side ta any great extent. The opening stages of the game took place in the home quarters, and Hallam was called upon to save his lines. This was promptly accomplished, and a round of passing initiated by Bate and Scott was the means of Warrington attack- ing for a brief period. Foulkes fumbled the ball, and Flockenhall almost got through after a tricky run,whilst hesitation by Dickenson lost his side the opportunity of opening the scoring. By Easy stages St Helens changed the venue by a brilliant dribbling movement. Warring- ton were penalised,and Pennington successfully negotia- ted the place kick, Following this reverse the locals infused more energy into their play, and the forwards followb.g up a series of kicks by Isherwood, Fish and Hallam had Foulkes in diffi- culties. The attack was maiotained and Scott and Bate repeatedly opened out the game, but laxity of finish spoiled many favourable openings. St. Helens were pressed in their quarters and after Scott had ' bluffed his opponents successfully and experienced the hard luck ef being pulled up on the line a fine move- ment by Bate, Scott, Isherwood and Dickenson saw the last-named struggle over and score the first try of the match. Fish fai.ed at the goal kick. Toe hot pace which had characterized the game throughout was maintained, and while the visitors relied on the robust work of their forwards the home backs checked any attempt to cross the half-way line. Repeated efforts to score by Isherwood and Dickenson were frustrated by the superb defence set up by Doherty, Unsworth and Morrison, but eventually the Lome bac,ks again got under weigh and the outcome of some fine exchanges between Scott, Bate and Isherwocd saw the centre serve Fish at the opportune moment, and that player easily rounded Foulkes and scored an unimproved try. War- rington continued their aggressive work until the in- terval, but no further scoring took place, and at half time the score was,Warrington two tries (six points). St. Helens a penalty goal (two points). Swift restarted operations and the visitors presented a bold front in the first few minutes. but Hallam, who displayed fine form throuehout, kicked with masterly skill and always got the better of the exchanges with Foulkes. A pretty movement taken part in by Taylor, Scholtze, and Eden was negatived by a forward pass. Doherty, distinguished himself by some excellent play and as a result Morrison scored a try. Pennington made a good attempt to place a goal. Warrington Iplayed up strongly after this reverse, and efforts by Fish and Isherwood were instrumental in Warrington forcing the game near the pavilion goal. Dickenson held the tall a shade too long when a pass to Fish would have resulted in srmething tangible, whilst hard luck was repeatedly experienced by the forwards when theyd -ha dribbled past all opposition. Eden was especially unfor- tunate in this connection and was within an ace of scoring. Final score :—Warrington two tries (six points). St Helens penaltygoal and a try (five points).

under the posts, the goal kick failing. Half time: Widnes "A" 11 points, Widnes Rangers nil. During the second half Stiallcrom and Tilley scored, aud Holford kicked a goal. Final: Widnes "A " two goals bye tries (19 points), Widnes Rangers nil.

div.head: " A" TEAM COMPETITION.
div.p: " A" TEAM COMPETITION.
Oldham v. Warrington.

Warrington second strinevisited the Watersheddings on Saturday. A capital match was witnessed ,the teams being fairly equal,and all through the game was evenly contested. Oidbam had the advantage from the kick- off, but Warrington was the first to score, Harris getting over with a good try, Scott failing to improve. Pearce equalised ',elm the interval, and afterwards scored his second try, from which Owen kicked a fine goal from a difficult position. Final :—Oldham, eight points ; Warrington, three points.

div.head: Latchford Rangers v. Runcorn Hornets.
div.p: Latchford Rangers v. Runcorn Hornets.

Played at Latchford on Saturday. Runcorn kicked off, and for some time play ruled in their favour. Scrambling play took the game to the other end, where after a fine bit of play Finnegan scored, the goal-kick failing. This livened Runcorn up, and Moulton scored. Not to be done, Latchford again rushed down, W Bate scoring, the goal-kick failing. Half-time: Latchford Rangers, six points ; Runcorn Hornets, three points. During the second half the home team had again the best of matters, and McWhirton scored after fine pass- ing, the kick at goal being a failure. Result: Latch- ford, three tries (nine points), Runcorn Hornets, one try (three points).

div.head: Widnes "A" v. Widnes Rangers.
div.p: Widnes "A" v. Widnes Rangers.

The first meeting of these local clubs on Saturday afternoon did not accuse much excitement in football circles. A good passing movement resulted in Tilley scoring a capital try at the corner, Holford failing at goal. Peacock remped over, and Roberts added the extra points. Just before half-time Wickham scored

Sankey Harriers Christmas Handicap. Thi. above club held their annual Coristmas handicap from headquarters, Sloop Hotel, on Satur- day. Trail was laid over seven miles of good country by E Davies, and an interesting race ended in a win for J Perdue (a sterling young novice), Closely followed by J Riley, jun., J Riley, sen., T Devlin (scratch), and ethers. The following is a list of patrons, who were donors of prizes :—J Llewellyn, J Reid, R Perdue, B Cunningham, A Jones, J Howard, T Green, A Dwerryhouse, G East- wood, P Houghton, A Clarke, T Burrows, J Riley, and J Potts. This was the most successful race the club has held, there being a prize for each runner, 14 men turning out.

div.head: Runcorn Recs. v. Widnes White Star.
div.p: Runcorn Recs. v. Widnes White Star.

At Runcorn. Williamsen started for the Recreation. Wright and Dunn got into the visitors' half, but passing 10-!tween Gleave, Peters, and Yates brought relief. The Recreation then pressed. Peters got a wily with a neat run, and scrimmaging followed in the Widnes half. The White Star then attacked, and Peters almoit placed a goal. Half-tinie—Recreation nil. White Star nil. The score remained unchanged when the game closed. Runcorn Parish Recs. v Widnes Recs.

The above teams met on the Runcorn. Parish ground, on Saturday. in ideal football weather. Ia the opening stages Ruricorn were decidedly superior, and presssed with vigour, but no score accrued. The play then became even, and from a for ward rush Widnes scored the first goal. In the second bait' Cooper scored for Run- corn, and later on another goal was registered by Sayle, and at the final Runcorn were leading by two goals to one.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
Warrington St. Mary's v. Runcorn Parish. Church.

Played at Warringtm on Saturday. The Saints opened the attack. Fleming placed nicely in the goal mouth, but G Blather kickel over the bar. Tricky play by J Henneghan caused the Ruac,)rn custodian to kick through his own goal. The visitors made a weak attack, but were beaten back by J Mather and Hill. G- Mahler scorea a sec3nd goal. Half-time; St Mary's, two goals; Runcorn, nil. ln the second halt Runcorn put a lot more spirit into their play, but could not break through the home defence. Hill kicked a penalty goal. Richardson sent in a good eh, which was eAsily cleared. Morley and Naylor had very hard luck just before time. Final :—Warrington Sc Mary's, three goals ; Runcorn Parish Church, nil.

div.head: COMBINATION.
div.p: THE COMBINATION.
Warrington v. White Star Wanderers.

This game— was played at Liverpool on saturday before a puer attendance. The visitors had only a fair team, whilst the home team were without the aid of their usual custodian: Roberts commencld for the Wanderers, both teams clmmencing with only ten men. The visitors lacked combination, and were put to an utter rout, the final aggregate reading—White Star Wanderers six goals, Warrington:nil.

div.head: NINETEEN HUNDRED.
div.p: NINETEEN HUNDRED.

This year of war draws to its do sing day, The century will soon have passed away, To mingla with forgotten time and be Engulfed in vast and dim eternity. We mourn the lose 4 who will return no mars. Who died alas ! upon a hostile shore. An Empire mourns o'er the departed brave, Who life dear life for England's honour gave. With anxinu4 hearts we viewed the clouds of war, And eager heard the measage from efir ; While cruel famine all Pis horror wrouv,ht, And where the bravest for an Empire fou;;ht.

Relieved, relieved, we heard the cheering ring Kimberley, Lady-smith. then Alafeking. Those scenes an Empire never will forget, And fancy sees the waving banners yet. As streaks of light through breaking clouds that stray, Foretell the storm will soon have passed away, So well we knew the darkest hour was o'er When famine reigned at Mafeking no more. Still year of war thou didst mankind appal With other horrors e'er the curtain fall, Upon the century that soon must be For ever mingled with eternity. Eternity forgotten, that has been Unknown eternal infinite unseen, To which we go, to what we cannot toll, In Him we trust, who dosth all things well. Why should we think with saltless on th,l brow, Bright hopes delusive, though we suffer now, we see not all, there is another part, Where love and friendship, bless the happy heart.
Then Lt nq hope, we soon shall welc-mne here. Another brighter, peaceful, happier year, When coffering war, and sorrow will he le;s, And our loved Empire all the world may bl-!cc.
S. KENYON.
Warrington, 1900.

div.head: EXAMINER URIDAY DECEMBER 23 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER URIDAY DECEMBER 23 1900.
VOLUNTEER PRIZE DIS- TRIBUTION.
Interesting Proceedings in the Parr Hall.

There was a large attendance in the Parr Hall on Fri- day evening on the occasion of the annual distribution of the shooting prizes gained by the members of the Ist V.B. (P.W.V.) South Lancasaire Regiment. Tae Volun- teer Band under the conductorship of Bandmaster Richardson was accommodated in the upper gaUerc and whilst the audience took their teats several inspiriting tunes were played Decorative materiel had been freely used about the platform,the edge of which bristled with bayonets. The presentation of prizes .was made by the Mayor who was accompanied on the platform by Colonel Ridgway. In commencing the proceediags, the Colonel extended a hearty welcome to the Mayor and proceeded to thank the prize-givers present for their generosity. Tney were very well aware, he said, that shooting was an important matter. They had learnt that in the war in South Africa. The prizs wiaich had been offered were a great incentive to the men to im- prove their shooting. He had also pleasure in thanking the Mayor and Corporation for the handsome manner they had treated the Battalion's South African Ceinpany —(applause)—and further for the generous terms they had given them in reference to their headquarters. He now desired to give a short resume of the position of the Battalion. Last year thsir strength was 653 moo; he was very pleased to say that this year they numbered 974 men an increase of 351 men. It was his ambition to make the Battalion one of the strongest in the district. (Hear, hear.) At the beginning of this year floe War Office on the representation made by him (the Colonel), assisted by the member for Warriagton, aliowed the Battalion to be increased by four companies—two of them feet, one cyclist, and one mounted infantry: (Applause.) He was very pleased to say that the mounted infantry com- pany was going on very satisfactorily. They wanted more young men who could ride to come forward and make it a good company, Tao streneth of their com- pany in South Africa was 96 —three officers and 93 men. They thought the men would have been home by this, but owing to the exigencies of this war, they had been keot at the front and were now, he believed at Gre4ory's Nek. He had received a letter from Captain Appleton—(applause)—in which he said they were go- ing on very well. Captain Appleton he was pleased to tell them had recovered and was out of hospital. (Ap- 1 plause.) The last be heard of Lieutenant Crosfieild was that he was recovering from his attack of enteric. (Ap- plause.) Fifteen of their volunteers had been invalided home and there had been three deaths in South Africa. The Battalion sympathised with their relatives and friends in their great lose. Their names were Privates W Blackwood, G Sudlow and F Wood. They had died a soldier's death whilst fighting for their Queen and country. (Applause.) Proceeding to refer to the last inspection, he said the men passed very satis- factorily. With regard to rifle ranges, he was doing his best to obtain one, and negotiations were new pro- ceeding for the acquisition of the necessary land. The grant of £3OO by the Government was useless, as the Battalion could not comply with the conditions, and the sum offered was totally inadequate. They would require from £lO,OOO to £20,000, and they desired the Govern- ment to lend them the necessary money at a reas nable rate of interest, and the Battalion would repay them in 35 years out of the capitation grant. (Hear heir.) They ' could not become a shooting regiment unless they had an accessible range. (Hear. hear). Toe MAYOR in the course of an address expressed regret that it was impossible to have with them the men of the Active Service Company, and then proceeded to refer lot feliciteas terms to his regret that he was not a volun- teer and poked fun at the re,trictioos which the War , Office imposed with reference to the height which pre- vented him from becoming a volunteer through no fault of his own. (Laughter.) He was proud to be associated as Mayor of the tow with the Battalion and it would be a pleasure as well as an honour to &an to endeavour to give any assistanoe. (Aoplauee ) The Prize List.

The followine is a list of priz 3 wmuers at the annual priz3 meeting held at the Altcar Range in August last . TEAM COMPE rinoN. THE BATTALION CELALLENGE SHIELD, Kindly presewed by the late Lieutenant-Colcnel W. Mac Carths-O'Lnary, when commanding the let Batta- lion P.W.V. (Seth Lancashire Regiment) to the best Company of this Bxttalion at Pm erical field musketry. To be competed for annually, and to be held by the winning company for the year, under the conditions of the donor. Ist prize, the shield and £l2 ; 2nd prize, £4. ;_3rd prize, £2.

Ist Prize,' D—oompany 62 points 2nd „ B „44 3rd „ Cyclists.. 41 ~ E Company 4O fg F „ 37 A „ 31 „ THE LADIES' TROPHY. (VOLLEY FIRING.) Open to teams eight men from each Coinpany, commanded by an officer or sergeant of tho com- pany. div.head: Annual Meeting. More Information Wanted
div.p: Annual Meeting. More Information Wanted

The annul meatiag of the Warrington Conservative Club was held at the Club on Thursday last week. Alder man Framomb, J P., presided, and there were also pre- sent :—Mr William Owen (hon. treasurer), Mr G Pillin g (hon. secretary), Mr Daintith (assistant secetary),V Mr Councillor A Jolley, Dr Nuttall, Messrs C L.igh, W W Westwell, El Ashcroft, C H Ward, WII Bellian, T Mason, W J Wilson, W Dooley, G Jolley, G Smith JOhri Cos, El Evans Carruthers, W Holbrook (Con- say ative agent) and others.

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: THE SECRETARY'S REPORT.

The SECRETARY said he had no report to present but as id former years he would make a satement. They hid hid suffiment new members to compensate them for 1)5505 by death and removals. The billiard tables had been re•covered as promised and prov idol with patent cushions. Tho decorating of the club was a little Le- hindhand,but the committe had had under consideration for some time the question of introducing electric light. At the last meeting of the committee it was decided to have electric light and the work of putting in the wires had already commenced. In a fortnighL's time they would have the club lighted by electricity provided the Corporation was able to supply them. As soon as the electric light had been instalied the Committee would proceed with the decoration of the premises. The billiard handicaps had been postponed until the electric light had been introduced so that all the competitors could have a good light. The club ball would be held in January next. Mr C LEIGH : Can you give us the number of members of the club?
The SECRETARY: We haven't the figures here. Mr DAINTITEI said the books wore at the auditors, but speaking from memory there were about 350 first .lass and 320 socond class.
Mr NI4soN prepaised the adoption F,f the report. Mr ASUCROFT seconded and the report was carried. THE TREASURER'S STATEMENT. A BALANCE SHEET WANTED.

Mr OWEN said his fiaancial statement like that of Mr Pilling's„was not written out, but he caul.' say that the books had been gone through by the auditor Mr Louis Voisey who c2rtitiad th.!m to be correct; in every respect. If he had to choose one word to point 'out their condi- tion as a club he should say the word was successful. (Hear, hear ) The cost of renovating the billiard tables was atsout £l5O. That expeaditure had been met and he thought that they would be able to pay the cost of iutroducing the electric light out of next year's income. (Hear, bear.) Early in the New Year the members would enjoy pure and wholesome air instead of air vitiated by the gas. Mr. C. LEIGH: Cannot we have a statement read ? We have no figures to go upon. I should like to ask if all the subscriptions have been got in ? The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Daiatlth told him that there would not be £lO in subscriptions out in both rootne. That was not a big itztra when they considered they had 700 members. _

Mr. Dot,EY : I think AI; Leigh wants the figures , showing how we stand. . , Mr, OWEN :• I can tell you we have money 'in hand. Hitherto the matter has been accepted by a simple statement, as we did not desire everyone in town to know our position. One reason for not naming the mount of money in hand is that you might be a little dined to be extravagant. (Laughter). Mr. LEIGH : All that is wanted is a proper balance sheet. (Eiear, hear.) The CHATEMAN : We don't want to expose our weak- nesses to everybody else. There was a time in the history of the club when it would have been very in- advisable for the punlic to know our position for We were very badly off, and now that we are in a prosper- ous coalition I think our modesty would stop us from boasting. Mr. LEIGH : It dwarfs the interest of the members.
The CHAIRMAN : There is such a thing as diplomacy. Mr LEltla : Quite so. The CHAIRMAN: If you think there is anything crooked we would adjourn the m2etiog. Cris of "No, no."

Mr EVAN 3 moved the adoption of the finan3ial state- ment. With due deference to what had been said it was not fair to the other members that they should be kept in the dark. He thought Mr Leigh had raised a point which ought to be thrashed out.
Mr CARRUTHERS seconded, and the financial statement was agreed to.

The CHATIMAN in the course of a few remarks said be did not think there was a better conducted club iG the country than their's. They never heard a wrong word spoken; they saw no drunkenness, no gambling or any- thing that could be taken exception to. He would not mind anyone coming there and seeing how things were conducted.

THE WORLD'S FIGURE-SKATING CHAMPIONSHIP. "Oa the Congnent tuere are not such delicate dis tinctions between amateur and professional athletes as there are in England, "writes G R Wood, in the Christ- mas number ot the WINDSOR MAGAZINE. "As regards. figure skating, the question of status does not arise in Great Britain, since there is no champireiehip, either professional or amateur, in this particular branch of sport. to other European countries a man is rated as professional if he teaches for money, and makes, or nartly makes, his living therein. Such men are not el- igible for the World's Figure-Skating Championship, which may, therefore, be said to be confined to amateurs. It often happens that a skiter is unable himself to bear all the heavy expenses incident on performing in the Championship competitione, in which case the skating cleto of which he is a member usually provides for his travelling and bare living expenses. The larger foreign clubs, such as those at Stockholm, Vienna, Berlin, and Munich, keep a profesvional skater, who picks out from the members of the club the one who is eiost likely to do the club credit in the Championship. This member is then properly trained and coached by the club pro- fessional at the club's expense, either locally or at the place appointed for the meeting. The arrangement of the big skating meetings is entirely in the hands of the 1 International Skating Union. The Union is administer- ed by a representative committee, elected at a biennial congress of all the members, and controls the Champion- ships of the weed and of Europe in speed and figure- skating. As fir as pessible the place at which the con- test is held is so selected that each country in rotatiou may have the honour of entertainine the champion skaters; but it often happens that, owing to lack of ice or to bad weather at the place originally selected, the meeting has to be transferred elsewhere. When the In- ternational Skating Union has decided the scene of the competition, it remains far the executive of the skat- ing club at the place selected to make all arrangements. To them are sent lists of judges, from which they select five at least, more if they are available. It is customs ary for those skating clubs which are sending represen- tatives also to send in names of judges, and these judges so suggested are usually selected, by the local committee. The Union appoints the referee, and also provides the championship medals and priz-a, while the local club adds on its own ac count an Ehrenpries—merit prize. The actual competition is divided into two sections. In the first part certain obligatory figures are performed ; in the second part—the free skating—the competitors choose their own figures. The Union has cemposed and published a set of seventeen figures, which are ac- cepted as the standard throughoet the Continent. From these the obligatory figures (Pflichtlaufen) for the cham- pionship are sele-eed ; they are usually five or six in number, and of increasing difficulty."

Corporation Contracts and Accounts. Sir,—ln answer to Mr Tanagen's lettee published in your issue of the 15th init. Ete remarks that he has been informed I have been a strong re...reporter of one of the political parties and that as I have suddenly dis- covered that not one of the Club nominees had grit enough to kick over the traces it must be a blow that fell heavily. No, Mr Flanagan, it did not, because that is not quite how the matter really stands. The change that has come over our Town Council has taken a few years to bring about. It com- menced from the day that Alderman Burgess Was put out of the Council Chamber; fur what reason or how that was brought about I will not go into. But there has been formed a clique which coesists cf members of both political parties who agree amongst themselves what political opinion the candidate must hold to be suceessful, in whatever ward he puts up for, in our Town Council. For instance, suppose there is a vacancy in the Town Hall Ward, and this clique have' agreed upon which party must have that seat and sup- peso a gentleman who does not believe in this arrange- ment was to COMA forward, what would happen ? Why both political clubs would combine as they have done before, and the workers of both parties would try their utmost to stop his being returned to the Council Cham- ber. So you see tbat this clique is powerful enough to disfranchise the whole of the ratepayers, a thing that the Government of this country dare not do, This being so (and nearly every ratepayer of this town who takes the slightest interest in town matters will know I only state a fact), just think what must be the power, of this clique in the matter of contracts and accounts, and what is the position of the Corporation officials ? If the ratepayers cannot protect themselves from this clique what sort of a posi- tion are the officials in ? As a matter of fact this clique is very much the master of the situation and simply has the whole of its own way. Now I know that the better class ef people, and by that I mean the straight- forward and pureminded ratepayers of this town are diseusted, and say so openly, at this state of things.and I Usr one am not prepared to blame the state of affairs simply on politics, although it is well known that I with many others have no strong feelings politically in refer- ence to municipal matters. But I do know this that black sheep will get into any society,l do not care what may be the purposes for which that society was formed and not only that but in many instances they will push their way to the front. But surely because they have got there it is no reason why they should stay there. My opinion is that these sort of people only prostitute their own party and the rank and file of each party ought to clear them out. It only makes me see that this class of people ought to be dealt with as they deserve which ever side they belong to. lam sure myself that there are in this town thousands of upright, honest, and pure minded men on both political sides who sadly deplore the very serious state of our town's affairs. Your readers are no doubt well aware that a large number of towns are, so to speak, under the meiery of a" spring cleaning." Has not the opportunity arrived for Warrington to come abreast of the times? Why is it (considering the correspondence n the subject) that not one word has appeared in the Public press from any town councillor or official Yours truly, Heathcot, Stockton Heath.
JOHN PEMBERTON.
