div.head: Passenger found_ _unconscious at Acton
div.p: A Passenger found_ _unconscious at Acton
Bridge.

Upon the arrival of the 2 20 train from Lime-street. Liverpool, at Acton Bridge, on Friday afternoon la3t week, a porter, on opening the door of a third-class compartment, was horrified to find a man lying on the floor in a p -ol of blood and in a state of semi-con- sciousness. The porter sought the assistance of the station master and the guard of the train, and they suc- ceeded in rouging the man, who, in answer to incoiries stated that he had been attacked by a fellow-passenger between Lime-street and Edge Bill.Aa the man appeared to be very seriously injured, it was deemed' advisebre to take him on to Crewe, two of tho station officials travelling in the same compartment from Acton Bridge. A measage wag deapatchei to the railway authorities a`..• Crewe Station, and they at once communicated with Dr Atkin- son, the Narth-Western Railway Company's chief surgeon, who met the train, and by his directions the man was placed in a cab and driven to the Company's hospital. Here he was attended by Dr Atkinson and his assistants, Drs Lawrence and Athill, who found that there were two deep gashes on the left side of the neck, and that the man's coat, vest and shirt were comnletely saturated with bloccl. The wounds, which were jigged, were very severe, and had evidently been ca.evci by a knife used with great force. Bath wounds were aboet an inch aecl a half in length, aril had to be stitched. By the time that the man reached tt e hospital,be had rallied sufficiently to be able to converse with those around, and he gave hi a name as James Williamson Mather, and his address as 11, Cecil-street, off Picton-road, Liverpool, his occupation being that of a scale porter, in the employ of the L. and N.-W. Railway Company at L'mr-atreet Station. On being further questioned, Mather said he had been branch secretary of a Tontine Christmas Club, and bad collected a sum of money—amounting to close upon £lO —from members in his district. This money was about to be distributed, and when he left Lime- street his intention WAS to proceed to Park-road Station where he was to have met the treasurer in order to hand over the money. He got into an empty com- partment, but just as the train was on the move he alleged that a man who was a complete stranger to him, jumped into the carriage, and at once entered into conversation by asking Mather for a bit of tobacco. He replied that be had not got any, and no sooner had he said that, than, according to Mather's statement, the stranger sprang upon him and began to rifle his pockets. Be took £6 in silver out of one trouser pocket and then inserted bls hand in the other and drew out a knife. Mather made a desperate effort to recover the money and a struggle ensued in the course of which the stranger, holding the cash in one hand, opened the knife which he had taken from Mather and plunged the blade twice into his throat. Mather stitl fought with his assailant who ultimately dealt him a heavy blow with his fiat above the eye. This stunned him and he remembered nothing more until he was discovered at Acton Bridge and roused by the station officials. Mather was then the only occu- pant of the compartment and he stated that the person who had attacked him must have jumped out of the train at one of the stations between Liverp,ol and Acton Bridge. The matter WAS promptly reported to the Crewe pelice,end Detective-Serenant Lees proceeded to the hospital, where he had an interview with Mather, who repeated the statement which he had made to the doctors. On searching the man's clothing the police found £3 in gold, and about ten shillings in silver, and this sum together with the £6 in silver which he alleged lied been stolen by hia assailant, made up the tetal amount that he intended handing over to the treasurer of the society referred to. From inquiries which have been made it appears that the knife could not lea found in the carriage, but Mather has supplied the police with a description of it. He has also furnished the medical staff at the hospital with a description of his assailant. Be states that he appeared to be a work- ing man, that he was clean shaven, about 5 feet 8 inches in height, and was wearing a hard hat and a brown overcoat. Mather is a middle-aged man apparently' about 45 years of age. On Saturday his wife and several other relatives journed frcm Liverpool to Cresee,and remained with him for soma' time at the company' hospital, where he is being detained as an in-patient. The wounds are regarded as of a dangerous character, being ef a considerable depth. During Friday nigh:: and also on Saturday his condition waa rather critical, but he is now pr ieressing as favourably as can be exoreted. The injured man still adheres to his statement that be was stabbed ard robbed by a fellow-passenger, who entered the compartment when he was alone as the train was moving out at Liverpool. Be described his assail. ant as apparently a workman and adds that he must Ihave known be was carrying a large sum of money.

div.head: FATAL STREET FIGHT.
div.p: FATAL STREET FIGHT.
Alleged Kicking Outrage at Earlestown
Accused b3fore the Magistrates.

On Friday night last, a fight whica had a fatal termination for a man named Thomas English, a collier, who resided in Athol-street, Newton Common,occurred at Earlestown. English and two or three other men were fighting in Wallington- street, some time atter 11 o'clock, and Engli-di was left lying on the ground in an unconscious condition. A man namsd James Fe lea was a witness of the fight and ho assisted to carry English to the resi- dence of his father, in L twrance-street, and it is supposed he was then. dead. At any rate he died. shortly after being carried to his .fathet' house. Foden saw 'one of .the men with whom English had been fighting kick him, butt he is not prepared to swear to the identity, of the individuhi , The wound was in the forehead, and" = 'was' very deep. English bad • '..p.reviouSly 'been fighting .with a man in .I.. Market-street A cap ' was found,, on tbe- . scene of the;, fight in Wellington-street, and following up.the clue tia afforded, P.C. Schofield succeeded in running to earth a man named Bernard lierrigitii, aliavViKer, aged 22 years, • at the house of his mo-her, Lancaster-road, Preston. Wit the asSistance of the Preston police an arrest was effected, and Kerrigan was brought in custody to Earlestown, but in reply to the charge of causing the death of English, he denied being guilty of the act. English leaves a widow and eight children totally unnrovided for. Opening of the Inquest Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, opened an inquiry at at the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday after- noon, into the circumstance 3 attending the death of Thomas English. Only evidence of identification was given, and the inquiry was adjourned unt" January 3rd.
Police Proceedings

/31P0RTANIT EVIDENCE Before Colonel Wood, at the Newton PaliC9 C3urt on Monday, Bernard Kerrigan, aged twenty-tw ) a hawker, of Lancaster-road Preston, was chargal with causing the death of Thomas English,a collier at Earle,etown, between eleven and half-past eleven o'clock on Friday night, the 21st inst. William Latham, a collier. of 59, Viaduct-street, Earlestown, stated that he mat the pri-oner and another man whom he was not acquainted with in Market-street, Earlestown, on Friday night last He remained in their company until shortly after eleven o'clock. Coming out of a chipped potato shop in Market-street, the deceased commenced to quarrel with the prisoner, and a severe fight fol- lowed. The prisoner got the better ot the deceased on the ground. Witness shouted that the police were eoming, and the prisoner and the deceased then ran off. Witness had walked a short distance down Legh-street when the prisoner came running after him besmirched with mud, and inforna-d witness that he had been almost butchered. Police-constable Schofield gave evidence to the effect that receiving information that the prisoner had left Earlestown on Saturday morning last for Preston,he journeyed to that town,and after search- ing town on Saturday night and the following morning, at about three o'clock in the afternoon he was informed that a man answering the des- cription of the fugitive had arrived at Preston. With the assistanee of the Preston police, he appre- hended the pris3ner at 4 p.m. at a house where his mother was lodging, in Lancaster-road, Preston. He was brought to Earlestown and there charged with causing the death of Thomas English. In reply, he said. " I deny that charge." The magistrate remanded the prisoner to the Newton Petty Sessions. The whereabouts of the other suspected person hasn't yet been traced.

Un- fortunately for the parish, the curate, the Rev S W Dunn, was taken ill op Saturday, as that the ser- vices of other clergymen were requisitioned for Sunday; the Ray L J T Dar wall, vicar of Waltoo, officiating at the celebration of Holy Communion, at eight a.m. ; the Rev S Scholes, curate at Runcorn Parish Chnrch, at the 10.30 a.m. service; and the Vicar of S'ockton Heath (Rev R V Pigot) at the evening service.

Naturally all municipalization schemes are very strongly opposed by those at present engaged in the liquor trade, but they are also regarded with dis- favour by many strong supporters of temperance. These urge that the liquor traffic must always be harmful, and that it is wrong to sa idle it thus upon the community, to involve the entire community in carrying it on, and to interest in it many persons not now interested; moreover good men, they say, would not come forward but would stand clear of the whole business; but a cloak of respectability would be thrown over the public-house and many _ _ . _
would drink who would have been ashamed to drink

before. Again it is urged that the collective desire for gain is not less dangerous than the individual desire, and more difficult to cops with, as there would be nothing left to appeal to. Even if it was strictly laid down that the profits were not to be applied to lightening any local burdens,there would be a danger of their being so applied in some under

hand wai, so that there 'Would' be a temptation to extend the traffic. Other objections are based on more general grounds. Only those things, which it is to the interest of the community to have supplied as freely and cheaply as possible e.g., gas, water, tramway facilities, &c.,. are justifiably monopolies in the hands of the muhicipalities. Liquor stands on a different footing; it should be the aim of the municipality to diminish the demand for it, to sell as little as possible, though of the best quality, but it would be difficult to conduct the sale Bads:.

_ fac•orlly, except on a strict business footing, and the reconciliation of these two aims, businesslike 'conduct and decrease of profits, at any rate would not be easy. It is doubtful too if the municipalities or other local bodies would be competent to man- age such a large business, and the immense sums of money involved would give ample opportunity and temptation for official corruption. Many of these'objec!ions could doubtless be met •by a careful organisation . Municipalisation on the Gothenburg lines, that is the conduc', of the liquor traffic by authorised companies with a statutory limit of profits the surplus to be devoted to public obkicts carefully guarded, with individual profit excluded, has been, as is well known largely tried

for many years in Norway and Sweden... There is great dispute as to its results, but it is certain that great reforms have been carried out CO1n61:11-; poranecuslY, whether those have been the direct outcome of the principles of the system or not. In this country the army canteens are based on the same priqciples, and private landowners and others have also applied them in single instances with great success. To argue. however, from foreign countries to our own is always a doubtful process, I and private experithents by their very nature exclude many et the dangers to which public ones are exposed. There is much that is very attractive in the
system, especially ths diminution of Drivate profit, the .aoplication of the immense profits of. the trade

to providing counter attractioas' to the public- house, and the basting of the drink influences from politics. There are, however, great dangers. The destination of the profits woald require to be most

carefully Bafeguarciled so as to avoia interestlnwthe community in the perpetuation or extension of the traffic. The danger of municipal corruption or mis- management is also a very real one. An 4 in spite

of the ousting of the liquor traders as a factor in politics, it might easily came to pass that local elections would turn on questions of managment, which would be not less hart:l2E4l than the present state of things. Exp4riment alone can settle on which side the advantage lies, and it is not too much to hope that some day a beginning will ba made by a trial of the system of local manage- ment on a small scale at first, say in some county town, not too large. Meantime local landowners, colliery proprietors, and other, if they are con- vincod that they must have public-houses, can do a great deal by rratning them on th'ese principles, for ~ho diminution of private profit cannot fail, if pro- perly enforced, to have great effActs. c Nctimo

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS R S E ItVE D. LICENSING REFORM,
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS R S E ItVE D. LICENSING REFORM,
IsY THE HIN. SIDNEY PEaL.
Popular Control of the Liquor
Traffic.

The scheme of reduction and compensation which we have outlined, has the effect of leaving the ground clear at the end of the given period for the adoption of any Scheme of reform which may seem desirable on its own merits Such proposals fall under two heads, permissive local prohibition, and municipalization or local management of the liquor traffic: both proposals embrace the principle of direct popular control. It would be beyond the scope of these articles to deal exhaustively with these subjects. Both go far beyond the immediate reforms put forward as desirable in this country:

if these framediate reforms canno be carried out, there would be little hopeof carrying more extreme measures, and it is a far wiser policy to proceed by degrees, without the risk of outrunning by too much the present public opinion. It will be suffi- cient to notice broadly the arguments advEmced for and against, and to explain the nature of the pro- posals made.

LOCAL PERMISSIVE PROHIBITION. Looking to the amount of pauperism, crime and distress, and to the general waste of national effi, ciency caused by the liquor traffic, it is not surpris- ing that ma,ny.people are desirous of abolishing it entirely. But the general use of alcoholic liquors as a beverage and the general attitude of the public on the subject, clearly render any such aim outside the range of practical politics Accord- ingly, they recognise that. the only course is to fall back upon the proposal for local permissive prohi- bition of the public sale of intoxicants The most practical proposal of the kind is that the ratepayers of a locality should have the power by a two-thirds or even larger) majority vote of prohibiting the issue.'of any liquor licenses in the district; or at any rate •of any licenses for - consumption on the premises. It is argued that the present licensing regula- tions have failed to protear the public from the evils of the drink trite!, and that no satisfactory protection can be afforded, except by entrusting; those who are most conaerned, namely; the inhabi- tants of the district, with the power of abolishing the traffic, if they wish to. Such local prohibition could not be in advance of the- public opinion of the locality, because the two-thirds majority would indicate such an overwheltning opinion,as to ensure enforcement of the law, and to guard against the dangers of fluctuation from no-license to license at recurring polls. A power of local prohibition is at present possessed by landlords,who may bya Clause in their leases forbid the sale of intoxicating liquors on their estates, and this power has been success- fully applied on many estates in this country; if the landlord possesses and exercises this power, a fo-tiori it ought to be possessed by those who are more directly concerned, the people themselves. Further, local veto is the- prevalent system in all English-speaking countries, and has been found to,be a success there as well as in Scandinavia. Local cont 01, in some .form or other, including the power of prohibition, is the law in all the States of the United States of America except four.; it is also the prevalent system in most of Canada, the Australian Colonies, and in Nbrway and Sweden; it is argued that, if a system: has spread so widely and been so long in existence, it cannot have been unsuccessful since the people who live under-it- themselves approve it. Objections to local veto are partly theoreticalan.d' partly practical in- their nature. The thebretical objections are two fold First, local veto would be: an unwarrantable interference, with the rights of iii 4;• dividualliberty ; it is beyond the funetion of legis- ,latied to say that a man shall ner, drink_vihat he 'pleases. This is perhaps the commonest' and most popular. argument against local veto. ltivo replies are made to it ; in the first place, 6haeithe•public house is a nuisance and an injury to the.loCalxty; it , is an interference with the rights of .•the. corn-, Munity.to allow it to remain, and against these :pablic..rights no private, rights ougheto be allowed, 5ti141,4 Z. second :place it is • not proposed tn prohibit the private consuetiption of intoxican bottralytheir public sale, andin:the• 'less extre,:itt*, plans op local option ontrttieir Public sale for publA.' consnraption on the premises. Thereis {l. clear ao-i tinctinn between' prohibiting,the public. and he 45f-irate- use-6f int exicatfrie liqnnrs ;tile same-IMT of .distinction is recoi.nised already in legislation. 4Vhere is no penalty Or private, bin:, only :,for public drunkenness. A man may with his devour the whole of a diseased sheep, if they', so-please; but as soon as they endeavour to sell a portion of it. to anyone else, they become subject to legal penalties, The principles of individual liberty would not therefore be infringed beyond a necessarypoint by prohibiting the public sale of intoxiCants. In the second place it is urged that local veto would be "robbing the poor man of his beer." While the rich man ha,d, his cellar and his club-to fall back on; the poor man would be deprived of what he regards as one of the essentials of life. To this it is replied that the matter is in the-poor-mans own hands ; poor men would be in-the majority, and if they took that view, it would be impossible to obtain the requisite two thirds majority for veto The practical objections are that local' veto would be an ineffective remedy for the evils of intemper- ance, because it would' only be used in a very few places, and those the ones which most needed it; where used, it would not be enforced; and, if enforced it would not diminish drinking but only drive it inwards into the house and the club; and that it has not been a success, when tried in other countries Now local veto has never been tried: in- this coun- try, and till it is tried', it is hopeless to decide upon these objections conclusively. The only certain con- clusion which can be drawn from the experience of other coun tries is that it is more likely to succeed in sparsely populated districts than in towns. Only a rash man would endeavour to pronounce authori- tatively on- its probable effects under the differing local conditions. of this country. We may, however, tentatively lay down the o3inion that it does not seem probable in the present state of public opinion, that it would prove a wide- spread remedy for the evils of interaperance,or that it would' receive such strong and continuous sup- port in many districts as to avert the dangers of fluctuation from no-license to license. It is on the strength orpublic opinion that the success of local option depends, and it does mat seem advisable to postpone universal and certain,. if less coMprehen-- sive reforms, in favour of what is admittedly a desperate, and in many localities at any rate a doubtful, remedy. In the interval allowed by the scheme for settling the compensation difficulty the. development of public opinion May bring about a change, and it might be a profitable object lesson, to England at least, if a measure of local control on the milder lines of permissive local prohibition of licenses for consumption on the premises, were applied first to Scotland or Wales, where public opinion is much more decidedly in its favour. LOCAL MANAGEMENT AND MIINICIPALISATTON SCHEMES.

The supporters of local Management admit, equally the necessity for popular control of the liquor traffic, but they dispute the practicability of prohi- bition. They argue that the real remedy is to ex- teud the principle of local government, place the liquor trade in the hands of the local authorities, eliminate all motives of private profit from the seller, and appropriate the profits for the good of the community. The same nrinciple of municipalization has been already applied to gas, water, tramways, &c., why not to intoxicating liquors? Instead of brewers and publicans directly interested in pushing sales, the best men would be got to serve with the public interest at heart, on the management committees, and actual sellers would have no private interest in pushing sales It would thus be easy to stop sales to drunken persons, to habitual inebriates, and to children, and to make the houses reasonably not meretriciously attractive and real houses of refresh- ment, not mere taps, without recourse to the cum- brous and unadaptahle machinery of legislation. It would. be possible at one blow and without any ditficulty to reduce the number a houses, and to make experiments in the hours of closing. The profits which now go to swell the pockets of some favoured individuals, would be applied to all sorts of projects for benefiting the community, and above all the importmt provision of counter attrac- tions to drinking. And lastly the vicious influence of the liquor traffic in local and imperial politics would b wirely removed. No longer would the morit;4 QI particular questions be obscured by the foro of bear?;oured freAy on the one side or the °Ater ; no longer would every public-house be a corn mittPe rolm or powerful political agency ready to cast, it influence, as the brewer may direct, for

div.head: MESSRS. GREENALL WHITLEY AND COMPANY SLIEDi FOR COSTS.
div.p: MESSRS. GREENALL WHITLEY AND COMPANY SLIEDi FOR COSTS.

frrteresting Caset At the Middlewich Petty S essions, on Wednesday. be- fore Colonel France-Hayhurst and Captain &enter' Leigh, an application wis made on behalf of the Urban Celina of aliddlewich. by Mr F Bettl ey-Coo se, for COStA against M,B9l'S Greened, W hitley and Company. Mr Cooke explained that two summonses were taken under the Housing of the Working Classes Act and under the rowns Improvement Clauses Act, 1547, in respect to certain freehold property belonging to Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Company,being in a ruinous and dangerous condition. The point that morning was simply a Ties- tion of coats, and when he said costs he meant a guinea should be paid to Dr. Garstang, who attended as medical officer, a guiaea to the Sur- veyer, 103 for the Inspector of Nuisances, and the court fess,—Mr. Fletcher's paint that day was that the costs should not be allowed, because the Council acted in a very arbitrary manner throughout the prcceedings e and his contention was that the Council had simply acted through a sense of duty. They had not acted exces- sively towards Messrs. Greenall,, Whitley and Company, but in a straightforward way, and he had given them ample opportunity to remedy the grievance. Messrs Greenall and Whitley purchased the property some months agoat a public atm ion,and in due time the Coun- cil's Inspector certified the property as dangerous and insanitary. He communicated either directly with the firm or through Mr Sheldon, their accredited archi- tect. The latter inspeoted the property, and from time to time certain repairs bad been executed in connection therewith, but notwithstanding the work done the Council and officials were of opinion that the property was still unfit for habitation. Eventually the whole of the houses were pulled down, and therefore, to his (Mr Cooke's) mind, that was the strongest point why the nests shou3d be allowed. The Council had written, com- municated, and inspected the property with Messrs Greenall's representatives, and on those grounds the Council were justified in taking the proceedings they did. Mr. Fletcher, in support of his protest against the application, observed that where there was no order their worships could not make an order for payment of costs. In the opinion of Messrs Greenall they had been very badly treated by the Urban Council. They were ratepayers of the town, and as such were entitled to the consideration and advice of the official whose expense they were asked to provide for. They would see at once that there had not only been an absence of any dis- position on the part of his clients to resist the duty of the Council, but on the contrary they had all along en- deavoured to meet their requirements in every particu- lar, inasmuch as they had gone so far as to sacrifice rent by removing the property out of existence altogether. The property was neither better nor worse ten years ago andit wae:only when it got into the hands of Messrs Green- all,Whitley and Co. ,who were brewers and looked upon as outsiders, that any pressure of this kind was brought to bear upon them. His friend admitted that as soon as they came into possession of the property they, on the advice of Mr Sheldon, spent from £4O to £5O on it. In addition to that plans bad been sent to the Council, which had not been returned, neither had any comment been passed upon them to their knowledge. Then, to the surprise of everybody,on Saturday,October 12th,and when there was nobody at the registered office of the Company, a notice was left to remove the whole of the property in three days. That was the first intimation of the Councira drastic measure. One of the ten- ants had been in fifty years, and ejectment orders wet.Vd have to be procured before we could turn them out. 1 hat being the case the notice was not eel ved uader reasonable circumstances. Following the notice was a summons en the 17th, which savoured ot Amp practice, They remembered the

grounds upon which the case was first adjourned was because of the hardship inircted on his clients in not 1 giving them due notice to prepare a defence, the quee- tion of costs being left over to see if they repaired the property to the satisfaction of the authorizy. They had satisfied them and surely they ought not to be mulcted in the costs. The three gentlemen were serrents of the ratepayers, bound to do whatever their respastive office called them to do. That was an almost unheard- of application. If the Middlewich Council- did not pay them to do the work, it ought to do. Even on those grounds Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., as rate- payers,had a grievance. They ought not to be mulcted In the expense of the attendance of public officials in the discharge of their duties. Mr. Cooke thought in fairness to the Council he should state that the au3horlt7 had not been aggressive for the short period mentioned by Mr. Fletcher. On the 24th July last he (the advocate) wrote Messrs. Greens'', Whitley. telling them it was useless spending money en the houses, because the Medical Officer had condemned them. _ _ _

The Chairman observel that the Bench considered that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Complny had done all that was required of them. They were also of opinion that they were unduly pressed in the matter, and they thought the clsts should not be allowed.
WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.

Annual Concert in Parr Hall. Successful in every respect was the concert given in the Parr Hall, on Thursday last week by the children its the upper standards at People's College School. The accommodation of the building was taxed to its utmost capacity, evtry seat being occupied. and the manner in which the scholars went through a long and attractive - programme, left nothing to be desired. It was not until • last year, that these concerts, which were so popular in bygone days were revived, but,. considering the success with which the re-com- mencement of them has been attended, they will no doubt be an annual event for many years , to come. The entertainment on Thursday evening was evidence of the time and labour which must have been expended in training the children, for throughout the concert there was not the slightest hitch. The per- formers had learnt their parts to perfection, and the various items were presented with that confidence which is se essential to a really successful children's concert. Though the programme was long there were no signs qf weariness on the part of the audience. who showed in a full measure their appreciation of the efforts of the scholars. The greatest praise is due to Mr El Payton, Mus. Ban., the singing master at the school, upon whom the duty of training the children largely devolved. There was a chorus of 350 voices,and Mr Payton presided at the organ with his customary taste and skill. The opening item was a most appro- priate one—" Rule Brittania" and it was -rendered with a verve which elicited the hearty approbation of the audience. A pleasing effect was produced in thedast verge by the children waving their programmss which had:been arranged 'lithe national colours—red.white and blue. "The Carnival "a tuneful melody was the next • item, and it was followed by" The Lost Chord" which was very expressively rendered. The female pnpil teachers, who were attired in picturesque Scotch •COS-. - tames gave" Caller Herria " and " The Keel Row" for which they were deservedly encored. A humorous chorus" The Three Beggars" was sung in an intelligent manner as were also "The Gift," and " Scar of Bethle- - lem," One of the most po, tear features of the first half of the programme was the spini-ed rendition of " Th lads in navy blue" by a number of boys clad as . Jack Tans. In addition they were put through a cutlass drill, which they executed with accuracy under the direction of R Monks, who won the high encomiums of tne audience for the way in which he fulfilled the part of captain. At the conclusion there were rounds of hearty applause and the last verse of the song-and also the drill, were repeated. A number of the younger girls contributed "Flowers, beautiful ffovrers " in which baskets containing brightly coloured flowers were effectively displayed. A humorous item, and one that "caught on" with the • audience was "The Piccaninnies "which was presented by several boys dressed in pierrot costumes. Their queer antics caused roars of laughter and a demand for a repetition had to be complied with. The concluding

chorus in the first portion of the entertainment was "The Old Brieade." and the children infused a great deal of enthusiasm into this patriotic composition. The • second part of the proeramme was equally interestfng. One of the choruses " Englandl still old England" was sung to music specially written for the occasion by Mr. W. R Payton. The music went with a merry swing and had a cordial recep— tion at the hands of the audience. The pupil teachers acquitted themselves admirably in the ermine song "Jest fancy " and also contributed a grac^ful dance. A humorous song " The Wonderful Musician„" in which imitations of several instruments were introduced, was capitally sung by "the pierrets." who were vociferously mewed. "The old folks at home" was feelingly retie - dared by the pupil teachers, the echolars joining in the chorus and supplying a humming accompaniment. Dnrinv an interval, Mr E Wallington, the head-mase ter, tendered the thanks of the teachers and scholars to, the audience for their attendance. In doing so he urged upon the parents the necessity of sending their children to school regularly. The attendance at present was not bad, but it might be better if the parents and scholars made an effort. At the end of the school year they had on the books of the upper school 920 children, and yet, the average attendance for the year was only gig• so that there were 104 children absent every morning and afternoon. They would see how that must interfere with the werk of the school and make the lessons unnecessarily difficult to both the teachers and scholars. Again out of 920 ,on the books there were only 16 children who were present every time and he thought it was to the credit of those children and their patents. Their names had been printed on cards of honour and hung in every chess. .rnorreat the school. He hoped that nev year, instead of 16 they would be able to pet down the names of 61 Scholars who had not missed once. In crinclusiein, Mr Wallington referred to the good work which was being done by the Bank Quay and Cairo-street, Infant Schools , end expressed the hope that these schools would be -better attended. (Applause). Tht evening's enjoyment was brought to a close with the singing of the National Anthem. . The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirrall, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take piece at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the epenine of the Court on MONDAY, the 31st day o December, 1900, at half-past eleven o'clock in the fore noon. The Court will be adjourned to the Court House, Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 2nd day of January, 1901, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. To make common Vegetables more inviting, always serve them with a good Corn Flour sauce. To make such a sauce simply mix a teaspoonful of good Corn Flour with a teacupful of milk, add a teaspoonful of butter, and cook for three minutes. Try' such a sauce with the commonest vegetables turnips, carrots, onions, leeks, parsnips, beetroot, &c., and you will be convinced how much they are improved by it.
